m:lb-tripoli-international-stadium|lm-7-.headline: Before the June 11 Stadium was built, the Municipal Stadium (now 7 October) was Tripoli's only football stadium, according to Wikipedia.
m:lb-tripoli-international-stadium|lm-7-.explanation: The 7 October Stadium was built in 1939 and was first called the Municipal Stadium. One Wikipedia article says it was the only football stadium in Tripoli until the June 11 Stadium was built. That makes the older ground the city's football home before the newer, larger one took over. The recorded year of 1970 is not confirmed, because the sources disagree on when the June 11 Stadium was built. The article says "the 1970s", and a Wikipedia timeline says 1982.
established: The 7 October Stadium was built in 1939 and was first called the Municipal Stadium (Docs 1 and 2).
Doc 1 says it was Tripoli's only football stadium before the June 11 Stadium was built.
Doc 1 says it is now a training ground for Al-Ittihad Club.
not_established: The year 1970 is not confirmed. Doc 1 says only 'the 1970s', and Doc 2 lists the June 11 Stadium opening in 1982.
The sources do not say how the Municipal Stadium was used under Gaddafi, or when it was renamed 7 October.
Both are Wikipedia pages, with no original records or eyewitness accounts behind them.
m:lb-tripoli-international-stadium|lm-7-.context: The June 11 Stadium is named after the date in 1970 when US forces left Wheelus base. The name does not by itself show when the stadium opened.

The map points may not mark the buildings that burned.

Neither profile says how the hotels were used under Gaddafi.

u:egypt|libya foreign relations.headline: In a September 1976 Tripoli speech, Qadhdhafi said he would have cut all ties with Egypt, but that the decision belonged to the Libyan people.
u:egypt|libya foreign relations.explanation: The one source is a transcript of a Qadhdhafi rally speech broadcast from Tripoli on 2 September 1976. In it he says decisions on Libya's relations with other countries now rest with the people, not a president or government. He then says that if the choice had been his, he would not have hesitated to sever all relations with Egypt. He gives Egypt's alliance with the United States and Israel as one reason. The speech shows Libya's open hostility toward Egypt and how Qadhdhafi described the way foreign policy was made. It does not show that relations were actually cut.
established: Qadhdhafi said that, had the decision been his, he would have severed all relations with the Egyptian government.
He accused Egypt of acting in alliance with the United States and Israel against the Libyan people.
He said decisions on foreign relations are now made by the people, not by a president or government.
The speech was broadcast from Tripoli and recorded on 2 September 1976.
not_established: The passage does not show that Libya actually broke relations with Egypt.
The last 50 minutes of the speech are marked indistinct, so the fuller argument is missing.
The transcript does not say what Egyptian actions he was referring to beyond the accusations quoted.
u:egypt|libya foreign relations.context: Libya's relations with Egypt were strained in the mid-1970s, after Egypt moved closer to the United States and toward dealings with Israel. Qadhdhafi described Libya's system as rule by popular congresses.

timeline.what: Qadhdhafi gives a rally speech, broadcast from Tripoli, criticising Egypt.

u:carlos the jackal|the institute.headline: A June 1979 CIA memo says Carlos was housed at "The Institute," a terrorist training camp near Tripoli, and planned attacks there with Libyan intelligence.
u:carlos the jackal|the institute.explanation: The memo names "The Institute" as a terrorist training camp near Tripoli. It says Carlos was housed there. It says he and the Libyan Intelligence Service planned operations together, and it gives the aborted 1977 attack on the US ambassador to Egypt as an example. The memo's main point is that Libya had probably ended this close relationship by 1979. It says Carlos had "dropped out of sight," and other reports placed him in other countries. For Tripoli, the memo shows that a camp near the city served as a base for a well-known international terrorist, with Libyan state involvement. It is a single American intelligence assessment, and much of it is not declassified.
established: The CIA memo of 1 June 1979 says Carlos was 'housed at The Institute,' a terrorist training camp near Tripoli.
It says Carlos and the Libyan Intelligence Service planned operations together, such as the aborted 1977 attack on the US ambassador to Egypt.
It says Tripoli probably decided to end its close relationship with Carlos, and that his whereabouts after 1977 were uncertain.
not_established: The memo gives no exact location for The Institute, only 'near Tripoli', and no dates for his stay there.

Part of the text is not declassified, so the memo's evidence for these claims is not shown.

u:gulf of sidra|map:bab.headline: After the March 1986 Gulf of Sidra clash with the US Navy, Gaddafi boasted about it in a speech at Bab al-Aziziya barracks in Tripoli.
u:gulf of sidra|map:bab.explanation: The link is an event, not a physical connection. The Gulf of Sidra is the stretch of sea where Libya's declared "line of death" met the US Sixth Fleet. Bab al-Aziziya is the Tripoli barracks where Gaddafi spoke afterward. Newsweek reports that he told a crowd there that Libya had "humiliated America" and repelled the fleet. This shows the compound as Gaddafi's stage for public messages about Libya's confrontations with the West. Both documents are copies of the same Newsweek article, so they count as one source, not two.
established: Newsweek (7 April 1986) says Gaddafi spoke to a crowd gathered at the Bab al-Aziziya barracks in Tripoli.
In that speech he boasted that his 'line of death' had repelled the US Sixth Fleet in the Gulf of Sidra.
He claimed his missiles shot down three American warplanes. The article reports this as his claim, not as fact.
The article describes the American fleet's operation in the Gulf of Sidra, including clashes with Libyan patrol boats.
not_established: The passages give no exact date for the speech, only the article's date of 7 April 1986.
The two documents are two scans of the same article, so they are not independent confirmation.
Gaddafi's claims about downed aircraft and the 'humiliation' of America are his own words and are not confirmed by these passages.
u:gulf of sidra|map:bab.context: The US naval exercise in the Gulf of Sidra in March 1986 was followed in April 1986 by US air strikes on Tripoli, including the Bab al-Aziziya compound.

Foreign Minister Belkeziz, then in Fez with the King, expected to return to Rabat late on 14 August or early on 15 August.

It does not say what was discussed in the talks beyond the treaty, or what the treaty changed in practice.

u:cairo|mansur kikhia.headline: Mansur Kikhia, a Libyan dissident, vanished from his Cairo hotel room in December 1993; a CIA commentary judged Libyan agents likely took him.
u:cairo|mansur kikhia.explanation: A CIA Counterterrorist Center commentary dated 15 December 1993 links Kikhia to Cairo. It says he went there for a human rights meeting and visited family in Alexandria. He came back to Cairo to meet his brother and planned to fly to Paris on 12 December. When his brother got into his hotel room that day, Kikhia was gone and his belongings, including his diabetes insulin, were still there. The CIA wrote that the evidence suggested Libyan operatives abducted him, and it cited strong circumstantial evidence of Libyan government involvement. This matters because it shows how Tripoli's reach under Gaddafi may have extended to opponents living abroad. The document is an assessment, not proof of who took him.

He was due to meet his brother in Cairo on 11 December and leave for Paris on 12 December.
On 12 December his brother got into his hotel room: Kikhia was gone, but his belongings and insulin remained.
The CIA assessed that Libyan operatives probably abducted him.
not_established: The passage does not name who carried out the abduction or show how it was done.
It does not say what happened to Kikhia afterwards.
The CIA's conclusion rests on circumstantial evidence, and the surviving text is partly cut off.
u:cairo|mansur kikhia.context: Mansur Kikhia was a former Libyan foreign minister who became an opponent of Gaddafi. His disappearance in Cairo in 1993 is widely reported, and his fate was unresolved for many years.

The summary says he announced the prisoners' release and recounted his revolution and the 1986 US strike.
The link reading says he mentions the 1986 strike on his tent at Bab al-Aziziyah in the same speech.
not_established: The passage shown does not itself contain the Bab al-Aziziyah reference; it is taken from the reader's reading of the document.

u:tripoli criminal court|tripoli prison.headline: One 1980 magazine article mentions both a Tripoli Criminal Court case against 28 intellectuals and a death under torture in Tripoli Prison.
u:tripoli criminal court|tripoli prison.explanation: The two places appear in the same article, a 1980 Cairo magazine piece republished by a U.S. translation service. It uses them as examples of how Gaddafi's government treated critics. The court is named in a case of 28 intellectuals accused of forming illegal organizations. The prison is named as the place where a well-known Libyan died under torture. The article does not say the two cases are connected, or that the accused were held in that prison. The link is therefore only that both are examples of repression in Tripoli, as reported by one hostile outside source.
established: The article says 28 intellectuals accused of forming illegal organizations were brought before the Tripoli Criminal Court at Gaddafi's command.
The article says a well-known Libyan died under torture in Tripoli Prison, and that large crowds attended his funeral.
Both are given as examples of repression of opponents.
not_established: The article does not say the 28 intellectuals were held in Tripoli Prison.
The article does not link the man who died in prison to the court case.
The claims come from one Cairo magazine and are not independently confirmed here.
u:tripoli criminal court|tripoli prison.context: Courts and prisons in Tripoli were commonly used against political opponents under Gaddafi, but this note rests only on the article.

timeline.what: The 28 intellectuals are said to have been detained, according to the article.
The report is published by JPRS.

u:kufra|libyan military headquarters.headline: A 1986 Washington Post article says U.S. intelligence found Gadhafi had moved Libya's military headquarters from the coast to Kufrah.
u:kufra|libyan military headquarters.explanation: The article links Kufra to the Libyan military headquarters by saying the headquarters was moved there. It says there was "reliable intelligence" for this. U.S. officials read the move as fear of American carrier-based bombers. The article places it in the 1986 planning of a psychological campaign against Gadhafi. It matters because it shows how Tripoli's leadership was thought to be reacting to U.S. military pressure in 1986. The article does not say when the move happened or how long it lasted. It does not say what stayed in Tripoli.
established: The article says U.S. officials had reliable intelligence that Gadhafi moved Libyan military headquarters from the coast inland, nearly 500 miles, to Kufrah.
It says officials concluded he was fearful and wanted the headquarters to be less accessible to U.S. carrier-based bombers.
The move is mentioned while describing U.S. planning before the 1 September 1986 anniversary of the revolution.
not_established: The article does not give the date of the move or say whether it was permanent or partial.
It does not describe the intelligence source, and it is a newspaper report from unnamed sources, not an official record of the move.

u:aadim al-hawwaaz|benghazi.headline: A U.S. Embassy officer in Benghazi says Hawwaaz asked him for money on December 2, 1969.
u:aadim al-hawwaaz|benghazi.explanation: A December 1969 U.S. Embassy cable proposes a public statement about Hawwaaz, the former Libyan Defense Minister. The draft says he spoke with an officer of the Embassy Branch Office in Benghazi after a routine meeting on December 2. He is said to have asked whether the U.S. government would give him a large sum of money to counter people he thought were working against Libya. The draft says the officer gave him no encouragement and that the U.S. refused on December 4. This ties Hawwaaz to Benghazi as the place of the approach. It matters because the Qadhafi government might later present the contact as sinister. The cable does not say where Hawwaaz lived or worked.
established: The cable's draft statement says Hawwaaz spoke to an officer of the Embassy Branch Office in Benghazi at the end of a routine meeting on December 2.
It says he asked whether the U.S. would give him a substantial sum of money to counter certain individuals.
It says the officer gave no encouragement and, on December 4, acting on instructions, told him the U.S. refused.
not_established: The passage does not say where the December 4 meeting took place.
It is a proposed statement, not a confirmed public account, so it gives the Embassy's version only.
It does not show that Hawwaaz lived in Benghazi or that the plot was based there.

u:abdel moneim huni|omar muhayshi.headline: In August 1976 a U.S. cable named Huni and Muhayshi as former RCC colleagues, both sheltered in Cairo and possible leaders of an anti-Qadhafi movement.
u:abdel moneim huni|omar muhayshi.explanation: A U.S. Embassy cable from Cairo, dated 14 August 1976, puts the two men side by side. It says both were former members of Libya's Revolutionary Command Council (RCC) and had been given asylum in Egypt. It also says Egypt saw them as possible leaders of an anti-Qadhafi political movement or government-in-exile. The link shows how Qadhafi's own early colleagues became opponents who lived abroad, and how Egypt used them against him. The cable gives no sign that the two men worked together. It reports only what Egypt and the U.S. Embassy thought of them.
established: The cable says Muhayshi and Al-Huni 'have, in fact, been given asylum in Cairo'.
It calls them 'former RCC members' and Libyan exiles in Egypt who 'provide potential leaders' for an anti-Qadhafi political movement or government-in-exile.
It says Egypt has used broadcasts by Muhayshi to try to discredit Qadhafi.
It places this within a wider assessment of Sadat's growing willingness to remove Qadhafi.
not_established: The cable does not say the two men cooperated, or that either agreed to lead a government-in-exile.
It does not say whether any such government was actually formed.
It gives no details of their roles in Libya before they left. The wording is an embassy assessment of Egyptian thinking.

u:gulf of sidra|sirte.headline: Sirte (Surt) lies on the Gulf of Sidra coast, and a 1986 CIA assessment saw a US run toward it as likely to provoke Libyan fire.
u:gulf of sidra|sirte.explanation: The Gulf of Sidra is the large body of water off Libya's central coast. Sirte, spelled "Surt" in the document, is a town on that coast. The 1986 CIA analysis looks at how Qadhafi might react if US ships entered the Gulf. It names Surt as an example of a sensitive target. It calls the town "Qadhafi's tribal heartland" and says a fast run toward it would likely lead Libya to order its forces to fire. The link helps explain why the Gulf was a flashpoint, and why Sirte mattered to Gaddafi beyond its size. The document does not cover Tripoli itself.
established: A January 1986 CIA analysis names Surt as an example of a target whose approach by US forces would likely prompt a Libyan order to fire.
It describes Surt as Qadhafi's tribal heartland.
It says the chance of a clash rises the longer US ships stay in the Gulf, the closer they get to the Libyan coast, and depending on how they approach Libyan civilian or military targets.
It notes that in August 1981 US ships entered the Gulf and Libyan ships did not fire.
not_established: The document does not say Surt is on the Gulf's shore. That comes from general geography, not from this passage.
It is an analyst's judgment about what Libya might do, not a record of what happened.
Nothing here concerns Tripoli directly.
u:gulf of sidra|sirte.context: Sirte lies on the coast of the Gulf of Sidra and was Gaddafi's home region. Libya claimed the Gulf as its waters, and the US disputed the claim, which led to clashes in 1981 and 1986.

u:gulf of sidra|misrata.headline: The Gulf of Sidra is the disputed sea off Libya's coast, and Misratah is a coastal city whose shore and port the sources tie to it.
u:gulf of sidra|misrata.explanation: Three documents from different years link the two places. In 1981, a Libyan military official said aircraft numbers rose around Tripoli, Benghazi and Misratah after the Gulf of Sidra dogfight. In 1985, a U.S. news report said Soviet SA-5 missiles were being unloaded at Misurata, possibly to challenge U.S. planes over the Gulf. In 1987, Gaddafi spoke in Misratah and described the meeting as being "on the shores of the Gulf of Sidra". The link is geographic and military: Misratah is a coastal place that Libya and U.S. reporters tied to the Gulf confrontation. This helps show that the Sidra dispute reached beyond the open sea into Libya's coastal towns, not only Tripoli. The sources do not say the Gulf of Sidra includes Misratah.
established: In April 1987 Gaddafi addressed a Pacific conference in Misratah and said he was meeting them "on the shores of the Gulf of Sidra".
In November 1985 ABC News, citing U.S. intelligence sources, reported Soviet ships unloading SA-5 missile equipment at the port of Misurata.
ABC said the SA-5 could give Libya its first effective weapon against American planes over the Gulf of Sidra.
After the August 1981 dogfight, a Libyan military official said aircraft numbers rose in the areas of Tripoli, Benghazi and Misratah.
not_established: The sources do not say Misratah lies on the Gulf of Sidra itself; the 1987 speech is loose about the location.
The ABC report gives only possible intent, from unnamed intelligence sources; it does not confirm the missiles were used or aimed at U.S. planes.
The summary's claim of demonstrations in Misratah is not shown in the passage given; only the aircraft remark is.
u:gulf of sidra|misrata.context: The Gulf of Sidra is a large bay on Libya's Mediterranean coast. Libya claimed it as territorial water, and the U.S. rejected that claim and held naval exercises there.

u:libya chemical weapons program|rabta.headline: A January 1989 U.S. cable treats the Rabta plant as the center of its concern over Libya's chemical weapons, which Libya denied.

The Rabta plant is the facility at the heart of that discussion. The U.S. side called it a chemical weapons production site. Libya said it made medicines only. The cable shows the U.S. position and Libya's denial. It does not prove what the plant actually produced. It also shows the U.S. trying to cut off foreign supplies to Libya's program.
established: The cable describes a U.S. effort to halt Libya's chemical warfare production capability and names the Rabta facility as the focus.
Libya maintained Rabta was a pharmaceutical plant and denied it was a chemical weapons production facility.
The U.S. said it had given detailed information to several countries to cut off supplies, and that the FRG had not questioned the U.S. assessment of Rabta, even in public.
not_established: The cable does not itself prove what Rabta produced; it records the U.S. view and Libya's denial.
It does not show any inspection of Rabta taking place.

u:map:wheelus|sebha airfield.headline: A 1982 U.S. imagery briefing says Foxbat jets seen at Sebha probably came from Okba Ibn Nafa airfield near Tripoli.
u:map:wheelus|sebha airfield.explanation: A January 1982 U.S. imagery briefing reports four Foxbat aircraft parked at Sebha airfield in southern Libya. It says this was the first time Foxbats had been identified there. The analysts judged the aircraft were probably based at Okba Ibn Nafa airfield, which they say houses the only Foxbat units in Libya. That ties the Tripoli-area base to a southern airfield. It shows that Libya's most advanced fighter force was based near Tripoli and could be sent south. The document gives no reason for the move and does not confirm where the aircraft came from. The link to the former Wheelus base depends on "Okba Ibn Nafa" meaning the same field. The document does not say this itself.
established: In January 1982 a U.S. imagery briefing board reported Foxbat aircraft at Sebha airfield, the first such identification there.
It counted two Foxbat A interceptors, one Foxbat A/C interceptor/trainer and one Foxbat B/D reconnaissance aircraft on the west-side transient cargo apron.
It judged the aircraft probably came from Okba Ibn Nafa airfield, which it says houses the only Foxbat units in Libya.
not_established: The origin is stated as probable. The briefing does not say the aircraft were tracked leaving Okba Ibn Nafa.
The document does not say why the Foxbats went to Sebha or how long they stayed.
The document does not mention Wheelus. That Okba Ibn Nafa is the former Wheelus base comes from outside background.

u:libyan maritime fishing company|zanzur.headline: A 1982 Tripoli newspaper article says the Zanzur tuna plant was controlled by the Libyan Maritime Fishing Company.

The link shows who ran one food plant near Tripoli and how state-run industry struggled in the early 1980s. It rests on one article, so the wording and the details of control are not confirmed elsewhere.
established: The article states the Zanzur tuna plant is controlled by the Libyan Maritime Fishing Company.
The plant reached only 43 percent of its target for the January–September 1982 period.
The causes given were worn equipment, no tuna because credit was delayed, no spare parts, and an unstable labour force.
not_established: The sources do not say how the company controlled the plant, for example whether it owned or managed it.

This is one newspaper's account, and no second source confirms it.

u:glock 17 pistols|qadhafi.headline: A 1986 newspaper column says Qaddafi was close to buying over 100 Austrian Glock 17 pistols, but the company denied any sale had happened.
u:glock 17 pistols|qadhafi.explanation: The link comes from a single Washington Post column by Jack Anderson and Dale Van Atta, dated 15 January 1986. It cites unnamed "intelligence sources". They said Qaddafi had nearly completed a deal for more than 100 Glock 17s, possibly up to 300. A Glock marketing official in Austria told the writers that no guns had been sold to Libya "at least not yet". So this is a report of talks, not a confirmed purchase. The column also suggests Austrian arms dealers were using the pistols as "sweeteners" for bigger sales. Nothing in it places the pistols or the deal in Tripoli, so its link to the city is indirect.
established: The column says intelligence sources told the writers Qaddafi had nearly completed a deal to buy more than 100 Glock 17s, possibly as many as 300.
It says Austrian arms merchants were using the pistols as 'sweeteners' for future sales of bigger items such as tanks.

m:mitiga|wp-mitiga-okba-ben-nafi-air-bas.headline: Both entries describe one place: the airfield at Mitiga, once Wheelus Air Base, later the Libyan air base Okba Ben Nafi.
m:mitiga|wp-mitiga-okba-ben-nafi-air-bas.explanation: The two map entries are the same airfield under different names. It was known as Mellaha under Italy, then Wheelus under US forces, then Okba Ben Nafi under Libya, and today as Mitiga airport. The sources given show the Wheelus part: the US left in June 1970, and Libya's new rulers planned to run the base themselves. They do not use the names Mitiga or Okba Ben Nafi. Those names, and the 1986 raid, rest on the atlas profile and Wikipedia, not on the passages here. For Tripoli, the link matters because one site was first a foreign base and then a Libyan military centre.
established: A 1974 survey says the US withdrew from Wheelus Air Base in Tripoli in June 1970. Until then, US advisers and an Air Force detachment trained and supported the Libyan Air Force.
A 1974 chronology lists the line 'June United States evacuates Wheelus Air Base' under 1970.
An October 1969 CIA cable says the new Libyan government planned to run Wheelus as a Libyan military facility. It expected to station five or six thousand army and air force troops there.
not_established: None of the four passages uses the names Okba Ben Nafi or Mitiga, so the renaming rests on the atlas profile and Wikipedia.
The passages say nothing about the 1986 US airstrike on this airfield. The one 1986 document given is about Qadhafi's political position afterwards.
The 1923 Italian founding and the Mellaha name are not covered by these passages.
m:mitiga|wp-mitiga-okba-ben-nafi-air-bas.context: Wheelus, near Tripoli, was a large US air base from the 1950s. It is widely known to have become Libya's Okba Ben Nafi base and later Mitiga airport.

m:mk-april1976|fateh|event.headline: The 7 April 1976 attack on protesting students took place at the University of Tripoli, which was renamed Al-Fateh University that year.
m:mk-april1976|fateh|event.explanation: The map records that police and regime loyalists attacked students protesting on this campus on 7 April 1976. The students were protesting military control of campus life and calling for free elections. The university is where the event happened, so it is the main place linked to that date. The link matters because it shows the campus as a place where protest was punished, and the same campus saw later events such as the 1984 hanging. I could not retrieve any source passage for this link. This note relies only on the stated reason and the two map profiles, and it does not check the cited sources.
established: The map's own stated reason says police and regime loyalists attacked students protesting on this campus on 7 April 1976.
The cited sources are an interview with former student Majda Sahli on Tarikhi and the Wikipedia article on the 1976 Libyan protests.
not_established: I could not read the cited sources, so I cannot confirm exactly what they say about the Tripoli campus.
No reliable death toll for Tripoli is given, and the number of students detained is not given either.
The profiles do not say which buildings or parts of the campus were involved.
m:mk-april1976|fateh|event.context: The university's name changed to Al-Fateh University in 1976, so sources may use either name. The profile also notes that protests took place at Benghazi as well as Tripoli.

u:civilian mobilization headquarters al-.explanation: The interview is with Maj. al-Khuwayldi al-Humaydi, who runs Libya's civilian mobilization project. The civilian mobilization headquarters on al-Sidi Street is only the setting or office tied to the interview. The link is a shared story and a shared city, not a direct connection between the two sites.

m:lh-janzur|janzour|same-place.headline: Janzur, Zanzur and Janzour are three spellings of the same coastal town west of Tripoli, so these two entries describe one place.
m:lh-janzur|janzour|same-place.explanation: The two map entries are one town under different spellings. The atlas profile for the first entry already lists "Zanzur" and "Janzour" as alternate names. The second entry lists "Janzur" and "Zanzur". The 1980s U.S. reports use the spelling "Zanzur" for a town west of Tripoli. They place it on the western rail line and name it as the site of a power station and a medical cotton plant. They do not say that Zanzur and Janzour are the same place, and they do not mention the 1986 raid or the naval academy. The identity rests on the shared names in the atlas and on the cited Wikipedia page. The two entries should probably be merged. The first entry's "Giorgimpopoli" name is not confirmed by these sources.
established: The documents spell the town "Zanzur" and place it west of Tripoli. DOC 2 lists it with Sabratha and Zuwara on the western rail track, and DOC 3 lists it on the western Tripoli–Ra's Ijdayr line.
DOC 1 names Zanzur as the site of a small gas-turbine power station.
DOC 4 mentions a medical cotton and gauze plant being built in Zanzur, with a capacity of 800 tons.
Both map entries list "Zanzur" among their alternate names.
not_established: None of the passages says in so many words that Zanzur and Janzour are the same town. This rests on the shared alternate names and the cited Wikipedia page.
The name "Giorgimpopoli" does not appear in any of the passages.
The passages say nothing about the 1986 raid, the naval academy or the Sidi Bilal port facility.
m:lh-janzur|janzour|same-place.context: Janzour is a coastal town just west of Tripoli. Zanzur, Zanzour, Janzur and Janzour are common English spellings of its Arabic name.

u:fort collins, colorado|libyan embassy.headline: Faisal Zagallai, a Libyan dissident living in Fort Collins, is linked in this article to the 1976 embassy takeover, but the town itself is not.
u:fort collins, colorado|libyan embassy.explanation: The article is about a 1981 trial in Fort Collins, Colorado. It says Faisal Zagallai and his wife had lived there for about ten years while studying at Colorado State University. The link to the 1976 embassy takeover goes through Zagallai, not the town. The passage we have does not mention the embassy takeover. The AI's note says the article mentions Zagallai's role in it, but the text shown cuts off before that. Fort Collins and the embassy takeover are therefore connected only through one person. For Tripoli under Gaddafi, this shows how the regime's critics abroad, who were first sent on regime scholarships, could become targets far from Libya.
established: Zagallai testified that he and his wife had lived in Fort Collins for 10 years while studying at Colorado State University, at first on scholarships from the Qaddafi regime.
The trial of Eugene Tafoya, over the shooting of Zagallai in October 1980, took place in Fort Collins.
Prosecutors claimed the shooting was an attempted assassination directed by Qaddafi's regime.

Nothing shows that the embassy takeover was planned in, or had any direct tie to, Fort Collins.
Zagallai's role in the takeover is not shown in the text given, only claimed in the link summary.

u:french embassy in tripoli|tripoli mob.headline: The 1981 interview mentions a "question of the French Embassy in Tripoli" but does not say mob violence damaged it.

Qadhdhafi addressed the crowd and called Tarhunah a new bastion of the revolution.

m:bab|abusalim|attack.headline: Arrests after the May 1984 attack on Bab al-Aziziya are said to have sent many detainees to Abu Salim prison.
m:bab|abusalim|attack.explanation: The link is about cause and effect. An armed group attacked Bab al-Aziziya, Gaddafi's compound, on 8 May 1984. Mass arrests followed across Libya. The stated reason says most of those arrested were believed to be held at Abu Salim, and that its first prisoners arrived in 1984. No source text could be retrieved for this note, so it rests only on the recorded reason and the two atlas profiles. The two places are not the same. One was a seat of power. The other was where people suspected of opposing that power were held. The link matters because it shows how an attack on the centre of government fed into long political detention.
established: The recorded reason states that most people arrested after the 8 May 1984 attack were believed held at Abu Salim.
The recorded reason states that Abu Salim's first prisoners arrived in 1984.
Two sources are cited: an Amnesty International 1992 report and the Wikipedia article on Abu Salim prison.
not_established: No passage from the cited sources was available, so the wording and the exact claims could not be checked here.
The word 'believed' suggests this is not firmly documented. The numbers of people arrested and held at Abu Salim are not given.
Whether any particular person was arrested because of the attack and then held at Abu Salim is not shown.
m:bab|abusalim|attack.context: Abu Salim was Libya's main prison for political detainees. It was built inside the Military Police Command compound, not at Bab al-Aziziya.

timeline.what: Armed opposition group attacks Bab al-Aziziya.

426 of 530 political prisoners at Abu Salim are released in an amnesty.

m:bab|abusalim|attack.open_question: The Amnesty International 1992 report and the Wikipedia article's own sources should be read directly. They should show what they say about the 1984 arrests and where the detainees were held. Testimony from former prisoners arrested in 1984 would also help.

u:morning glory tanker|sidra.headline: In March 2014 the tanker Morning Glory loaded stolen Libyan crude oil at the port of Sidra before US forces seized it at sea.
u:morning glory tanker|sidra.explanation: The Wikipedia article says the Morning Glory was ordered to Libyan waters off Sidra, where rebel gunmen seized it. The episode shows how a militia in the east of the country could challenge the government in Tripoli over oil. u:benghazi|foreign liaison office tripol.headline: Benghazi and the Foreign Liaison Office in Tripoli appear in one 1981 news digest, but nothing in it ties them together.

u:libyan cw production facility|rabat.headline: The cable's "Rabat plant" most likely means the Libyan plant at Rabta, not the Moroccan capital, so this link looks mistaken.
u:libyan cw production facility|rabat.explanation: The 1988 cable reports Morocco's ambassador asking the U.S. to hold back on the Libyan chemical weapons plant. The word "Rabat" appears in two senses. It stands for the Moroccan government ("Rabat had noted..."). It also appears in the phrase "the Rabat plant", which the Libyans said made medicines. The cable gives no sign that a Libyan plant stood in Morocco. Morocco was briefed because it was a friendly government, which is not the same as the plant being in its capital. The plant's name is probably a misspelling of Rabta, a site near Tripoli. For Tripoli under Gaddafi, the useful point is that Libya's chemical weapons programme drew Western concern in 1988. This cable does not link the plant to the city of Rabat.

not_established: The passages do not show who organised the demonstration or whether Libyan authorities directed it.

The source gives no dates, no numbers and no named prisoners. We therefore cannot say when the transfers happened or whether they took place in the 1969–1989 period. The link rests on a short background article with no references shown.

The article says many of its prisoners were often later transferred to Abu Salim prison.

u:misratah port|tubruq port tobruk.headline: A January 1983 U.S. imagery note says helicopter containers arriving off Tobruk would probably be moved on to Misratah port.

The note judged they were unlikely to be unloaded there and would probably go on to Misratah port. Misratah was named because delivery of similar containers had been observed there earlier. The link is a prediction, not a recorded delivery. It shows how Libya's eastern and western ports were used for military shipments. It does not concern Tripoli directly.

Delivery of HAZE A containers observed at Misratah, according to the note.

u:bin ghashir|tarabulus military facilit.headline: A 1982 US photo-analysis note suggests the Scud missile launchers seen at Bin Ghashir may have been moved there from the Kulliyat garrison.
u:bin ghashir|tarabulus military facilit.explanation: Bin Ghashir lies south of Tripoli and Kulliyat lies north of it. The note says Scud and FROG-7 short-range missile units were seen at Bin Ghashir for the first time. The analysts say this could mean units were moved there or that new ones were being set up. The note's summary links the equipment to Kulliyat as a possible source. This matters because it shows how Libya's missile forces around Tripoli may have been shifted between bases in early 1982. established: The note, dated January 1982, reports elements of at least two Scud brigades and one FROG-7 battalion at Bin Ghashir for the first time.

The summary places Bin Ghashir about 7 nautical miles south of Tripoli and Kulliyat about 6 nautical miles north, and says the equipment may have come from Kulliyat.
not_established: The visible text does not show the statement that all but four Scud launchers had left Kulliyat, so that detail is unchecked here.
The note does not confirm that the equipment actually came from Kulliyat. It offers this only as a possibility.
It does not say who ordered any move, or when.
u:bin ghashir|tarabulus military facilit.context: Kulliyat is a military site near Tripoli. Libya held Soviet-supplied Scud and FROG-7 short-range missiles in this period.

u:muhammad al-magrif|rome fiumicino airp.headline: A 1981 news digest quotes an exiled Libyan saying Muhammad al-Magrif was targeted by an assassination squad at Rome's Fiumicino Airport on 24 February.
u:muhammad al-magrif|rome fiumicino airp.explanation: The link comes from one report, a U.S. digest of foreign broadcasts and news from March 1981. u:oujda treaty|qadhafi.headline: The Oujda Treaty was a 1984 union between Morocco and Libya, the country Qaddafi led, but this cable never names him.
u:oujda treaty|qadhafi.explanation: A 1984 U.S. cable from Algiers describes the Oujda Treaty as a "Moroccan-Libyan Treaty of Union". It reports that Algeria saw the treaty as aimed at itself and expected Libya to give Morocco financial help. Qaddafi led Libya at the time, so the treaty ties to him as Libya's head. The passages given do not name him or describe what he did. The link is therefore an inference from Libya being a party. The cable is about regional diplomacy, not about life in Tripoli.
established: The cable calls the Oujda Treaty a Moroccan-Libyan Treaty of Union.
Algeria saw the treaty as directed against it and expected Libyan financial help for Morocco in the Western Sahara conflict.
The cable was written in September 1984 to prepare the Vice President for a meeting with Algeria's foreign minister.
not_established: The passages do not name Qaddafi or describe his part in negotiating or signing the treaty.
They do not say how long the union lasted or what it meant for Tripoli.

u:map:tip|tunis.headline: In November 1979, an Iranian delegation stopped at Tripoli's international airport on its way to Tunis, according to Libyan radio.

u:abdullah senussi|tripoli villa former.headline: A Wikipedia article says Mansour Kikhia's body was found in 2012 in a Tripoli villa of former military intelligence, tied to Abdullah Senussi.

u:libyan arab people's bureau|rome.headline: A 1984 Libyan news report says the secretary of Libya's People's Bureau in Rome was shot at outside his home.
u:libyan arab people's bureau|rome.explanation: The "People's Bureau" was Libya's name for its embassy-type offices abroad. This report says the bureau in Rome had a secretary, 'Ammar at-Taqqazi, who was fired on near his residence in the Italian capital on 21 January 1984. The report comes from Libya's state news agency, which blames supporters of Yasir Arafat. The link is a direct one between the bureau and the city. It tells us about Libya's offices abroad, not about daily life in Tripoli itself.
established: JANA reported that 'Ammar at-Taqqazi, secretary of the Libyan Arab People's Bureau in Rome, was fired on by unidentified assailants at noon on 21 January 1984.
The shooting was said to be outside his residence in the Italian capital.
JANA said political circles in Rome believed supporters of Arafat were behind it.
not_established: Who actually carried out the shooting is not shown; the blame on Arafat supporters is a belief reported by a Libyan state source.
The passage does not say whether he was hurt or what followed.
The name may be garbled by OCR, so the spelling should not be over-relied on.
u:libyan arab people's bureau|rome.context: Libya called its embassies "People's Bureaus" after 1979. In the early 1980s Libyan officials abroad were sometimes targets of attacks.

timeline.what: Arafat is quoted at a rally near Tripoli, Lebanon, making a threat of revenge.
Shots are fired at the bureau's secretary outside his residence in Rome.

Its stated reason is that the Sidi Bilal camp lay beside the Libyan naval academy on the Janzour coast. No source passage could be retrieved for this note, so it rests only on that stated reason and the two atlas profiles. That suggests the two entries may describe one target, or two parts of one site. The wording "beside" fits neighbouring sites better than a single one. It matters because it affects whether one raid target appears once or twice on the map.
established: The project's stated reason is that the camp lay beside the naval academy on the Janzour coast.
Both atlas profiles tie the site to the US bombing of 15 April 1986 and to US claims of naval commando training.
The camp's map point is a nearby mosque in OpenStreetMap, and a naval academy is mapped nearby.
not_established: No retrieved source passage was available, so the Wikipedia claim could not be checked here.
It is not shown whether the camp and the academy are one site, overlapping sites, or separate neighbouring ones.
The camp's exact boundary was not found, and the US description of its purpose was disputed by Libya.
m:wp-murat-sidi-bilal-camp|naval-academy.context: The US bombed targets in and near Tripoli and Benghazi on 15 April 1986, after the 5 April 1986 Berlin discotheque bombing.

US aircraft bombed the Sidi Bilal camp and port facility.

u:libyan people's bureau|london.headline: A CIA chronology places the Libyan People's Bureau, Libya's embassy, in London, where a policewoman was shot and killed in 1984.
u:libyan people's bureau|london.explanation: The Libyan People's Bureau was Libya's embassy in London. The CIA chronology says gunfire from that building killed a British policewoman and wounded 11 anti-Qadhafi demonstrators. A siege followed. The document says British authorities then found weapons and spent shell casings in the empty building. It also says British citizens in Libya were arrested as hostages during the siege. The link shows how events in Tripoli's foreign policy reached London. The document is a U.S. intelligence assessment, so it is one source and not independent proof. The passage gives no year for this entry, though the layout of the text suggests it falls in the 1980–85 chronology.
established: The CIA chronology says a British policewoman was killed and 11 anti-Qadhafi demonstrators were wounded by gunfire from the London Libyan People's Bureau.
It says there was a siege of the Bureau, and that British authorities found weapons and spent shell casings in the vacated embassy.
It says a number of British subjects in Libya were arrested on trumped-up charges as hostages to pressure the British government during the siege.
not_established: The passage does not name the shooter or say who gave the order.
The exact date of this entry is not clear in the OCR text, and the document does not give the policewoman's name.
The hostage claim and the 'trumped-up charges' wording are the CIA's own view; no other source is given.
u:libyan people's bureau|london.context: The shooting in April 1984 outside the Libyan embassy in St James's Square is widely known. The victim was Yvonne Fletcher. Britain broke off diplomatic relations with Libya afterward.

timeline.what: Period covered by the CIA chronology of Libyan incidents abroad.
Shots fired from the People's Bureau in London; a policewoman is killed and 11 demonstrators are wounded.
British authorities find weapons and spent shell casings in the vacated building.

u:ali treiki|libyan mission to the unite.headline: Ali Treiki used to lead Libya's Mission to the UN, and a 1984 news report says the FBI watched the mission for suspected funding of U.S. activists.
u:ali treiki|libyan mission to the unite.explanation: A 1984 New York Times article, kept in a U.S. government file, says Ali A. Treiki had headed the Libyan Mission to the United Nations and had just become Libya's Foreign Minister. The same article says the FBI had watched the mission since 1981. Officials suspected Libya was funding black activists in the U.S. to support Qaddafi and oppose Reagan's re-election. The link between Treiki and the mission as his former post is clearly stated. His personal role in any funding is only suspicion, not shown. It matters because it shows how Libya's UN office in New York was seen by U.S. officials as more than a diplomatic post.
established: The 1984 article describes Treiki as the former head of the Libyan Mission to the UN who had just become Libya's Foreign Minister.
The FBI is reported to have kept the mission under surveillance from 1981.
Officials suspected the mission was involved in funding black activists in the U.S.
not_established: The source does not prove that Treiki himself directed or paid for any funding.
The funding claim is described as suspicion from officials, with no proof or charges given in the summary.
The exact years Treiki led the mission are not given.
u:ali treiki|libyan mission to the unite.context: Libya's UN mission in New York was its main diplomatic office to the United Nations. Relations between Libya and the Reagan administration were very tense in the early 1980s.

timeline.what: FBI reportedly begins surveillance of the Libyan Mission to the UN.
New York Times reports the inquiry; Treiki, former head of the mission, has just become Foreign Minister.

u:ali treiki|libyan mission to the unite.open_question: FBI surveillance records or later court or congressional papers could show whether Treiki had any part in the suspected funding while he led the mission.

u:libyan air force|map:wheelus.headline: The Libyan Air Force was built up with U.S. help from Wheelus, and after the U.S. left it used the base, renamed Okba Ben Nafi.
u:libyan air force|map:wheelus.explanation: Three U.S. government documents tie the Libyan Air Force to Wheelus at different stages. A 1969 meeting treated U.S. influence over the air force as something to use in talks about Wheelus's future. A later Kissinger memo says U.S. airmen at Wheelus helped the Libyans start their air force, and that this support would end when the U.S. left in June (1970). A 1971 intelligence estimate says the base, now called Okba Ben Nafi (written "Ukbah Bin Nafi"), is used by the Libyan Air Force. The link shows how a U.S. base became a Libyan military one after the 1969 revolution.
established: The Kissinger memo says the U.S. Air Force at Wheelus helped the Libyans get their own air force started, and that this basic support would end when U.S. activities at Wheelus ended in June.
In November 1969 U.S. officials planned to use their ability to influence the Libyan Air Force as leverage in talks on Wheelus's future, which were due to begin December 15.
The U.S. provided training and second-level maintenance to the Libyan Air Force, and F-5 jets were to be delivered (DOC 2). The memo says ten F-5s had been delivered and eight more were scheduled.
The 1971 estimate says Okba Ben Nafi (formerly Wheelus) Air Base is used by the Libyan Air Force, assisted by Greek and Pakistani training missions.
not_established: The sources do not say how many Libyan Air Force units were based there, or which aircraft.
They do not give the date the base was handed over or renamed.
DOC 1 is catalogued as 1965 but its content points to early 1970. The year is not stated in the passages given.
u:libyan air force|map:wheelus.context: Wheelus Air Base, near Tripoli, was a major U.S. air base in Libya. The U.S. left it in 1970, after the 1969 coup that brought Gaddafi to power.

timeline.what: U.S. hoped helping the Libyan Air Force might support continued use of Wheelus (DOC 1).
U.S. officials plan to use their influence over the Libyan Air Force in Wheelus talks (DOC 2).
Talks on the base's future due to begin (DOC 2).
U.S. activities at Wheelus due to end, ending U.S. Air Force support there (DOC 1).
Estimate says the former Wheelus, now Okba Ben Nafi, is used by the Libyan Air Force (DOC 3).

quotes.text: Ukbah Bin Nafi (formerly Wheelus) Air Base, which is used by the Libyan Air Force, assisted by Greek and Pakistani training missions.

quotes.text: During our years at Wheelus Air Base, the U.S. Air Force helped the Libyans get their own air force started.

m:lh-mellaha-wheelus-mitiga|wp-mitiga-ok.headline: Both entries describe one airfield east of Tripoli, known over time as Mellaha, Wheelus, Okba Ben Nafi and Mitiga.
m:lh-mellaha-wheelus-mitiga|wp-mitiga-ok.explanation: The two entries are the same place under different names and at different stages of its history. The Wikipedia article on Mitiga airport says it was built in 1923 as the Italian base Mellaha. It later became the US base Wheelus, then the Libyan air base Okba Ben Nafi, and in 1995 the civilian Mitiga airport. One entry covers the long history. The other focuses on the base's later years and the 1986 US raid. Readers can treat them as one site. The map should probably merge them or cross-reference them, so the airfield's story is not split in two.
established: The Mitiga article says the airport was built in 1923 by the Italian Air Force as Mellaha Air Base.
It says the Americans renamed it Wheelus Air Base in 1945, and after they left it became Okba Ben Nafi Air Base, used by Libyan and Soviet air forces.
It says the US bombed the base in 1986 during Operation El Dorado Canyon, and that it became a civilian airport called Mitiga in 1995.
The second source (on the 2019–2020 fighting) mentions Mitiga Airport as a place that was attacked, which shows the name is still in use.
not_established: The passages do not settle the exact handover date from the US to Libya; other sources give March or 11 June 1970.
The passages do not give the exact date of the 1986 raid, which is 15 or 16 April depending on time zone.
m:lh-mellaha-wheelus-mitiga|wp-mitiga-ok.context: Mitiga is the airfield on the coast just east of central Tripoli. Many Tripoli residents knew it as Wheelus in the 1950s and 1960s.

timeline.what: Built by the Italian Air Force as Mellaha.
Captured by the British 8th Army and passed to US forces.
Renamed Wheelus.
US forces left; renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base.
Bombed by the US during Operation El Dorado Canyon.

quotes.text: When the Americans left, the base was renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base (قاعدة عقبة بن نافع الجوية) after the Islamic general who conquered North Africa.

quotes.text: In 1995, the air base was converted to a second civilian airport for Tripoli, and was given its current name.

m:lh-mellaha-wheelus-mitiga|wp-mitiga-ok.open_question: Libyan or US records of the handover in 1970 would settle the exact date the base changed hands.

m:bab|lb-tripoli-central-hospital|casual.headline: Seventeen bodies found in a sealed hospital morgue in 2011 were suspected to be victims of executions after the 1984 attack on Bab al-Aziziya.
m:bab|lb-tripoli-central-hospital|casual.explanation: On 8 May 1984 an armed opposition group attacked the Bab al-Aziziya compound, and mass arrests followed across Libya. In October 2011, fighters broke into a sealed section of Tripoli Central Hospital and found a morgue with 17 bodies. Officials suspected these people were executed after the 1984 attack. The link between the compound and the hospital is therefore indirect. It runs through that suspicion, not through any proven finding. No source text could be retrieved for this note, so it rests on the recorded reason and the atlas profiles alone.
established: The atlas records that an armed group attacked Bab al-Aziziya on 8 May 1984 and that mass arrests followed.
The atlas records that in October 2011 fighters found 17 bodies, including a baby, in a sealed section of Tripoli Central Hospital.
The recorded link rests on two cited sources, an IOL report from October 2011 and the Wikipedia page on the hospital. Their text was not available to check.
not_established: No source here shows who the dead were, how or when they died, or that they were executed.
The tie to 1984 is the suspicion of officials, not a proven finding.
The sources do not show that the hospital held the bodies on orders linked to the compound.
m:bab|lb-tripoli-central-hospital|casual.context: After the 1984 attack, many people arrested across Libya were held in prisons such as Abu Salim. The atlas notes that the morgue's link to 1984 is only suspected.

timeline.what: Armed opposition group attacks Bab al-Aziziya; mass arrests follow.
Fighters break into a sealed section of Tripoli Central Hospital and find 17 bodies.
Officials suspect the dead were executed after the 1984 attack.

m:bab|lb-tripoli-central-hospital|casual.open_question: Forensic examination of the 17 bodies, hospital and morgue records from 1984, and testimony from staff or families could show who they were and when they died.

u:banina airport|benghazi.headline: Banina airport is the airport that serves Benghazi, and one report places a bomb on the road to it.
u:banina airport|benghazi.explanation: The only source here is a 1982 report. As summarized, it says an explosive device was placed in a commercial center on the road to Banina airport in Benghazi. Gaddafi was due to open that center. This links the airport to the city by location, since the airport lies on the city's edge. The source passage itself was not provided, so we cannot check the wording, the date of the event, or who was responsible. The link matters mainly as a sign of how Gaddafi's public openings and travel could be targets for opposition attacks in Libya's second city. It tells us little about Tripoli directly.
established: The summary of the 1982 report places Banina airport in Benghazi.
It says an explosive device was put in a commercial center on the road to the airport.
It says Gaddafi was scheduled to open that center.
not_established: The passage text was not supplied, so the exact wording and date of the event are unchecked.
The source does not say who placed the device, or whether it went off or caused harm.
Nothing here shows whether Gaddafi actually visited.
u:banina airport|benghazi.context: Banina is the airport of Benghazi, Libya's second-largest city, in the east of the country.

timeline.what: Date of the report that mentions the device.

u:banina airport|benghazi.open_question: The full text of the report, or other news from mid-1982, would show the date, the outcome and who was blamed.

m:as-benashour|ben-ashour|same-place.headline: The 1986 US raid's stray bombs fell on homes in Ben Ashour, a district of embassies, and damaged the French embassy.
m:as-benashour|ben-ashour|same-place.explanation: One end is an event, the damage to homes in the 1986 raid. The other end is the place where that damage happened, the Ben Ashour district. The map's own profiles agree that bombs meant for Bab al-Aziziya fell on a crowded residential area with many embassies. They say civilians were killed and the French embassy was hit. This matters because it shows how the raid affected ordinary families in a diplomatic neighbourhood of Tripoli. No source passage could be retrieved for this note. It rests only on the stated reason and the two atlas profiles, which are the family's own summaries. The two ends describe the same place and event from two sides, so the link is sound but its details are not independently checked here.
established: The recorded reason says stray bombs hit homes in Ben Ashour, killed civilians and damaged the French embassy.
Both atlas profiles say the bombs missed their intended target and fell on a residential area with many embassies.
The atlas profile for the strike says a 1987 press report in CIA files describes one F-111 mistakenly hitting a residential area near the French embassy.
not_established: No source text was available to check the claims here; the cited Wikipedia and MERIP pages were not read for this note.
The exact streets hit and the number of civilians killed in Ben Ashour are not settled in the sources.
The CIA-file press report says 'near the French embassy'. It does not name Ben Ashour in the passage as summarised.
m:as-benashour|ben-ashour|same-place.context: The US air raid on Tripoli and Benghazi took place on 15 April 1986. Its main targets in Tripoli included Bab al-Aziziya, Gaddafi's compound.

timeline.what: US air raid on Tripoli; some bombs fall on homes in a residential, embassy-heavy area.
Libyan officials take foreign journalists to the damaged streets (per the Ben Ashour profile).
A press report in CIA files says one F-111 mistakenly hit a residential area near the French embassy.

m:as-benashour|ben-ashour|same-place.open_question: The cited MERIP article and contemporary press or embassy reports could settle which streets were hit and how many civilians died in Ben Ashour.

m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-tripoli-me.headline: A Wikipedia article on a different hospital names Tripoli Medical Center as one of two main teaching hospitals for Al Fateh University's medical sciences.
m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-tripoli-me.explanation: The link is that Tripoli Medical Center is a teaching hospital for the university's medical side. The only passage given is from the article on Tripoli Central Hospital, not on the Medical Center itself. It says Central Hospital is "one of the main two teaching hospitals" for Al Fateh University's medical-sciences department, "the other being the Tripoli Medical Center." So the university link is stated, but only in passing and by one undated, open-source article. The recorded reason says it is "the main" teaching hospital. The passage says it is one of two. established: A Wikipedia article on Tripoli Central Hospital calls Tripoli Medical Center one of the two main teaching hospitals for Al Fateh University's medical-sciences department.
The other main teaching hospital named there is Tripoli Central Hospital.
not_established: That Tripoli Medical Center is the main teaching hospital. The passage gives it as one of two.
That the hospital stands on or beside the university campus, which a 'same-place' label would suggest.
When the teaching arrangement began, or how it worked in practice under Gaddafi. The passage is undated and about the present day.

u:jamahiriyah guard|libyan people's bure.headline: A April 1986 CIA memo discusses both bodies as parts of one question: how Qadhafi might respond to a US strike.
u:jamahiriyah guard|libyan people's bure.explanation: The two organisations appear in the same CIA assessment, but the memo does not describe any direct link between them. The Jamahiriyah Guard is described as Qadhafi's coup protection force. The memo says a US strike on its facilities alone would probably make Libya less inclined to target US officials. The People's Bureau is mentioned separately, as a place where some radicals might attack US citizens on their own after a US strike. So the link is that both figure in the analysts' picture of possible reactions. It is not a stated working relationship. It helps show how US analysts saw Qadhafi's security forces and his overseas missions in 1986.
established: The memo calls the Jamahiriyah Guard 'Qadhafi's coup protection force'.
It judges that a US strike only on Guard facilities would probably reduce Libya's inclination to target US officials.
It says a US attack might push some radicals assigned to the Libyan People's Bureau to attack US citizens without explicit instructions from Tripoli.
not_established: The memo does not say the Guard and the People's Bureau worked together or had any organisational tie.
It is an analysts' forecast, not a record of what happened after any strike.
The wording of the memo here is partly cut off, so the full context is not visible.
u:jamahiriyah guard|libyan people's bure.context: The memo is dated 11 April 1986, shortly before the US air strikes on Libya that month. The People's Bureau was the name Libya used for its embassies abroad.

timeline.what: CIA memo assesses Qadhafi's likely response to a US military strike.

u:gulf of sidra|libyan closure line at 3.headline: The "closure line" at 32°30' is the northern edge of the waters Libya claimed in the Gulf of Sidra, so the two ends describe the same dispute.
u:gulf of sidra|libyan closure line at 3.explanation: A 1982 US interagency memo says Libya claimed the Gulf of Sidra as internal waters in October 1973, out to latitude 32°30' north. The memo calls this limit the Libyan "closure line". US naval exercises were described as staying above it, or going below it. The line is therefore the edge of the claim that the Gulf of Sidra exercises were about. This shows how the dispute over the Gulf shaped Libya's relations with the US, but the memo is about military planning and does not describe life in Tripoli.
established: In October 1973 Libya claimed the Gulf of Sidra as internal waters, north to latitude 32°30'.
The memo says the US penetrated below the 32°30' closure line with aircraft and ships when it resumed exercises in August 1981.
The US held exercises in the Gulf for years, including some below the line, then paused them in 1980 after Libyan protests.
not_established: The memo does not say how Libya enforced the line, other than mentioning an attack on US fighters (the text is cut off).
It does not show what the line meant for people in Tripoli.
u:gulf of sidra|libyan closure line at 3.context: The Gulf of Sidra is a large bay off Libya's coast. The US did not accept Libya's claim and treated the waters as international.

timeline.what: Libya claims the Gulf of Sidra as internal waters north to 32°30'.
After Libyan protests, the US stops exercises in the claimed waters.
The US resumes exercises and goes below the 32°30' line.

m:dahra|zawiyat-dahmani|same-place.headline: Dahra and Zawiyat al-Dahmani are recorded as neighbouring areas of Tripoli, not as one place.
m:dahra|zawiyat-dahmani|same-place.explanation: The link is recorded as "same-place", but the only reason given is that an Arabic Wikipedia article on Dahra names Zawiyat al-Dahmani as bordering it to the east. The two profiles also describe different places: Dahra is a central district of embassies and state offices, and Zawiyat al-Dahmani (Shar al-Shatt) is the site of the 1911 battle and reprisals. The link is useful only as a note that they sit next to each other, and the "same-place" label should be changed.
established: The recorded reason says an Arabic Wikipedia article names Zawiyat al-Dahmani as bordering Dahra to the east.
not_established: No source text was available to confirm the border statement.
Nothing shows that Dahra and Zawiyat al-Dahmani are the same place or share a name.
Nothing links the 1911 events at Shar al-Shatt to Dahra or to its embassies and offices.
m:dahra|zawiyat-dahmani|same-place.context: Tripoli's districts adjoin one another, so neighbouring areas are common. Being neighbours does not make them the same place.

u:as-saddadah|gulf of sidra.headline: A 1983 Gaddafi speech named As-Saddadah, a battle site against Italy, and the Gulf of Sidra in the same comparison of Italy and America.
u:as-saddadah|gulf of sidra.explanation: The two places appear in one speech given on 7 October 1983, the anniversary of the Italian expulsion. Gaddafi spoke at a cemetery of martyrs and said Rome had sent armies and generals to attack As-Saddadah. He then said America now thinks it can use the Gulf of Sidra to force Libya to surrender. The link is one of theme: he compares the old Italian threat with the present American one. The speech does not say the two places are near each other or tie As-Saddadah to the Gulf of Sidra in any physical way. The passage is also poorly scanned, so some wording is uncertain.
established: A Libyan radio speech of 7 October 1983 marked the anniversary of the Italian expulsion and honoured martyrs buried in a cemetery.
The speaker said Rome sent armies and generals to attack As-Saddadah.
The speaker said the United States believes it can force Libya to surrender through the Gulf of Sidra.
He drew a parallel between Italy's past conduct and America's present conduct.
not_established: The text does not say where As-Saddadah is, or that it lies near the Gulf of Sidra.
The scanned text is garbled, so the exact cemetery location and some wording are uncertain.
Nothing connects either place to a specific site or event in Tripoli.
u:as-saddadah|gulf of sidra.context: The Gulf of Sidra was the scene of U.S.–Libyan naval confrontations in the early 1980s. The Italian invasion of Libya began in 1911. Both are widely known background, not evidence from this document.

Gaddafi gave the speech on the anniversary of the Italian expulsion, naming As-Saddadah and the Gulf of Sidra.

u:great man-made river|kufra.headline: The Great Manmade River was planned to draw water from the underground lake at Kufra Oasis in southern Libya and carry it to the coast.
u:great man-made river|kufra.explanation: A 1985 newspaper column describes Qaddafi's pipeline as running about 1,200 miles from an underground lake in southern Libya to the Mediterranean coast. It names the Kufra Oasis as that lake's location and quotes Qaddafi calling al-Kufra "the source of the Great Manmade River." The stated aim was to irrigate farmland where most Libyans live, which includes the Tripoli region. The column also reports suspicions that the project had a political aim toward Egypt and Sudan. Those suspicions are not proven in the text.
established: The column says the pipeline would run about 1,200 miles from an underground lake in southern Libya to the Mediterranean coast.
It refers to draining the underground lake in the Kufra Oasis and to a pipeline from Kufra to the Mediterranean.
It quotes Qaddafi calling al-Kufra the source of the Great Manmade River.
The stated aim was to irrigate 450,000 acres where most of Libya's people live, at a cost of up to $25 billion.
not_established: The column does not show that the suspected plan to harm Egypt or Sudan was real. It rests on unnamed intelligence sources and Egyptian and Sudanese fears.
It says nothing specific about Tripoli, and it does not describe how the project was built or how it worked in practice.

m:hadba|mk-feb2011|context.headline: Hadba al-Khadra prison held Gaddafi-era figures, including Saadi Gaddafi, tried after 2011 over the crackdown, but no source text was available to check this.
m:hadba|mk-feb2011|context.explanation: The link is recorded as background. It says that after 2011, senior Gaddafi-era figures, including Saadi Gaddafi, were held at al-Hadba prison. Officials were also tried over the 2011 crackdown. So the place appears here as a later jail, not as a site of the February 2011 events. We could not retrieve any passage from the two cited sources, so this note rests only on the reason as recorded. It helps readers see where the legal aftermath played out. It does not show that the prison had any role in the crackdown itself.
established: The recorded reason says Saadi Gaddafi and other senior figures were held at al-Hadba prison during the post-2011 trial.
Two sources are cited, an HRW piece from October 2015 and an Amnesty International document from 2015, but no passages were retrieved to read.
not_established: No source text was checked, so the detention claim and the link to the trial are unverified here.
Nothing shows that the prison, or the Hadba district, was involved in the 20–25 February 2011 shootings.
It is not established whether the al-Hadba buildings were used for detention before 2011.
m:hadba|mk-feb2011|context.context: The al-Hadba prison is documented as a prison only after 2011. The February 2011 crackdown took place in other parts of Tripoli, such as Green Square, Fashloum, Tajoura and Ben Ashour.

m:as-sidibilal|wp-murat-sidi-bilal-camp|.headline: Both entries describe the same site: the Sidi Bilal naval training camp west of Tripoli, bombed by three US F-111s on 15 April 1986.
m:as-sidibilal|wp-murat-sidi-bilal-camp|.explanation: The two entries look like one place recorded twice. One is filed as an event, the 1986 US strike. The other is filed as the camp itself, under the name Murat Sidi Bilal. Both give the same site name, the same date, the same number of aircraft and the same US description as a naval training camp. No source passage could be retrieved for this note, so it rests only on the two profiles and the stated reason. The entries are probably duplicates. Keeping them together still shows how the raid and the place relate in Tripoli's story.
established: The two profiles use the same name (Sidi Bilal) and the same event: three F-111s hitting the camp in 1986.
The recorded reason says both describe the Murat Sidi Bilal naval commando camp, hit on 15 April 1986.
The profiles cite Wikipedia and the US Air Force Historical Support Division, but no passages from them were available to check.
not_established: No source text was retrieved here, so the dates, aircraft count and camp description are not confirmed from the sources themselves.
The camp's exact boundary is unknown. The map point is a nearby mosque in OpenStreetMap.
The US description of the camp's purpose is the US government's own. Libya disputed the civilian-versus-military framing.
m:as-sidibilal|wp-murat-sidi-bilal-camp|.context: On 15 April 1986 the United States bombed targets in and around Tripoli and Benghazi. It said the raid was a reprisal for the 5 April 1986 bombing of a Berlin discotheque.

Three US F-111s bomb the Sidi Bilal camp west of Tripoli.

u:icelandic eagle air|libyan arab airlin.headline: A 1986 CIA memo says Icelandic Eagle Air leased Boeing 707s to Libya, and one was flying for Libyan Arab Airlines.
u:icelandic eagle air|libyan arab airlin.explanation: The CIA memo looks at how US sanctions affected Libya's civil airline fleet. It says Icelandic Eagle Air has leased Boeing 707 aircraft to Libya from time to time. One of these planes had been leased since 1984 and, at the time of writing, was operating for Libyan Arab Airlines. This shows how the national airline kept its fleet going despite the 1982 US embargo, by leasing aircraft from foreign firms. The memo does not describe the terms of the lease or who signed it for Libya.
established: Icelandic Eagle Air has periodically leased Boeing 707s to Libya.
A lease signed in 1981 was allowed to lapse shortly after the 1982 sanctions took effect.
One Icelandic 707 has been leased to Libya since 1984 and is, as of the memo, operating for Libyan Arab Airlines.
not_established: The memo does not give the lease terms, price, or the number of aircraft involved.
It does not say whether the lessee was Libyan Arab Airlines itself or another Libyan body that passed the plane to it.
It is a single CIA assessment from 1986, so it does not show what happened later.
u:icelandic eagle air|libyan arab airlin.context: The US imposed an embargo on Libya in March 1982. This restricted the sale and leasing of US-made aircraft and parts to Libya.

US sanctions take effect; the 1981 lease is allowed to lapse.
One Icelandic 707 is leased to Libya again.
CIA memo says that aircraft is operating for Libyan Arab Airlines.

u:al wigh airfield|sebha airfield.headline: A 1982 U.S. imagery note says the new Al Wigh airfield lies 172 nautical miles south of Sebha airfield.
u:al wigh airfield|sebha airfield.explanation: The two places are different airfields in southern Libya. They are linked only by distance and direction. The note, from the U.S. National Photographic Interpretation Center, uses Sebha airfield as a reference point to place the new Al Wigh airfield. It also gives the distance from the Libya-Chad border. This helps show how far Libya's air network was growing into the remote south, well away from Tripoli. The note does not say the two fields were connected in any other way.

It also places Al Wigh 74 nm north of the Libya-Chad border.
Al Wigh was a new jet-capable airfield, seen in mid-stage construction in southwestern Libya.
not_established: The passage does not show any operational, command or supply link between the two airfields.
It does not say how the distance was measured, for example whether it was measured in a straight line.
u:al wigh airfield|sebha airfield.context: Sebha is a major town in southern Libya. In this note its airfield serves as a known landmark for locating the new site.

u:billy carter|libyan officials houdairi.headline: A July 1980 White House prep memo links Billy Carter to Libyan officials, including meetings with a man named Houdairi.
u:billy carter|libyan officials houdairi.explanation: The memo records Zbigniew Brzezinski preparing for congressional hearings about Billy Carter's contacts with Libya. It lists a November 20 initiative, a November 27 meeting, and "subsequent meetings with Houdairi," plus a March phone call. The notes treat these as contacts with Libyan officials during the hostage crisis. They are planning notes for testimony, not a finished account. They do not describe what was said, and they do not say outright that Billy Carter attended each meeting. For Tripoli, the memo shows how Libya's officials came to deal with the U.S. President's family.
established: The memo lists the November 20 initiative, a November 27 meeting, and any later meetings with Libyans in January, February and March.
It refers to 'subsequent meetings with Houdairi' and says Vance was briefed on all the meetings with 'Houdari' (spelling varies).
Brzezinski was preparing a statement on 'Simple facts and chronology pertaining to Billy Carter'.
The memo notes a phone call from Brzezinski to Billy Carter sometime between March 26 and April 2, 1980.
not_established: The memo does not say who Houdairi was, what office he held, or exactly who attended each meeting.
It does not say what was discussed or what came of the meetings.
These are internal preparation notes, not a record of the meetings themselves.
u:billy carter|libyan officials houdairi.context: Billy Carter, the President's brother, later faced a U.S. Senate inquiry over his dealings with Libya and payments from the Libyan government. The Libyan contacts in this memo were linked to efforts during the Iran hostage crisis.

Meeting is held.
Later meetings with Houdairi and other Libyans, and a March phone call.
Brzezinski's staff prepare for the hearings.

u:abu bakr yunis jabir|map:tip.headline: Abu Bakr Yunis Jabir, Libya's top military officer, met visiting defense leaders at Tripoli's airport in 1979 and 1983.
u:abu bakr yunis jabir|map:tip.explanation: Two news reports place Jabir at Tripoli International Airport in his official role. In January 1983 he welcomed the defense minister of South Yemen (PDRY) when he arrived. In November 1979 he led the official farewell for Raul Castro of Cuba and Vo Nguyen Giap of Vietnam. This shows the airport was where the armed forces' leadership carried out state hospitality for foreign military guests. The reports are Libyan state news as translated by the U.S. government, so they show the ceremonies, not any wider role Jabir had at the airport.
established: In January 1983, JANA reported that Jabir, called commander in chief of the Libyan Armed Forces, welcomed PDRY Defense Minister Salih Muslih Qasim and his delegation at Tripoli International Airport.
In November 1979, the official farewell for Giap and Raul Castro at Tripoli international airport was headed by Jabir, then described as chief of staff.
not_established: The sources do not show whether the 'Tripoli military airport' on the map is the same site as the 'Tripoli International Airport' named in the reports, though the names suggest it is.
They do not show that Jabir had any ongoing command or other role at the airport beyond these ceremonies.
u:abu bakr yunis jabir|map:tip.context: Jabir was a senior officer in Gaddafi's government and one of the original officers of the 1969 revolution. His title is given differently in the two reports.

PDRY Defense Minister Salih Muslih Qasim arrives in Tripoli and is welcomed by Jabir at the airport.

u:az-zintan|tunisia.headline: In a March 1976 speech at Az-Zintan, Qadhdhafi threatened the Tunisian government, so the town is where the threat was spoken.
u:az-zintan|tunisia.explanation: The link is a single radio report. It says Colonel Qadhdhafi spoke to crowds at Az-Zintan on 30 March 1976. The speech marked the anniversary of the battle of Al-Kardun. In it he praised the Az-Zintan tribe and said Libyans could unite with the Tunisian and Egyptian peoples. He also said that one Libyan tribe crossing the border could "eliminate" the Tunisian regime. Az-Zintan was the setting for the speech. It was not part of any Tunisian matter. The link shows how Libya's leader used a local gathering to send a message to a neighbouring state. The summary also says he denied plots against Tunisian and Egyptian figures, but the passage given does not show that part.
established: Qadhdhafi gave a speech to crowds at Az-Zintan on 30 March 1976, broadcast by Tripoli radio.
In it he said a single Libyan tribe could eliminate the Tunisian regime by crossing the border.
He spoke of the Libyan people uniting with the Egyptian and Tunisian peoples.
not_established: The passage shown is cut off, so the denial of plots against Tunisian figures is not visible in it; only the summary mentions it.
The sources do not show any action taken against Tunisia after the speech.
The text is excerpted OCR of a translated broadcast, so wording may be imperfect.
u:az-zintan|tunisia.context: Libya and Tunisia had tense relations in the mid-1970s, after a proposed union between them in 1974 was dropped.

timeline.what: Qadhdhafi speaks at Az-Zintan for the anniversary of the battle of Al-Kardun.
Tripoli radio broadcasts the recorded excerpts.
