u:gulf of sidra|libya territorial waters.headline: A 1979 Tripoli radio commentary says Libya has declared the whole Gulf of Sidra a Libyan gulf, with 12-mile territorial waters.
u:gulf of sidra|libya territorial waters.explanation: The Gulf of Sidra is the sea area off Libya's coast. The "territorial waters claim" is Libya's declared right to control that sea. In this August 1979 commentary, Tripoli radio says Libya has announced the Gulf is a Libyan gulf and that its territorial waters reach 12 miles. The commentary is an official Libyan government voice answering the United States. It shows how the government described the Gulf as a matter of national security and was ready to defend it. It does not give the date of the original proclamation or say how other countries responded.
established: A Tripoli radio commentary, reported by FBIS on 14 August 1979, says Libya announced the Gulf of Sidra's waters were Arab waters and the whole Gulf a Libyan gulf.
The same commentary says Libyan territorial waters extend to 12 miles.
It says the proclamation took national security into account and that Libya can defend these waters.
not_established: The passage does not say when the proclamation was first made.
It does not show the legal basis of the claim or whether any other state accepted it.
It is propaganda commentary, so it shows Libya's stated position, not an independent account.
u:gulf of sidra|libya territorial waters.context: The Gulf of Sidra later became a repeated point of dispute between Libya and the United States. The U.S. generally holds that the Gulf is international waters.

timeline.what: Libya proclaims the Gulf of Sidra a Libyan gulf with 12-mile territorial waters (date not given).
FBIS reports a Tripoli radio commentary repeating the claim and attacking the U.S. position.

quotes.text: the entire Gulf of Sidra was a Libyan gulf and that the Arab Libyan territorial waters extend to 12 miles

u:gulf of sidra|libya territorial waters.open_question: The original Libyan proclamation, with its date and wording, would show when and how the claim was first made.

u:gulf of sidra|shari' al-zawiyah basic.headline: A Gaddafi speech to the Shari' al-Zawiyah congress in Tripoli mentions the Gulf of Sidra as a point of confrontation with the U.S.
u:gulf of sidra|shari' al-zawiyah basic.explanation: The two ends are linked by one speech. Gaddafi spoke to the Basic People's Congress of Shari' al-Zawiyah in Tripoli. In it he talked about the U.S. fleet near Libya and the Gulf of Sidra. He said a clash would have followed if American ships had crossed the latitude 30.5 degrees, which he gave as the start of the Gulf. This shows how a local congress in Tripoli was used to explain and rally support for Libya's confrontation with the U.S. The Gulf is not the subject of the congress itself. It is one topic in a longer speech about mobilization and an economic struggle.
established: The document is a transcript of a Gaddafi speech at the Basic People's Congress of Shari' al-Zawiyah in Tripoli.
The speech refers to American fleets off the Libyan coast and to a possible clash if they reached the Gulf of Sidra at latitude 30.5 degrees.
The speech also discusses the Gulf of Sidra as a place where the U.S. faced confrontation.
not_established: The congress did not itself take any decision about the Gulf of Sidra, as far as these passages show.
The document header date (1985-01-14) and the summary's January 1986 date do not agree, so the exact date of the speech is unclear.
The passages do not say whether any clash actually took place in the Gulf.
u:gulf of sidra|shari' al-zawiyah basic.context: The Gulf of Sidra was a long-running source of tension between Libya and the U.S., which disputed Libya's claim to the waters. Basic People's Congresses were the local assemblies of Libya's official system.

timeline.what: Gaddafi speaks to the Shari' al-Zawiyah Basic People's Congress in Tripoli and mentions the Gulf of Sidra.

u:abu nidal organization|libyan people's.headline: A 1986 CIA note ties grenades seized in Ankara to Abu Nidal attacks and says Tripoli passes weapons through its diplomatic missions.
u:abu nidal organization|libyan people's.explanation: Two copies of the same CIA note say grenades taken from Libyans arrested in Turkey match Bulgarian grenades used in Abu Nidal attacks. The note says this supports earlier reporting that Tripoli supports the group and uses its diplomatic installations to pass weapons. The Libyan People's Bureau in Ankara is the Libyan embassy-type office there, so it fits that description. The passages shown do not name the Ankara bureau as the source of the grenades. The link is therefore a reasonable inference from a general statement about Libyan missions, not a direct statement about this office.
established: Grenades were seized from Libyans arrested in Ankara in April 1986 (per the document summaries).
The grenades were made in Bulgaria in 1980 and carry the same markings as grenades used by suspected Abu Nidal terrorists in Rome, Vienna and Malta in 1985.
The CIA comment says Tripoli supports the Abu Nidal group and uses its diplomatic installations to pass weapons to terrorists.
not_established: The passages shown do not say in words that the Ankara grenades came from the Libyan People's Bureau there.
The note does not show that the Ankara bureau dealt directly with the Abu Nidal group.
It is an intelligence assessment; it gives no court findings or named witnesses.
u:abu nidal organization|libyan people's.context: Libyan embassies were commonly called "People's Bureaus" after 1979. Abu Nidal's group was a Palestinian militant organisation that was reported to have had a base in Libya in the mid-1980s.

m:lb-libyan-academy-graduate-studies|lh-.headline: The Libyan Academy is located in Janzur, a town just west of Tripoli, according to a general reference article.
m:lb-libyan-academy-graduate-studies|lh-.explanation: The link says the Libyan Academy sits in the town of Janzur. The Wikipedia article on Janzur lists the Libyan Academy among the important institutions there, along with some University of Tripoli faculties. This helps place the Academy at the western edge of greater Tripoli, outside the old city centre. The source is a general reference, not an eyewitness or official record. It does not say when the Academy moved there or which of its sites is meant. The "same-place" label is a loose fit: the Academy is in Janzur, not the same thing as Janzur.

It also lists University of Tripoli faculties (Arts, Medicine, Engineering) and vocational colleges there.
not_established: The passage does not say when the Academy was set up in Janzur, or whether it was there under Gaddafi.
It does not say whether Janzur holds the Academy's main site or only one of several.
The Italian name Giorgimpopoli does not appear in the passage.

u:omar muhayshi|tripoli barracks.headline: Two Wikipedia articles say Umar Muhayshi took over the Tripoli barracks during the 1 September 1969 coup.
u:omar muhayshi|tripoli barracks.explanation: Both articles describe how the Free Officers seized key sites on 1 September 1969. They say Gaddafi captured the Barqa barracks in Benghazi, and Umar Muhayshi took over the Tripoli barracks. Muhayshi was later a member of the Revolutionary Command Council and then turned against Gaddafi. This link shows him in an active military role in Tripoli on the first day of the new government. The two articles use almost the same wording, so they are probably not independent confirmation. Neither names which barracks in Tripoli.
established: Both articles state that Umar Muhayshi took over the Tripoli barracks during the 1 September 1969 coup.
They place this alongside Gaddafi taking the Barqa barracks in Benghazi and Jalloud seizing Tripoli's anti-aircraft batteries.
Military control of Tripoli was said to be established within a few days, with no deaths or violent incidents reported.
not_established: Which Tripoli barracks is meant, and how it was taken, is not stated.
The two articles are near-identical secondary summaries, with no eyewitness account or primary record cited in these passages.
Nothing here confirms that this Umar Muhayshi is the later RCC member and critic, though that is generally accepted.

Military control is established in Tripoli and elsewhere.

m:lb-abu-salim-prison|central-security|c.headline: A 2018 UN report is said to record that in 2017 Abu Salim prison was held by an armed group called Central Security/Abu Salim.
m:lb-abu-salim-prison|central-security|c.explanation: The link says that in 2017, long after Gaddafi's fall, Abu Salim prison was run by an armed group using the name Central Security (or Central Security/Abu Salim). This comes only from the stated reason and the cited UN report, "Abuse Behind Bars" (2018). I could not retrieve a passage from that report, so I have not checked it. The link does not show that the 2017 group was the same body as the Interior Ministry's Central Security under Gaddafi. It also does not show any link between the two during Gaddafi's rule. It matters mainly as a later chapter: the prison outlived the government that built it, and control passed to armed groups.

m:camp-27|janzour|same-place.explanation: The only basis for this link is a one-line reason entered by the map's builders: Camp 27 lies west of Janzour on the coast road. The article's title suggests it covers fighting over Camp 27, but we could not read it. The atlas profile for Janzour mentions the 1986 US raid and the naval academy, and nothing in it ties either to Camp 27.
established: The record states that Camp 27 lies west of Janzour on the coast road.
The cited source is a Libya Security Monitor article about clashes over Camp 27.

Nothing shows that Camp 27 and Janzour are the same place; the stated reason describes them as separate, neighbouring places.

u:map:tajura-camp|ounianga kebir old air.headline: A 1983 U.S. imagery note puts Tajura Barracks and Ounianga Kebir airfield in one report on Libya's war in Chad.

m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-ibn-al-man.headline: The Faculty of Dentistry is recorded as one of the faculties of the University of Tripoli, but no source text was available to check this.
m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-ibn-al-man.explanation: The map links the university as a whole to one of its faculties, the dental college at Ibn al-Manzour. The only support is the recorded reason: the dental college is a faculty of the University of Tripoli. That is a cited Wikipedia page, and no passage from it could be retrieved. The link is plausible and fits how universities are organised. It helps readers see the dental college as part of the wider university, which was renamed Al Fateh University in 1976. Nothing here shows that the dental faculty took part in the events on the main campus, such as the student protests or the hangings.
established: The link record states that the dental college is a faculty of the University of Tripoli.
The record cites the Wikipedia article on the University of Tripoli, but no passage from it was available for this note.
not_established: No source text was checked, so the claim rests on the recorded reason alone.
Nothing shows when the dental faculty was founded or where it stood during the Gaddafi years.
Nothing links the dental faculty to the 1976–77 protests, the hangings or the 2011 student uprising.
m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-ibn-al-man.context: Universities in Libya, as elsewhere, were made up of faculties, often in separate buildings around the city. The dental college may therefore sit apart from the main campus.
m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-ibn-al-man.open_question: The cited Wikipedia page, or a university or Ministry of Education record, could confirm the faculty's founding date, its name over the years and its address.

m:lh-hani-battle-monument|lh-shar-al-sha.headline: A memorial in the Hani area is thought to mark the October 1911 Shar al-Shatt battle, but no source we could read says so.
m:lh-hani-battle-monument|lh-shar-al-sha.explanation: The recorded reason is that the Hani fighting in late October 1911 was part of the Shar al-Shatt battle. We could not retrieve any source passage, so this note relies only on that stated reason and the atlas profiles. The profiles place the Hani memorials in the eastern oasis belt, about 1.5 km from the coordinates given for the battle. That fits the battle's setting, but it is a guess from location. The profiles also say none of the pages opened name Hani as the Libyan name for this battle. The link is therefore a reasonable inference, not a documented fact, and the "documented" label looks too strong.
established: The recorded reason says the Hani fighting in late October 1911 was part of the Shar al-Shatt battle.
The atlas profile says the Hani memorial points lie about 1.5 km south-east of the coordinates Wikipedia gives for the battle area.
not_established: No retrieved passage names Hani as the Libyan name for the Shar al-Shatt battle.
The memorial's date, builder and the battle year it marks are unknown.
It is not shown that the memorials stand on the battlefield itself, since Wikipedia's coordinates give only the general battle area.
m:lh-hani-battle-monument|lh-shar-al-sha.context: The 1911 fighting took place soon after Italy landed at Tripoli in the Italo-Turkish War. Libyan memorials to it are likely to date from a later period.

u:map:tip|qadhafi.headline: A Libyan state radio report says Gaddafi flew back into Tripoli International Airport on 13 March 1982 after visiting Austria and stopping in Malta.
u:map:tip|qadhafi.explanation: The link is an arrival. Libya's official news agency, JANA, reported that Gaddafi came home at 1900 and was welcomed at Tripoli International Airport. Senior armed forces officers met him there. The report shows the airport was where the leader came back into the city after foreign trips, and that the state marked the return with a military welcome. It is one report from state media, so it tells us what Libya chose to announce. It says nothing about the airport's wider role.
established: JANA reported that Gaddafi returned home at 1900 after a 4-day official visit to Austria, made at the invitation of Chancellor Kreisky.
He was welcomed at Tripoli International Airport by the Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces and other senior officers, including the Chief of Staff.
The summary says he stopped in Malta on the way, met Prime Minister Mintoff, and agreed to submit the continental shelf dispute to the International Court of Justice.
not_established: The passage does not say whether this was the military airport or the civil terminal. It names only Tripoli International Airport, so the link to the 'military airport' label rests on the map treating them as one place.
The passage is cut off, and the names and titles of the officers are partly garbled by OCR.

timeline.what: Gaddafi begins a 4-day official visit to Austria.
He stops over in Malta, then returns to Tripoli at 1900 and is welcomed at the airport.
JANA broadcasts his statement on returning, saying the Austria visit was extremely positive.

quotes.text: The brother commander returned home at 1900 today.

u:great man-made river|us companies.headline: A 1986 CIA briefing says US companies left the Great Man-Made River project, slowing Gaddafi's priority water scheme.
u:great man-made river|us companies.explanation: The document is a set of talking points on how US trade sanctions were affecting Libya's economy. It says progress on the Great Man-Made River, which it calls Qadhafi's priority project, was slowed because US companies working on it departed. This shows that American firms had a part in the early work on the scheme, and that sanctions cut that involvement. It matters because it shows how foreign politics reached into Libya's large development projects. The passage does not name the companies or say how much the work was delayed.
established: A CIA document dated 28 August 1986 says progress on the Great Man-Made River was slowed by the departure of US companies working on it.
It describes the project as Qadhafi's priority.
It places this within a wider account of US sanctions affecting Libya's development program.
not_established: The passage does not name the US companies involved in the river project.
It does not say what work they did, when they left, or how long the delay was.
The US oil companies named elsewhere in the passage are listed as leaving oil operations, not this project.
u:great man-made river|us companies.context: The Great Man-Made River was Libya's large scheme to pipe water from underground sources in the desert to the coast. The US imposed sanctions on Libya in 1986.

timeline.what: US oil companies ceased Libyan operations under US orders (per the document).
CIA talking points note the river project slowed after US companies left.

quotes.text: Progress on Qadhafi's priority Great Man-Made River project also has been slowed as a result of the departure of US companies working on the scheme.

m:abusalim|mk-abusalim|same-place.headline: The 1996 massacre took place inside Abu Salim prison, so the two entries describe one event and the place where it happened.
m:abusalim|mk-abusalim|same-place.explanation: Abu Salim prison was the building in Tripoli. The massacre was the mass killing of prisoners held there in June 1996. The supplied passages call it the "Abu Salim Prison massacre" and place it in that prison. They give a date of 29 June 1996 and an estimate of about 1,270 dead. This matters because the prison, built to hold political prisoners, became the site of the worst single killing of the Gaddafi years. Families' protests over it later fed into the 2011 uprising. The sources here are background articles, not eyewitness accounts.
established: A Wikipedia overview says the Abu Salim Prison massacre was a mass killing of prisoners on June 29, 1996, with an estimated 1,270 killed.
The same article describes poor conditions and torture of prisoners before the massacre, which it says led to the events.
Other background articles name the 1996 Abu Salim prison massacre and link Gaddafi's government and its intelligence chief, Abdullah Senussi, to it as an accusation.
not_established: The passages do not give an eyewitness account of the killings inside the prison.
The death toll is an estimate, and the sources say figures are disputed. The recorded reason says about 1,200, while one passage says 1,270.
The two cited sources (Human Rights Watch 2009 and the Abu Salim prison article) were not among the passages shown, so they could not be checked here.
m:abusalim|mk-abusalim|same-place.context: Abu Salim is also the name of a district of Tripoli. The prison stood in the Military Police Command compound there. The massacre is widely reported to have followed a prisoner protest over conditions.

Families' protests over the killings helped spark the uprising (from the atlas profile).

u:sebha airfield|sebha sam site.headline: A December 1982 U.S. briefing note says a newly spotted SA-2 missile site near Sebha was probably placed to defend Sebha airfield.

A U.S. photographic interpretation note from December 1982 describes the site as about 3 nautical miles east of the airfield. It says the site is "probably" there to defend the airfield. The wording is a judgement, not a confirmed fact. Sebha is in central Libya, far from Tripoli. This link shows how Libya's air defences were spread across the country, but it says little about Tripoli itself.

It puts the site about 3 nautical miles east of Sebha airfield.
It says the site is probably deployed in defence of the airfield.
It lists six SA-2 launchers, a Fan Song guidance radar and a Spoon Rest early-warning radar, and two SA-3 sites already in the area.
not_established: The note does not confirm the site's purpose; 'probably' is an analyst's judgement.
It does not show who operated the site or what it did in practice.
It has no direct connection to Tripoli.

u:tarabulus military installation east-s.headline: A 1982 CIA report places a SAM support facility at, or within, the Tarabulus military installation east-southeast of Tripoli, where an SA-8 battery was seen.
u:tarabulus military installation east-s.explanation: The report says the first SA-8 missile system in Libya was identified in January 1982 at the Tarabulus Military Installation East-Southeast. It adds that this installation houses a major training facility for all types of surface-to-air missile (SAM) equipment. The next sentence says an SA-8 battery was seen at the Tarabulus SAM Support Facility. The two names probably point to the same area, with the support facility being the part of the installation where the battery was seen. The report does not say this outright. It also says the SA-8 had not yet been deployed for actual use, so this was a training and support setting, not a combat site.
established: The first SA-8 identification in Libya was at Tarabulus Military Installation East-Southeast in January 1982.
The installation houses a major training facility for all types of SAM equipment.
An SA-8 battery was observed at Tarabulus SAM Support Facility.
The SA-8 had not yet been tactically deployed in Libya.
not_established: The report does not say in so many words that the support facility lies inside the installation.
It does not give exact coordinates, so it cannot show whether the two names mark the same spot or two nearby ones.
The passage is cut off after the facility's name, so any site identifier is missing.
u:tarabulus military installation east-s.context: SAM means surface-to-air missile. The SA-8 is a Soviet-made mobile short-range air defence system.

u:geneva|qadhafi.headline: A 1974 CIA cable fragment places Qadhafi in Geneva, where he was expected to meet Tunisia's President Bourguiba.
u:geneva|qadhafi.explanation: The document is a short, badly scanned cable from January 1974. It says Tunisian government and party members were in Geneva, and that press reports suggested Qadhafi and Bourguiba might meet there that afternoon. It also suggests Qadhafi's delegation had arrived only a few hours earlier. The link is about Qadhafi's travel and diplomacy abroad, not about daily life in Tripoli. It shows that the Libyan leader was dealing with Tunisia's leaders in Switzerland at this time. The text is heavily garbled, so details should be read with care.
established: The document's title and text place Qadhafi's delegation in Geneva in January 1974.
Press reports cited in the cable said Qadhafi and Bourguiba might meet that afternoon.
Tunisian government and party members were also in Geneva.
not_established: Whether the meeting between Qadhafi and Bourguiba actually took place.
What was discussed, or the outcome.
The reason for the trip, since the text is mostly illegible.
u:geneva|qadhafi.context: In January 1974 Libya and Tunisia announced a plan to merge, which was later dropped. This background is not drawn from the document's legible text.

timeline.what: Cable dated; reports Qadhafi's delegation arriving in Geneva and a possible meeting with Bourguiba.

u:al jufrah airfield|tripoli tarabulus.headline: A 1983 U.S. photo-analysis note places Al Jufrah airfield about 260 nautical miles southeast of Tripoli, as a distance reference only.
u:al jufrah airfield|tripoli tarabulus.explanation: The document is a December 1983 briefing note from a U.S. photo-interpretation centre. It says the Al Jufrah airfield in central Libya, reportedly built with Soviet help, is now working and can handle advanced jets. It gives Tripoli (written "Tarabulus") only as a reference point: the airfield is 260 nautical miles to the southeast. So the link is about distance and direction, not a Tripoli site. It helps readers see how far from the capital this military base lay.
established: The note states the airfield is 260 nautical miles southeast of Tarabulus (Tripoli).
It reports the airfield as operational and able to handle advanced jet aircraft, and says it was reportedly being built by the Soviets.

The Soviet involvement is described only as 'reportedly'; the note does not confirm it.

u:gulf of sidra|libyan coast.headline: The Gulf of Sidra is a stretch of water on the Libyan coast, and a February 1983 Tripoli broadcast treats the two together.
u:gulf of sidra|libyan coast.explanation: The two ends are not the same thing. The Libyan coast is the wider shoreline. The Gulf of Sidra is one large bay on it. In this 1983 Tripoli radio report, news of U.S. military movement "toward the Libyan coast" is linked to Qadhdhafi's warning about the gulf's waters. The passage does not say that the gulf is part of the coast, so that point rests on geography. It does show how Tripoli described the dispute: Libya said it would not allow the United States or any other state into the gulf's territorial waters. The link helps explain how the coast and the gulf were presented together as a matter of national defense.
established: A Tripoli broadcast of 18 February 1983 called the U.S. military movement toward the Libyan coast the lead story in world and Arab media.
It reported Qadhdhafi telling the General People's Congress that Libya would not allow the United States or any other state into the territorial waters in the Gulf of Sidra.
It said Libyans were ready to turn the gulf into a "red gulf" in defense of their waters, land and air.
not_established: The passage does not state that the Gulf of Sidra lies on the Libyan coast. That is only implied.
It does not say where the U.S. ships actually went, or whether they entered the gulf.
The summary's mention of Sixth Fleet units is only partly visible in the passage shown.
u:gulf of sidra|libyan coast.context: The Gulf of Sidra is a large bay on Libya's Mediterranean coast. Libya claimed it as territorial water, and the United States and others disputed that claim.

u:libyan peoples' bureau in rome|rome.headline: The Libyan Peoples' Bureau was Libya's official office in Rome, and a 1983 CIA paper says it threatened exiles there in 1980.
u:libyan peoples' bureau in rome|rome.explanation: The link is between an organisation and the city where it sat. The CIA assessment places the Libyan Peoples' Bureau in Rome and says it reacted to the 1980 murders of two Libyan exiles. It reports that the Bureau, echoing Qadhafi, threatened "liquidation" of exiles who would not return to Libya. This shows how Tripoli's government used its overseas offices to reach opponents abroad. The AI's reason says it responded to a "crackdown". The passage actually describes the Bureau responding to Italian outrage and an Italian security crackdown on the killings.
established: The document names the Libyan Peoples' Bureau in Rome and describes it acting in Rome.
Two Libyan exiles were murdered in Rome in spring 1980.
The Bureau reacted defiantly, threatening 'liquidation' of exiles who refused to return to Libya.
Italian security officials increased protection, and the assassination activity ended, according to the CIA.
not_established: The passage does not say who carried out the murders, nor does it say the Bureau took part in them.
It does not show who in Tripoli ordered the Bureau's statement beyond saying it was 'echoing Qadhafi'.
It is a single CIA assessment, and nothing here confirms its claims independently.
u:libyan peoples' bureau in rome|rome.context: Libyan embassies were renamed 'Peoples' Bureaus' in the late 1970s. Libyan exiles were attacked in several European cities around 1980.

timeline.what: Two Libyan exiles are murdered in Rome.

m:mitiga|wp-mitiga-okba-ben-nafi-air-bas.headline: Both entries describe the same Tripoli airfield, once Wheelus Air Base and later Mitiga (Okba Ben Nafi), so this is one place recorded twice.
m:mitiga|wp-mitiga-okba-ben-nafi-air-bas.explanation: The two entries cover the same site east of Tripoli. It began as the Italian-built Mellaha field and was known as Wheelus Air Base under US use. After the Americans left in June 1970, Libya ran it as a military base. The recorded reason, a military base and a civilian airport on one site, fits this. The sources given here show the handover of Wheelus and Libyan plans to use it as a military base. They say nothing about civilian flights or the names Mitiga and Okba Ben Nafi. For a reader of the map, the two entries should be treated as one place, not two.
established: A 1974 survey says the US withdrew from Wheelus Air Base in Tripoli in June 1970.
The 1974 chronology says the US evacuated Wheelus in June 1970.
A October 1969 CIA cable says the Libyan ruling council planned to run Wheelus as a Libyan military facility, with five or six thousand army and air force troops.
The 1969 cable calls Wheelus the future central Libyan military installation.
not_established: None of the passages uses the names Mitiga or Okba Ben Nafi, so the renaming rests on the atlas profiles and Wikipedia.
The passages do not mention civilian airport use, so the 'dual' military and civilian claim is not shown by these sources.
The 1986 raid on the airfield is not described in the passages given.
m:mitiga|wp-mitiga-okba-ben-nafi-air-bas.context: Wheelus, Mellaha, Okba Ben Nafi and Mitiga are widely understood to be names for the same airfield at different times. The civilian Mitiga airport shares the site.

u:map:bab|national front for the salvati.headline: The National Front for the Salvation of Libya attacked Gaddafi's Bab al-Aziziya compound in Tripoli in May 1984, and the attack failed.
u:map:bab|national front for the salvati.explanation: Two sources link the opposition group to the Bab al-Aziziya compound. The column says Gaddafi was behind Soviet-made tanks and antiaircraft guns.
Wikipedia says the group's most notable coup attempt was its 1984 armed assault on the Bab al-Azizia compound in Tripoli.

u:lockheed|omar muhayshi.headline: A 1976 State Department cable links Lockheed to Umar Muhayshi through Qadhafi's public claim that Lockheed had bribed him.

The cable's summary says Qadhafi publicly attacked Muhayshi and that Muhayshi was alleged to have been bribed by Lockheed.

m:wheelus|wp-mitiga-okba-ben-nafi-air-ba.headline: Both entries describe one place: the airfield east of Tripoli, once Wheelus Air Base, renamed Okba Ben Nafi in 1970 and now Mitiga airport.
m:wheelus|wp-mitiga-okba-ben-nafi-air-ba.explanation: These two map entries are the same base, described twice. The airfield was built by Italy in 1923. The US later ran it as Wheelus. After the 1969 coup and the end of the American lease, Libya renamed it Okba Ben Nafi. It became a civilian airport called Mitiga in 1995. Keeping the two entries linked helps a reader see that the US base, the Libyan and Soviet-used air base, and the 1986 bombing target were all one site.
established: The airport article says the base was built in 1923 as an Italian base, Mellaha, and was renamed Wheelus Air Base by the US in 1945.
It says American use continued until the 1969 coup and the end of the lease, and that the base was then renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base.
It says the Libyan and Soviet air forces used the base, and that the US bombed it in 1986.
It says the base became a civilian airport in 1995 and took the name Mitiga.
not_established: The passage does not give an exact date in 1970 for the handover or the renaming.
Only one Wikipedia passage was supplied. The Wheelus article cited in the record was not shown, and Wikipedia is a secondary source.

m:fashloum|lm-martyrs-square|same-place.headline: Fashloum is a district of Tripoli lying southeast of Martyrs' Square, so the two are neighbours, not the same place.

That makes the link one of location: a poorer district close to the city's main square. It is not a link between two names for one place, so "same-place" is the wrong label. The article does not say the two uprisings were linked or coordinated.

It describes Fashloom as one of the more impoverished districts of the city.

m:lb-tripoli-supreme-court|mk-abusalim|c.headline: Libya's Supreme Court is recorded as ruling in 2021 that the 1996 Abu Salim killings were genocide and sending the case back to a lower court.
m:lb-tripoli-supreme-court|mk-abusalim|c.explanation: The link comes from one stated reason: on 2 May 2021 the Supreme Court ruled on the Abu Salim massacre. It is cited to a Wikipedia page about Abu Salim Prison. We could not retrieve any passage from that page, so we have not checked the claim against the text. The link shows how the killings of 1996 were still being dealt with in court 25 years later, long after Gaddafi's rule ended. The atlas profile notes that the ruling comes from a source about the prison, not about the court building. So it tells us about the court's role in the case, not about the building or its place in Tripoli.
established: The recorded reason says the Supreme Court ruled on 2 May 2021 that the 1996 Abu Salim massacre was a genocide.
The same record says the case was sent back to a lower court.
not_established: No source text was available, so we could not check the ruling, its date, its wording or the court's exact decision.

The cited page is about the prison, not the court.
m:lb-tripoli-supreme-court|mk-abusalim|c.context: The Abu Salim killings took place in the prison in Tripoli in 1996. Families of the dead pressed for answers for many years, and the government long denied what had happened.

not_established: No source text was retrieved, so the claim of closeness could not be checked here.

m:ainzara|ain-zara-prison|same-place.headline: Both entries appear to describe the same Ain Zara prison, but the sources given do not show that it was a political prison under Gaddafi.

u:abdessalam jalloud|map:wheelus.headline: Jalloud, a senior Gaddafi aide, is said to have led Libya's side in talks on the American departure from Wheelus Air Base.
u:abdessalam jalloud|map:wheelus.explanation: Abdessalam Jalloud was one of Gaddafi's closest colleagues after the 1969 coup. Wheelus was the large American air base near Tripoli, later renamed Okba Ben Nafi. The link is that Jalloud is said to have headed the Libyan negotiators when the Americans agreed to leave, and the base passed to Libya in 1970. This matters because the base's handover was an early sign of the new government's independence. The one source is a Wikipedia biography. The part of it we can read is cut off before it reaches Wheelus, so the claim rests on the document's summary and the earlier reading of it.
established: The biography describes Jalloud as a classmate of Gaddafi, a leading figure among the 1969 coup officers, and deputy chairman of the Revolutionary Command Council.
He was Minister of Treasury from 1970 to 1972 and Prime Minister from 1972 to 1977.
The document summary says the article covers his Wheelus negotiations.
not_established: The passage we can read does not mention Wheelus or the base's handover. It breaks off at 'The same year, Jalloud also succeeded…'.
The source does not give the dates of the talks, who sat on the American side, or the terms agreed.
It is a single background reference, not an eyewitness or official record.
u:abdessalam jalloud|map:wheelus.context: The United States left Wheelus Air Base in June 1970. Libya then renamed it Okba Ben Nafi and used it for its own forces.

Jalloud is Treasury Minister. The summary places the Wheelus talks around this time, and the base is handed to Libya.
Jalloud serves as Prime Minister.

u:abdessalam jalloud|map:wheelus.open_question: The full text of the Wikipedia section on Wheelus, or U.S. and Libyan records of the 1969–70 evacuation talks, would show Jalloud's exact role.

u:faya-largeau|ogoui.headline: A 1983 imagery report places Libyan aircraft at Ogoui, a forward airfield in Chad, during the push to retake Faya Largeau.
u:faya-largeau|ogoui.explanation: Both places are in northern Chad, not in Tripoli. The report says Libyan light-strike aircraft and helicopters were moved to forward airfields at Ogoui and Ounianga Kebir before the August 1983 assault on Faya Largeau. So Ogoui was part of the staging for that operation. The passage given does not mention a road between the two places or a mechanized infantry battalion moving along it, so that part of the claimed link is not supported here. It matters for Tripoli only as background: it shows how far Libya's military reach extended from Tripoli into Chad.

Libyan light-strike aircraft and helicopters were moved to forward airfields at Ogoui and Ounianga Kebir.

u:bin ghashir|map:qasr-ben-ghashir.headline: Bin Ghashir and Qasr bin Ghashir appear to be the same place just south of Tripoli, named in two different documents.
u:bin ghashir|map:qasr-ben-ghashir.explanation: Both ends point to the Bin Ghashir area south of Tripoli. A 1991 U.S. State Department report lists Bin Ghashir as a site used to train people from abroad in terrorist and guerrilla tactics. A 1976 radio report places a Qadhdhafi rally "near Tripoli" at Bin Ghashir. Qasr bin Ghashir is the name of the town on the map, so the two entries probably describe one location under a shorter and a longer name. The sources do not themselves say they are the same, and they describe very different uses of the place fifteen years apart.
established: The 1991 report places Bin Ghashir just south of Tripoli and says it was used to train dissidents from Africa, Asia and Latin America.
The 1976 radio item says Qadhdhafi spoke at a popular rally near Tripoli, at Bin Ghashir.
not_established: Neither source uses the full name Qasr bin Ghashir or says the two names mean the same place.
The sources do not show that the 1976 rally and the later training use were at the same exact site.
The 1991 claims are a U.S. government assertion; no independent confirmation is given in the passage.

u:polisario front|tindouf.headline: In 1987 Morocco feared Libyan planes landing at Tindouf, in Algeria, were carrying arms to the Polisario Front.
u:polisario front|tindouf.explanation: Tindouf is a town in Algeria near the Moroccan border. The Polisario Front is the movement fighting Morocco over Western Sahara. A U.S. embassy memo from Rabat says Morocco counted 11 Libyan flights to Tindouf in five days. King Hassan feared these were an "air bridge" of arms to the Polisario. This shows how Libya under Gaddafi was thought to be backing the Polisario, using Tindouf as the landing point. It is Morocco's concern as passed to the Americans, not a confirmed finding.
established: A U.S. embassy memo of March 4, 1987 records a Moroccan message that Libya may have resumed arms aid to the Polisario.
Morocco said it registered 11 Libyan flights to Tindouf in Algeria from February 28 through March 4.
The Moroccans thought the aircraft might be Soviet-built Antonov transports, each staying on the ground about an hour.
not_established: The memo does not show what the planes carried; the arms link is Morocco's suspicion.
It does not show that the cargo was handed to the Polisario at Tindouf.
The excerpt does not give any U.S. view on whether the Moroccan claim was true.
u:polisario front|tindouf.context: Tindouf, in southwestern Algeria, is widely known as a base for Sahrawi refugee camps and for the Polisario Front's leadership.

timeline.what: Morocco registers 11 Libyan flights to Tindouf.
Moroccan officials pass King Hassan's concern to the U.S. at a reception in Rabat.

quotes.text: the Moroccans have registered 11 Libyan flights to Tindouf in Algeria near the Moroccan border.

u:palmaria sp howitzer|tarabulus army ba.headline: A 1982 U.S. imagery report places one Italian-built Palmaria self-propelled howitzer at Tarabulus Army Barracks East, the first seen in Libya.
u:palmaria sp howitzer|tarabulus army ba.explanation: Two copies of a September 1982 note from the U.S. National Photographic Interpretation Center say the same thing. They report one Italian-made 155mm Palmaria howitzer, parked in travel-lock position, at Tarabulus Army Barracks East. The note says this was the first such weapon identified in Libya. It reads the weapon as another sign that Libya was spreading its arms purchases across more suppliers. For Tripoli, it shows that this barracks held foreign-bought heavy weapons by 1982. The two documents appear to be duplicates, not independent confirmation.
established: Both documents state that one Palmaria 155mm self-propelled howitzer was identified at Tarabulus Army Barracks East on imagery.
The weapon was parked in travel-lock position, and the note gives coordinates 32-53-37N 013-19-32E.
The note calls this the first identification of an Italian self-propelled howitzer in Libya.
not_established: The sources do not say when Libya bought the weapon, or from whom, or how many it ordered.
The note says the weapon might have been there earlier, but image quality prevented identification, so the arrival date is unknown.
Only one vehicle is reported. The sources do not say whether it stayed at the barracks.
u:palmaria sp howitzer|tarabulus army ba.context: The Palmaria was an Italian self-propelled howitzer made by OTO-Melara for export. The two documents are dated a few days apart and look like copies of the same note, with different reference numbers.

timeline.what: The weapon might already have been present, but the imagery was too poor to identify it.
The imagery note reports one Palmaria howitzer at Tarabulus Army Barracks East.

He is executed

u:gargaresh tripoli temporary prison|kha.headline: An Arabic Wikipedia article says the Khamis Brigade killed prisoners held in a temporary prison near Gargaresh in August 2011.

The same article also mentions a reported killing of prisoners in a warehouse in Tripoli in August 2011.
not_established: The passage supplied does not show who the evidence for the killings came from, such as witnesses, survivors or later investigators.
The summary does not confirm the figure of 17 prisoners or the date of 21 August 2011. Those come from the link note.

u:gargaresh tripoli temporary prison|kha.context: The Khamis Brigade was commanded by Khamis Gaddafi, one of Muammar Gaddafi's sons. It was among the best-equipped units that fought the 2011 uprising. Tripoli fell to opposition forces in late August 2011.

timeline.what: Reported strike on the brigade's headquarters near Tripoli.
Reported killing of 17 prisoners in a temporary prison near Gargaresh (date and number from the link note).
Reported killing of prisoners in a warehouse in Tripoli.

Libya and Morocco made a treaty, which the column links to Muhayshi's handover.

m:abusalim|lb-abu-salim-prison|same-plac.headline: Both entries describe the same place: Abu Salim prison in Tripoli, built in 1984, though the supplied passages never state the 1984 date.
m:abusalim|lb-abu-salim-prison|same-plac.explanation: The two entries are one prison under two spellings, "Abu Salim" and "Abu Slim". Both profiles say it opened after the 1984 attack on Bab al-Aziziya and later held political prisoners. The passages supplied here do not describe the building or its 1984 start. They only show that Abu Salim was a prison used for political detainees and for the 1996 killings. Treat the two entries as duplicates and merge them. Keep the details from each: the 1988 amnesty and the construction details.
established: The sources name Abu Salim prison as a place where Libyan Islamist prisoners were held and, per Belhaj's account, tortured (DOC 1, DOC 3).
They link the prison to the 1996 massacre (DOC 2, DOC 4).
Belhaj is said to have been held there for about seven years after his 2004 return to Libya, then released in 2010 (DOC 1).
not_established: None of the passages gives the 1984 completion date, the construction details or the 1988 amnesty figures.

Tafoya said he was working for the CIA, and the agency denied it. Prosecutors suggested he was a paid Libyan hit man, and a grand jury later looked into his ties to ex-CIA agent Edwin Wilson. The case matters because it shows Qaddafi's government was suspected of reaching dissidents abroad. It happened in the United States, not Tripoli.

m:lm-tripoli-international-airport|mitig.headline: After Tripoli International Airport was badly damaged in 2014 fighting, passenger flights in Tripoli moved to Mitiga, the city's former Wheelus air base.

The sources agree on the general shift. They differ on timing, because one says Mitiga was the sole airport from 2018 and another says Tripoli reopened briefly in 2017. For Tripoli under Gaddafi, this shows how the two airports, one civilian and one a former foreign base, later swapped roles.

u:april 14 american bombing raid against.headline: The 14 April 1986 US air raid on Libya was the backdrop to a later US plan to unsettle Gaddafi.
u:april 14 american bombing raid against.explanation: A Washington Post article from October 1986 describes a secret US plan, approved in August 1986, to make Gaddafi believe another attack was coming. It says officials justified the plan by citing new intelligence, which they said came "following a four-month lull after the April 14 American bombing raid against Libya." So the raid is mentioned as the starting point of that period, and Gaddafi is the target of both the raid and the later plan. The article does not say the raid was aimed at Gaddafi personally, and it does not describe the raid itself. For Tripoli, it shows how the raid still shaped US–Libyan tension months afterward.

Officials said new intelligence showed Gaddafi was stepping up his terrorist plans again.
A plan to deceive Gaddafi was discussed at a White House meeting on 14 August 1986 and approved in general terms.
The article says a memo to Reagan described Gaddafi as temporarily quiescent in his support of terrorism.
not_established: The passage does not describe the raid itself, its targets or its results.
It does not say the raid was aimed at Gaddafi personally.
Other sources said there was no significant, reliable intelligence in mid-August to support the claim of renewed plans.
u:april 14 american bombing raid against.context: The US bombed targets in Libya, including in Tripoli, on 14 April 1986, after accusing Libya of involvement in terrorism.

It also says the main Libyan ground deployment in Chad was there. So Faya Largeau was a central place in this part of the Chad conflict. The document has nothing about Tripoli itself. It matters only because it shows how far Libya's military reach extended from Tripoli.

It says Libyan ground units had pushed as far south as Faya Largeau, about 420 nautical miles northeast of Ndjamena.

It states that the primary Libyan ground force deployment in Chad was at Faya Largeau.

u:kufra airfield|map:wheelus.headline: A 1982 US imagery note says two Blinder bombers at Kufra probably flew in from Okba Ibn Nafa airfield, the former Wheelus base near Tripoli.
u:kufra airfield|map:wheelus.explanation: The note is a short briefing from the US National Photographic Interpretation Center. It reports two Blinder aircraft (a Soviet-built bomber type) at Kufra airfield in southeastern Libya. It says they "probably" came from Okba Ibn Nafa airfield. The same passage says two Blinder were missing from Okba Ibn Nafa, though the OCR text there is broken. This shows that Okba Ibn Nafa, on the Tripoli side of the country, was a base for these aircraft and that they could be sent far to the south. The note does not say the base was Wheelus; that identification comes from background knowledge. Kufra is far from Tripoli, so this is background only.

It does not give the reason for the deployment.

u:oau chairmanship|qadhafi.headline: Qaddafi was due to become chairman of the Organization of African Unity in summer 1982, and both the US and Morocco worried about it.
u:oau chairmanship|qadhafi.explanation: Two 1982 US government documents link Qaddafi to the OAU chairmanship. A January State Department cable says he was scheduled to take the chair that summer. It says the US wanted a Western Sahara cease-fire and referendum worked out before then. A May CIA memo records King Hassan II of Morocco calling it "inconceivable" that Qaddafi could head the OAU. The King wanted to build a bloc to block a quorum at the summit. This shows how Libya's leader was seen abroad, and how his role in African politics became tied to the Western Sahara dispute. The documents say nothing about how Qaddafi got the chairmanship or what happened at the summit.
established: A January 1982 State Department cable says the OAU chairmanship was scheduled to be taken up by Qadhafi that summer.
The US wanted progress on a Western Sahara cease-fire and referendum before he took the chair.
A May 1982 CIA memo of a meeting with King Hassan II lists the OAU Summit and Qadhafi's chairmanship as a main topic.
King Hassan said Morocco needed one-third of OAU members on its side to block a quorum, and that a concerted action against Qadhafi's chairmanship could then be developed.
not_established: The documents do not show whether the summit took place or whether Qaddafi actually became chairman.
Parts of the May memo are not declassified, so Morocco's full plan is unclear.
The January cable mentions Qadhafi only briefly; its main subject is Western Sahara.
u:oau chairmanship|qadhafi.context: The Organization of African Unity was the continental body of African states. Its chair rotated yearly among member leaders. Morocco and Libya were on opposing sides over the Western Sahara and the Polisario.

The link is a historical one between two places in the order's story. The passage does not mention Tripoli.

u:douglas schlachter|edwin wilson.headline: Douglas Schlachter, a former aide to Edwin Wilson, was charged and later pleaded guilty over the Libyan explosives and terrorist training work.
u:douglas schlachter|edwin wilson.explanation: Three 1981–82 newspaper articles tie Schlachter directly to Wilson. They say he managed Wilson's Virginia farm. In August 1976 he left to supervise the Libyan operation that Wilson and Frank Terpil ran under a 1976 contract. He was indicted with them. In 1982 he pleaded guilty and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors. This matters because Schlachter's account was a route for U.S. investigators into how Wilson's work for Libya was set up. In February 1982 he pleaded guilty to shipping explosives to Libya and helping set up an explosives school there, working for Wilson and Terpil.
He agreed to cooperate with prosecutors in the Wilson-Terpil investigation in exchange for pleading guilty to two lesser charges.
not_established: The articles do not say where in Libya, or whether in Tripoli, the school or training took place.
Schlachter's lawyer said he believed he was working within an operation sanctioned by U.S. government agencies. The articles do not show whether that was true.
They do not say what Schlachter told investigators or whether his testimony was ever used against Wilson.

u:billy carter|frank terpil.headline: A 1981 news article says Billy Carter met arms dealer Frank Terpil in Libya in 1979 and later said Terpil had asked about machine guns.
u:billy carter|frank terpil.explanation: Two copies of the same 1981 newspaper article say Billy Carter met former CIA man Frank Terpil at a dinner and watched a parade with him on his 1979 trip to Libya. The article says Carter later told a Justice Department official and an FBI agent that Terpil had contacted him about getting many machine guns for Libya. A 1980 Washington Star article adds that a photo in Time magazine seemed to show Terpil next to Carter, but Terpil denied it was him. The sources therefore agree that the two were linked, but the 1979 meeting is reported, not proven, and Terpil disputed it. Both men matter because they show how private Americans dealt with Libya's government in these years.

The same article says that in January 1980 Carter told Justice Department official Joel Lisker and an FBI agent that Terpil had recently contacted him about getting many machine guns for Libya.
The article says prosecutors in the Terpil case believe the link with Carter was never adequately explored.
A July 1980 Washington Star article says a Time magazine photo was disputed: Terpil said the man beside Carter was not him.
not_established: No source shows that any machine-gun deal was made or that Carter took part in one.
Whether the man in the Time photo was Terpil is disputed. Terpil denied it, and the Star says intelligence sources were uncertain.
The Star says Carter told a reporter in January 1980 'I don't know the guy', which conflicts with the later account of a meeting.

u:great man-made river|jifarah plain.headline: Falling groundwater in the Jifarah Plain, Libya's best farmland near Tripoli, is the problem the Great Man-Made River was meant to ease.
u:great man-made river|jifarah plain.explanation: The 1987 study says the Jifarah Plain near Tripoli was Libya's most productive farming region. It was irrigated mostly by wells, and overirrigation was lowering its water tables. That was a serious long-term threat to farming there. The Great Man-Made River was Libya's project to bring in water from elsewhere. The link is plausible and fits the account. The passages we have only show the problem and a possible later link to Tripoli. They don't show the project was built to supply the Jifarah Plain's farms. The AI's summary says the falling water tables "prompted" the project, but the visible text doesn't say that. The text is also cut off just where it would discuss the project.

Most farms there were irrigated by individual wells and electric pumps, drawing on an underground aquifer.
Falling water tables caused by overirrigation in the best farmland were called a severe long-term ecological threat.

u:great man-made river|jifarah plain.context: The Great Man-Made River was a large Libyan scheme that piped groundwater from desert aquifers in the south to the coastal cities. It was announced in the 1980s.

The atlas gives the toll as more than 140 killed in November 1945, 12 in June 1948 and 18 in June 1967.
The cited source is a general Wikipedia list of massacres in Libya.
not_established: No source text was available to check the 'centred on the Old City' claim, the casualty figures or the street-level detail.
It is not shown here which streets or buildings were attacked in each wave.
m:mk-riots|old-city|same-place.context: Libya's Jewish community was one of the oldest in North Africa. Most of its members left after the 1945 and 1948 violence, and nearly all of the rest left after 1967.

timeline.what: First riots; more than 140 people killed, according to the atlas.
Second wave; 12 killed.
Third wave; 18 killed.
Gaddafi takes power; almost no Jewish residents remain.

m:mk-riots|old-city|same-place.open_question: A history of Libyan Jews, or survivor accounts from the Hara Kabira and Hara Saghira, could confirm where each wave of violence struck and how many people left.

u:kufra|umar al-mukhtar.headline: Kufra, the last Sanusi stronghold, fell in 1931, the same year Umar al-Mukhtar was captured and hanged.
u:kufra|umar al-mukhtar.explanation: A 1987 Library of Congress study puts the two in the same short passage on the end of Sanusi resistance to Italy. It says Al Kufrah, the last Sanusi stronghold, fell in 1931. It says Mukhtar was captured in September of that year and then hanged. The link is one of timing and shared history. Mukhtar was not at Kufra, and the source does not say he was. For Tripoli under Gaddafi, the link helps explain why Mukhtar became a national symbol of resistance to foreign rule.
established: Al Kufrah is called the last Sanusi stronghold and is said to have fallen in 1931.
Mukhtar was captured in September 1931, given a summary court-martial and hanged before a crowd of 20,000 Arabs.
After his death Sanusi resistance collapsed and the Italian pacification of Libya was complete.
Mukhtar remained a symbol of Arab defiance and was revered as a national hero.
not_established: The source does not say Mukhtar was at Kufra or took part in its defence.
It does not say the fall of Kufra caused his capture, only that one came before the other.
It does not give the month of Kufra's fall, so the exact gap between the two events is unknown.
u:kufra|umar al-mukhtar.context: Kufra is a remote oasis in the south-east of Libya. Mukhtar led Sanusi fighters in Cyrenaica, in the east, against Italian rule.

timeline.what: Al Kufrah, the last Sanusi stronghold, falls to the Italians.
Mukhtar is captured, tried by summary court-martial and hanged.
Sanusi resistance collapses and Italian pacification is completed.

quotes.text: Al Kufrah, the last Sanusi stronghold, fell in 1931, and in September of that year Mukhtar was captured.

doc.t: Libya - The Second Italo-Sanusi War

quotes.text: With the death of Mukhtar, Sanusi resistance collapsed, and the Italian pacification of Libya was completed.

doc.t: Libya - The Second Italo-Sanusi War

u:kufra|umar al-mukhtar.open_question: A detailed history of the 1931 Italian campaign could give the month Kufra fell and say whether Mukhtar's forces were connected to it.

u:gulf of sidra|sidra.headline: "Sidra" here is the name of a place on the Gulf of Sidra coast, so the two ends are related but not the same.
u:gulf of sidra|sidra.explanation: The Gulf of Sidra is the large bay off Libya's northern coast. The 1986 article says U.S. planes attacked a SAM-5 missile site "at Sidra". The summary reads this as a site on the gulf coast. The two names share a root, and the gulf takes its name from the place. The article does not say how far apart they are. The link is probably loose or partly overlapping, and the sources don't settle it. The article is about the U.S.–Libya naval confrontation, not Tripoli itself.
established: The article reports that the U.S. Navy finished its exercise in the Gulf of Sidra in March 1986.
The summary of the article says it describes attacks on a SAM-5 site at Sidra.
not_established: The passages shown do not describe exactly where the town or site of Sidra lies.
The shown text does not state that Sidra is on the gulf coast; that comes from the summary.
The shown text does not mention the SAM-5 attack in detail.
u:gulf of sidra|sidra.context: The Gulf of Sidra (also spelled Sirte) is the bay on Libya's central-northern coast, east of Tripoli. Gaddafi called its northern limit a "line of death".

timeline.what: The U.S. announces its Navy has completed the Gulf of Sidra exercise.

quotes.text: Navy ships and planes had completed their exercise in the Gulf of Sidra and had moved north of the guif region.

doc.t: U.S. SAYS NAVY HAS COMPLETED LIBYAN EXERCISE

u:gulf of sidra|sidra.open_question: A map or fuller text of the article showing where "Sidra" is, and whether it means the gulf or a coastal town, would settle this.

u:ali al-houderi|libyan people's bureau.headline: A January 1980 US memo names Ali al-Houderi as a member of the Libyan People's Bureau who brought a message from Qadhafi.
u:ali al-houderi|libyan people's bureau.explanation: The memo from Brzezinski to President Carter says Ali al-Houderi "of the Libyan People's Bureau" had just returned from Tripoli. He brought a message from Colonel Qadhafi and read it to Brzezinski by phone. So the source ties him directly to the Bureau, which acted as Libya's channel to Washington. This shows how messages from Tripoli reached the US government. The memo gives no detail on his exact job or how long he held it.
established: The memo names Ali al-Houderi as being 'of the Libyan People's Bureau'.
He had returned urgently from Tripoli the day before the memo, January 3, 1980, to deliver Qadhafi's message.
He phoned Brzezinski at noon and read out the message to be passed to President Carter.
not_established: His exact title or rank within the Bureau is not given.
The passage does not say how long he worked there or what else he did.
u:ali al-houderi|libyan people's bureau.context: Libyan "People's Bureaus" were what Libya called its embassies after 1979. The one in Washington was Libya's main official link to the US government.

timeline.what: Houderi returns urgently from Tripoli with Qadhafi's message.
He phones Brzezinski at noon and reads the message; Brzezinski writes to Carter.

quotes.text: Ali al-Houderi of the Libyan People’s Bureau returned urgently from a visit to Tripoli yesterday to deliver a message from Col. Qadhafi.

u:gulf of sidra|sixth fleet.headline: The U.S. Sixth Fleet is tied to the Gulf of Sidra in both sources: as a possible 1981 pressure tactic and in a 1982 announced exercise.
u:gulf of sidra|sixth fleet.explanation: The Gulf of Sidra is the stretch of sea off Libya's coast where the U.S. Sixth Fleet, based in the Mediterranean, operated. A October 1981 Newsweek article says the fleet "could be sent back" there to distract Libya's air force if Libya provoked Sudan or others. A March 1982 Libyan news item reacts to a report that the U.S. Navy secretary said the Sixth Fleet would hold manoeuvres there over six months. Libya's official voice called this a possible prelude to invasion. Together they show the gulf was a point of confrontation between Washington and Tripoli in these years.
established: Newsweek (Oct 1981) says the Sixth Fleet could be sent back into the Gulf of Sidra in response to an attack on Sudan or other Libyan provocations.
JANA (16 Mar 1982), citing French news agency, says Navy Secretary John Lehman announced Sixth Fleet manoeuvres in the Gulf of Sidra over the next six months.
JANA's political editor treated the plan as possible preparation for invasion and called an attack on the gulf an attack on Libyan territory.
not_established: Neither source describes what actually happened at sea in the gulf.
The Lehman announcement is second-hand (via French news agency and Libyan radio), and JANA itself doubted it was confirmed.
The Newsweek plan was a contingency under consideration, not a decision.
u:gulf of sidra|sixth fleet.context: The words "sent back" in the 1981 article refer to earlier U.S. naval exercises in the gulf. Libya claims the gulf as its territorial waters, and the U.S. rejects that claim.

timeline.what: Newsweek reports the Sixth Fleet could be sent back into the Gulf of Sidra if Libya provokes Sudan or others.
JANA responds to a reported U.S. Navy announcement of Sixth Fleet manoeuvres in the gulf.

quotes.text: the USS. Sixth Fleet could be sent back into the Gulf of Sidra to distract Kaddafi’s air force

doc.t: UNITING AGAINST LIBYA

quotes.text: For an aggression on the Gulf of Sidra is an aggression on Libyan territories and on the integrity of Libyan soil.

doc.t: FBIS Daily Report: Middle East & Africa, Vol. V No. 052, 17 March 1982

u:gulf of sidra|sixth fleet.open_question: U.S. Navy records of the actual exercises, and Libyan accounts of them, would show what took place in the gulf after these statements.

u:jamal 'abd an-nasir base|tobruk.headline: Gaddafi spoke at a rally in Tobruk and named the Jamal 'Abd an-Nasir Base, which the link says lies in that region.
u:jamal 'abd an-nasir base|tobruk.explanation: The document is a broadcast of Gaddafi's speech at a Tobruk rally on 28 March 1981. It marked the anniversary of British bases leaving Libya. In the speech he talks about the Jamal 'Abd an-Nasir Base, saying Egyptian pilots graduated there and that it was freed from the British. The text given does not say where the base is. It does not say the base is in Tobruk or that it was once called Al-Adem. The link therefore rests on the base being discussed at a Tobruk rally, plus outside knowledge. The speech shows how the government used Tobruk and this base to tell a story about ending foreign control. It is not about Tripoli itself.
established: Gaddafi gave a speech at a public rally in Tobruk on 28 March 1981, marking the anniversary of the British bases' evacuation.
In the speech he says Egyptian pilots graduated from the Jamal 'Abd an-Nasir Base.
He says the base was liberated from the British and then opened to Arab forces and Egypt.
not_established: The excerpts do not state that the base is in the Tobruk region.
The excerpts do not give the former name Al-Adem.
u:jamal 'abd an-nasir base|tobruk.context: The base was formerly the British Royal Air Force station at El Adem, near Tobruk, and was renamed after Egypt's President Nasser. This is background knowledge, not shown in the source.

timeline.what: According to the speech, British aircraft flew from the base to strike Egypt.
Gaddafi speaks at the Tobruk rally and mentions the base.

quotes.text: Egyptian pilots graduated from the Jamal ‘Abd an'Nasir Base. After we liberated the base from the British we opened it to the Arab forces and to Egypt.

doc.t: FBIS Daily Report: Middle East & Africa, Vol. V No. 060, 30 March 1981

u:jamal 'abd an-nasir base|tobruk.open_question: A map, gazetteer or other record naming the base's location and its former name Al-Adem would settle the link.

u:libya-chad border|matan as sarra airfi.headline: A December 1983 US imagery note places Matan as Sarra airfield in southeast Libya, about 75 nautical miles north of the Chad border.
u:libya-chad border|matan as sarra airfi.explanation: The two ends are a border and an airfield that sits near it, so they are different places. The US imagery note gives the distance directly: the airfield is 75 nautical miles north of the Libya-Chad border. It says the airfield had been under construction since February 1983 and was in its late stages. For Tripoli under Gaddafi, this shows Libya building up military facilities in its remote south, close to the Chad frontier, in the early 1980s. The note does not say why the airfield was built or what it was meant to be used for.
established: The note states Matan as Sarra airfield is 75 nm north of the Libya-Chad border, in southeast Libya.
The airfield had been under construction since February 1983 and was in the late stages.
It was supporting small numbers of light tactical aircraft, with a tent camp and a communications site.
not_established: The note does not say what the airfield was for or whether it was meant for use in Chad.
It does not say exactly where on the border the distance is measured from.
u:libya-chad border|matan as sarra airfi.context: Libya and Chad were in conflict in the 1980s, partly over the border region. This is background, not shown by this note.

timeline.what: Construction of the airfield begins, according to the note.
A tent camp is first seen at the airfield.
The imagery note is issued, with the airfield in late stages of construction.

quotes.text: MATAN AS SARRA AIRFIELD, 75 NM NORTH OF THE LIBYA-CHAD BORDER IN SOUTHEAST LIBYA, HAS BEEN UNDER CONSTRUCTION SINCE FEBRUARY 1983

m:lb-us-embassy-tripoli|palace|event.headline: A march is recorded as having gone from the American Embassy to the People's Palace in Tripoli in 1979, but no passage was available to check.
m:lb-us-embassy-tripoli|palace|event.explanation: The only basis for this link is a short stated reason: a march moved from the American Embassy to the People's Palace. It is attributed to two FBIS daily reports from March 1979, but we could not retrieve any text from them. So we cannot confirm the wording, the date, who marched or why. If the report is right, it shows the two places linked in one public demonstration, with the embassy as the starting point and the former royal palace, then used by the government, as the destination. Treat it as a second-hand note until the original reports are read.
established: The link is recorded as an event: a march from the American Embassy to the People's Palace.
Two FBIS Daily Report issues from March 1979 (Vol. V No. 057, 22 March, and No. 063, 30 March) are cited as sources.
not_established: No source text was retrieved, so the march's date, size, organisers and purpose are not confirmed here.
It is not shown which of the two cited reports describes the march, or whether both do.
The embassy's exact location in 1979 is unclear, so the route is unknown.
m:lb-us-embassy-tripoli|palace|event.context: The People's Palace was the former royal palace renamed after the 1969 coup. The US embassy was burned by protesters on 2 December 1979, later than these March reports. That is a separate event.

timeline.what: FBIS Daily Report (Vol. V No. 057) cited as a source
FBIS Daily Report (Vol. V No. 063) cited as a source
Embassy set on fire by protesters (from the atlas profile, a separate event)

m:lb-us-embassy-tripoli|palace|event.open_question: The text of the two FBIS reports (22 and 30 March 1979) would show whether a march really went from the embassy to the People's Palace, when it happened, and why.

m:abusalim|mk-feb2011|casualties.headline: Human Rights Watch linked Abu Salim to the February 2011 Tripoli crackdown through a reported morgue count and a fear that detainees were held in the prison.
m:abusalim|mk-feb2011|casualties.explanation: The only basis for this link is the reason recorded by the family's researchers. It says Human Rights Watch (HRW) heard that at least 50 bodies lay in the Abu Salim hospital morgue after the shootings of 21–22 February 2011. It also says HRW feared that detainees were held at Abu Salim prison. These are two separate points. One concerns the hospital in the Abu Salim area, and the other concerns the prison. No source text could be retrieved, so we could not check either claim against the HRW pages. The link matters because it ties the prison, long a place of political detention, to the events of the 2011 uprising. It rests on second-hand information and a stated concern, not on confirmed facts.
established: The recorded reason says HRW heard that at least 50 bodies were in the Abu Salim hospital morgue after the 21–22 February 2011 shootings.
The recorded reason says HRW feared detainees were held at Abu Salim prison.
Two HRW pages, dated 22 February and 13 March 2011, are cited.
not_established: No passage was available, so the wording and context of the HRW statements could not be checked.
It is not shown that the bodies came from the prison or that the prison held people arrested in the crackdown. The hospital and the prison are different places.
The cause of death for the bodies in the morgue is not given here.
m:abusalim|mk-feb2011|casualties.context: Abu Salim is both the name of a Tripoli district and of the prison within it. The hospital morgue is in the district, not in the prison.

timeline.what: Security forces fire on protesters in Tripoli.
HRW hears of at least 50 bodies in the Abu Salim hospital morgue.
HRW publishes 'Commanders should face justice for killings'.
HRW publishes 'End violent crackdown in Tripoli'.

m:abusalim|mk-feb2011|casualties.open_question: The full text of the two HRW pages would show exactly what HRW said about the morgue and about detainees at the prison. Hospital records or witness accounts from Abu Salim would show whether anyone was held there during the crackdown.

m:hadba|abu-salim|same-place.headline: Hadba al-Khadra and Abu Salim are neighbouring areas of Tripoli, named together as the last loyalist-held districts in August 2011.
m:hadba|abu-salim|same-place.explanation: The recorded link says they are the same place, but the sources show two separate, neighbouring areas. Both English Wikipedia articles name them side by side as places still held by Gaddafi loyalists in late August 2011. That fits the recorded claim that they are close, but neither article says Hadba al-Khadra belongs to the Abu Salim municipality or lies to its west. That claim rests on the Arabic Wikipedia article, which we did not see. For understanding Tripoli, the link matters because Hadba al-Khadra has no documented prison use before 2011. Its tie to Abu Salim, the main political prison, should not be taken as showing the two sites were the same or that Hadba al-Khadra held prisoners earlier.
established: Both articles describe Abu Salim and Hadba al-Khadra as areas still under loyalist control around 24-25 August 2011.
The two names are treated as separate districts, not as one place.
not_established: The passages do not say that Hadba al-Khadra is part of the Abu Salim municipality.
The passages do not say which side of Abu Salim Hadba al-Khadra lies on.
They say nothing about Hadba al-Khadra being used as a prison before 2011.
m:hadba|abu-salim|same-place.context: Abu Salim is the district best known for the prison where the 1996 massacre took place. The "same-place" label is better read as "adjacent or overlapping areas".

timeline.what: Rebels reportedly believed only the area near Bab al-Azizia, al-Hadhba and Abu Salim were still under Gaddafi's control.
Opposition forces were still trying to fight their way into Abu Salim and Al Hadba al Khadra.

quotes.text: Opposition forces were also still trying to fight their way into the Abu Salim and Al Hadba al Khadra areas, where loyalists were still in control.

quotes.text: the only areas still under Gaddafi's control, other than the immediate neighbourhood of Bab al-Azizia, were al-Hadhba and Abu Salim

doc.t: Libyan civil war (2011) (Wikipedia)

m:hadba|abu-salim|same-place.open_question: The Arabic Wikipedia article, or a municipal boundary map of Tripoli, would show whether Hadba al-Khadra lies inside the Abu Salim municipality.

m:naval-academy|janzour|same-place.headline: The naval academy and the Sidi Bilal port are recorded as lying on the shore at Janzour, but no source text was available to check this.
m:naval-academy|janzour|same-place.explanation: The map links the Libyan Naval Academy to the town of Janzour because the academy and the Sidi Bilal port facility are said to sit on the Janzour shore. This matters because the US air raid of 15 April 1986 hit the Sidi Bilal facility, which the US described as a training site for naval commandos. No source passage could be retrieved for this note. It rests only on the map's own stated reason and the profile text. The link is a place-within-place one (an institution in a town), not a link between two names for the same thing. It is plausible, but this note cannot confirm it from the sources.
established: The map's stated reason says the navy academy and Sidi Bilal port sit on the Janzour shore.
The atlas profiles say the US raid of 15 April 1986 struck the Sidi Bilal port facility.
The profiles say the US described Sidi Bilal as a training site for naval commandos.
not_established: No source text was retrieved, so the location of the academy in Janzour is not checked here.
It is not shown whether the academy and the Sidi Bilal port facility are the same site or two neighbouring sites.
The cited Wikipedia page was not read for this note, so the 'documented' label is unconfirmed.
m:naval-academy|janzour|same-place.context: The 15 April 1986 US air raids on Libya included targets in and near Tripoli. Sidi Bilal is commonly described as a naval training site west of the city.

timeline.what: US aircraft bomb the Sidi Bilal port facility, which the US said trained naval commandos.

m:naval-academy|janzour|same-place.open_question: A map or gazetteer entry placing the academy and Sidi Bilal inside Janzour, or the relevant section of the cited Wikipedia article, would settle whether they are one site or neighbouring ones.

u:otrag rocket test launch|sebha.headline: A German magazine reports that Otrag's rocket test launch on 1 March 1981 took place at the oasis of Sebha, in southern Libya.
u:otrag rocket test launch|sebha.explanation: The 1981 Der Spiegel article, translated by the U.S. government, says Otrag's 12-meter rocket left its launch pad at the oasis of Sebha. Sebha is described as 800 km south of Tripoli. The firm, based in Munich, then left Libya after a dispute among its people. This links a foreign rocket venture to a desert site far from the capital. It shows that Libya hosted this activity during the Gaddafi years. The article is a single, translated source, and the OCR text may contain errors.
established: The article says a 12-meter Otrag rocket was launched at 11:20 am local time on 1 March 1981 from the launching pad at the oasis of Sebha.
Sebha is placed 800 kilometers south of Tripoli.
Otrag, a Munich rocket firm, left Libya after an internal dispute.
not_established: The article does not say who in the Libyan government approved or took part in the launch, in the text given.
The passage does not say whether Sebha was Otrag's only test site in Libya.
u:otrag rocket test launch|sebha.context: Otrag was a private German company that tested low-cost rockets in remote desert areas, including in Libya in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

timeline.what: Otrag rocket launched from the oasis of Sebha at 11:20 am local time.
Otrag leaves Libya after violent internal dispute.
Der Spiegel publishes the article (translated by JPRS on 25 November 1981).

quotes.text: at 11:20 am local time on 1 March 1981, the 12=-meter long rocket left the launching pad at the oasis of Sebha, 800 kilometers south of the Libyan capital of Tripoli

doc.t: Near East/North Africa. Report No. 2442

u:otrag rocket test launch|sebha.open_question: Libyan or Otrag records of the test range, and other press reports, could confirm the exact site and the Libyan role.

u:malta|map:tip.headline: Gaddafi ended a 19-day tour with a stop in Malta, then landed at Tripoli International Airport on the afternoon of 3 July 1978.
u:malta|map:tip.explanation: A Libyan radio report, reprinted in a U.S. daily report, says Gaddafi met Maltese Prime Minister Dom Mintoff in Malta on the morning of 3 July 1978. The same day the radio said he returned to Tripoli at the end of his tour of socialist countries and Malta. It gives his arrival at Tripoli International Airport as 1400. So the link is a trip home from Malta to Tripoli's airport. It shows the airport as the place where Gaddafi's foreign visits began and ended. The report does not say he flew directly from Malta, though that is the likely reading.
established: On 3 July 1978 at 1000, Gaddafi met Maltese Prime Minister Dom Mintoff at Government House in Malta for about an hour and a half.
Libyan radio said he returned to Tripoli that afternoon, at the end of a 19-day tour of socialist bloc countries and Malta.
The report says he arrived at Tripoli International Airport at 1400.
not_established: The text shown does not say he flew directly from Malta to Tripoli, or give the flight details.
The report does not say whether the airport is the same site as the 'military airport' label on the map. It uses only the name Tripoli International Airport.

timeline.what: Gaddafi meets Dom Mintoff at Government House, Malta.
Gaddafi arrives at Tripoli International Airport.
The U.S. FBIS daily report publishes the Libyan radio items.

quotes.text: He arrived at ‘Tripoli International Airport at 1400 today.

quotes.text: returned to Tripoli this afternoon at the end of a 19-day ‘our of peace, friendship and cooperation to socialist bloc countries and Malta.
