m:yarmouk-camp|hamza-camp|control.headline: Yarmouk camp and Hamza camp are linked because both were reportedly held by Haftar forces until the GNA said it retook them in May 2020.
m:yarmouk-camp|hamza-camp|control.explanation: The link comes from one stated reason: Haftar forces held Yarmouk, al-Sawarikh and Hamza camps until the GNA (the Tripoli-based government) said it retook them on 23 May 2020. So the two camps are connected by sharing the same later holder and the same recapture. No source text could be retrieved for this note. It rests only on the recorded reason and the cited Al Jazeera article, which we have not seen. This is a link from after Gaddafi's fall, not from his time. It shows that former Gaddafi-era military sites near Tripoli were still strategically important in later fighting.
established: The recorded reason says Haftar forces held Yarmouk, al-Sawarikh and Hamza camps until the GNA said it retook them on 23 May 2020.
The cited source is an Al Jazeera article dated 23 May 2020, titled 'GNA retakes military camps near Tripoli'.
not_established: No passage from the Al Jazeera article was available, so we could not check the wording or details.
The GNA's claim of recapture is reported as a claim; independent confirmation is not shown here.
Nothing here shows how long each camp was held, or whether they were held in the same way.
m:yarmouk-camp|hamza-camp|control.context: Haftar's forces (the Libyan National Army) fought the UN-backed GNA for Tripoli from April 2019. Both camps were military sites on the edge of Tripoli that existed in Gaddafi's time.

timeline.what: Haftar forces reportedly held the camps during the fight for Tripoli (per the recorded reason).
The GNA said it retook Yarmouk, al-Sawarikh and Hamza camps.

m:yarmouk-camp|hamza-camp|control.open_question: The text of the Al Jazeera article, and independent reports from late May 2020, would show exactly which camps were retaken and how far the GNA's claim held up.

u:gulf of sidra|surt sirte.headline: A Libyan missile site near Surt fired at US aircraft over the Gulf of Sidra in March 1986.
u:gulf of sidra|surt sirte.explanation: The Gulf of Sidra is the large bay of the Libyan coast, and Surt (Sirte) is a coastal town on that shore. The one source here describes a missile site near Surt that fired Soviet-made SA-5 missiles at American fighter jets operating over the Gulf on 24 March 1986. So Surt appears as the launch point and the Gulf as the area of the confrontation. This matters for understanding Libya under Gaddafi because it shows the coast around Surt as a place of armed standoff with the United States. The source says nothing about Tripoli itself.
established: A Libyan missile installation near Surt launched two SA-5 missiles at 07:52 on 24 March 1986 toward US F-14A Tomcats.
The missiles missed and fell into the sea.
Two more SA-5 missiles were fired at 13:52 at F-14s on patrol; the source says an EA-6B Prowler jammed them.
US aircraft had crossed the 'Line of Death' and entered the Gulf of Sidra on 23 March.
not_established: The passage does not give the exact location or size of the missile site beyond 'near Surt'.
It does not say how the town of Surt itself was affected.
Libyan and Soviet claims of hits conflict with the US account; the passage does not settle this.
u:gulf of sidra|surt sirte.context: The Gulf of Sidra lies along Libya's central coast, and Surt sits on its southern shore. Libya claimed the Gulf as territorial waters, which the US disputed.

timeline.what: US aircraft from three carriers cross the 'Line of Death' and operate in the Gulf of Sidra.
Two SA-5 missiles fired from near Surt at F-14s; they miss.
Two more SA-5 missiles fired at F-14s; the source says they were jammed.

quotes.text: A Libyan missile installation near Surt (Sirte) launched two Soviet-made SA-5 "Gammon" surface-to-air missiles (SAMs) at 07:52 (CET), toward F-14A Tomcats of America's VF-102.

m:mk-april1976|mk-hang-1984|context.headline: Both events were state violence against university students in Tripoli, eight years apart, but no source we could read ties them together.
m:mk-april1976|mk-hang-1984|context.explanation: The 1976 crackdown and the 1984 campus hanging both involved students at the university in Tripoli being punished by the state for dissent. The link was recorded as background context, not as a direct chain of cause. The stated reason is that both belong to one campaign against student dissent that made 7 April a date of reprisals. No source passage could be retrieved for this note, so that reason rests only on the atlas's own wording and a cited Asharq Al-Awsat article we could not read. The 1984 hanging is dated to about 16 April, not 7 April, so it is not an anniversary event in the strict sense. Readers should treat this as a reasonable thematic connection, not a proven one.
established: The atlas profile says the 7 April 1976 attack hit student protesters at the universities in Tripoli and Benghazi, with many detained for months.
The atlas profile says Rashid Mansour Kaabar was hanged at the University of Tripoli in April 1984, with other students made to watch.
The atlas profile says the 1984 date is not 7 April and probably falls on 16 April.
not_established: No retrieved source shows that the 1984 hangings were planned as part of one campaign that began in 1976.
The cited Asharq Al-Awsat article on the 7 April hangings was not available to check, so its content is unconfirmed here.
The exact date and campus venue of the 1984 hanging rest on limited newspaper and exile accounts.
m:mk-april1976|mk-hang-1984|context.context: Public hangings of students were used in Libya in 1977 and again in 1984 as a warning to others. This is widely reported background, not evidence from this link's sources.

timeline.what: Students in Tripoli and Benghazi attacked and many detained after protesting.
Students sentenced by a military tribunal in Tripoli hanged in public in Benghazi.
Rashid Mansour Kaabar hanged at the University of Tripoli; another student hanged in Benghazi.

m:mk-april1976|mk-hang-1984|context.open_question: The Asharq Al-Awsat article, and exile or press accounts from April 1984, would show whether contemporaries or the authorities linked the 1984 hangings to the 7 April anniversary and the earlier crackdown.

m:lm-tripoli-international-airport|lh-ca.headline: These two entries describe the same airport, Castel Benito, later Idris el Awal, then Tripoli International Airport.
m:lm-tripoli-international-airport|lh-ca.explanation: Both entries cover one airfield south of Tripoli, opened in 1934 and known under different names over time. The atlas profiles give the same history: Castel Benito, then Idris el Awal in 1951, then Tripoli International after 1969. The CIA-era documents only show that "Tripoli International Airport" was the name in use in 1977 and 1985. They do not state the earlier names or the link to Castel Benito. For readers, it means the airport that received Gaddafi-era visitors was the old Italian field. The two map entries could be merged into one.
established: The documents show Tripoli International Airport in use as a name in 1977 and 1985, receiving a Yugoslav official, President Ceausescu and Sudanese officers.
Both atlas profiles give the same 1934 origin, the same 1951 renaming and the same new terminal on 28 July 1978.
The recorded link cites Wikipedia for the renaming after 1969.
not_established: None of the four passages mentions Castel Benito or Idris el Awal, so they do not confirm the name change.
The exact date or decree of the post-1969 renaming is not given in the sources shown.
Wikipedia, as described, does not mention Gaddafi in its account.
m:lm-tripoli-international-airport|lh-ca.context: Under the monarchy the airport was named after King Idris. After the 1969 revolution the new government dropped that name.

u:abdelbaset al-megrahi|malta.headline: A 1989 CIA cable reports that al-Magrahi, under an alias, visited Malta in late September 1989 and met business contacts and an intelligence chief.
u:abdelbaset al-megrahi|malta.explanation: The cable records what a source ("P/1") told a CIA officer on 16 October 1989. The source said al-Magrahi went to Malta with Lamin Fihma, a former Libyan Arab Airlines manager in Valletta. They met Vincent Vassallo, a Maltese citizen, about a travel agency the three own together, "Medtourist Services." They also met the ESO chief in Malta, and left after two or three days. The source said he got this directly from Vassallo, so it is a second-hand report. It shows a link between al-Magrahi and Malta that was recorded before the Pan Am bombing was solved. It says nothing about Tripoli itself.
established: The cable says its source identified al-Magrahi as travelling to Malta in late September 1989 under the alias 'Abd al Baset Ali.
He travelled with Lamin Fihma, a former Libyan Arab Airlines manager in Valletta.
They met Maltese citizen Vincent Vassallo, who jointly owns the travel agency Medtourist Services with them.
They also met the ESO chief in Malta, and left after two or three days.
not_established: The cable does not show that the trip had anything to do with the Pan Am bombing, despite its title.
It does not independently confirm the trip. The account comes from one source, who heard it from Vassallo.
It does not say what was discussed at the meetings or what the ESO chief's role was.
u:abdelbaset al-megrahi|malta.context: Al-Magrahi was later convicted for the 1988 Pan Am 103 bombing over Lockerbie. Malta was part of the case against him, but this cable does not address that.

u:ghurdabiyah airfield|sirte.headline: A 1982 U.S. imagery note places Ghurdabiyah airfield about 9 nautical miles south of Sirte, on Libya's Mediterranean coast.
u:ghurdabiyah airfield|sirte.explanation: The two places are linked by distance and position. Ghurdabiyah is an airfield in north-central Libya, and the note says it lies 9 nautical miles south of Surt (Sirte). Sirte was the nearest town of note, so it served as the reference point for finding the airfield. The note is mainly about a Libyan Air Force crash near the airfield in 1982. For Tripoli, it shows that Libyan military air activity was spread along the coast and well away from the capital.
established: The note, dated May 1982, states that Ghurdabiyah airfield is in north-central Libya, 9 nm south of Surt, on the Mediterranean coast.
It reports that a possible Fitter aircraft crashed and burned near one end of Ghurdabiyah airfield, apparently while landing.
not_established: The note does not say what the airfield was used for or which units were based there.
It does not describe any link between the airfield and the town of Sirte beyond distance and location.
The coordinates printed in the OCR text are unclear about which set belongs to which airfield, so they should not be relied on here.
u:ghurdabiyah airfield|sirte.context: Surt is another spelling of Sirte, the coastal city east of Tripoli. Neither the airfield nor Sirte is in Tripoli.

u:map:port|tobruk.headline: A 1986 CIA memo discusses Soviet naval use of both Tripoli harbor and Tobruk, but treats them as separate places.
u:map:port|tobruk.explanation: The memo is a CIA assessment of how the Soviet Union might increase its support for Libya after the 1986 clashes with the United States. It mentions Tripoli harbor and Tobruk in the same discussion of Soviet naval activity. Tripoli harbor is where a Soviet ship is said to be stationed and could pass on warnings. Tobruk is a port the Soviet Navy might use more often to resupply and repair ships. The two places are linked only by being named in the same forecast. The memo does not say they are connected in any other way.
established: The memo says a Soviet ship is stationed in Tripoli harbor and is used to pass on early-warning information in crises.
It says the Soviet Navy will probably use Tobruk more regularly to replenish and repair submarines and ships.
It says the Soviets may be willing to keep a naval ship in port to assure Qadhafi of timely warning.
not_established: The memo does not describe any direct operational link between Tripoli harbor and Tobruk.
The Tobruk use is a forecast ('probably'), not a confirmed arrangement.
The memo's summary says it gives no specific places in Tripoli, and 'Tripoli harbor' is the only Tripoli location mentioned in the passages shown.
u:map:port|tobruk.context: Tobruk is a port in eastern Libya, far from Tripoli in the west. Both were Libyan harbors that the Soviet Navy could, in principle, visit.

u:balidogle|bur acaba.headline: A 1999 CIA report links a flight into the Balidogle air base to a Libyan-Iraqi look at uranium deposits at Bur Acaba in Somalia.
u:balidogle|bur acaba.explanation: One CIA information report, dated 13 March 1999, mentions both places. It says an aircraft landed at the former Somali air base at Balidogle on 7 March 1999. On board was a 15-person delegation of specialists in extracting uranium from ground deposits. The report ties this to earlier Libyan activity: five Libyans had arrived on 5 March to discuss extracting uranium from deposits at Bur Acaba. So Balidogle is where the delegation landed, and Bur Acaba is where the uranium was said to be. The report does not say the delegation went on to Bur Acaba. This matters for Tripoli because it suggests Libya was looking for uranium in Somalia, far from the capital.
established: On 7 March 1999 an aircraft carrying a 15-person delegation arrived at the former Somali air force base at Balidogle.
The delegation was described as technical specialists in extracting uranium: seven Iraqis, four Iranians and four Libyans.
Five Libyans had arrived in Somalia on 5 March 1999 to evaluate extracting uranium from deposits at Bur Acaba, about 180 km west of Mogadishu.
The report calls the Balidogle arrival 'earlier activity connected to this delegation' in its wording about the Libyans' visit.
not_established: The passage does not say the delegation travelled from Balidogle to Bur Acaba.
It does not show that uranium was actually found, extracted or moved.
It is a single, not-finally-evaluated intelligence report, and the source of its information is not given in the passage.
u:balidogle|bur acaba.context: Balidogle (often spelled Baledogle) is a former air base in southern Somalia. Bur Acaba (Buurhakaba) is a town in the same region, west of Mogadishu.

timeline.what: Five Libyans arrive in Somalia to discuss extracting uranium at Bur Acaba.

u:map:tajoura-nuclear|soviet union.headline: A 1984 US memo says the Soviet Union supplied Libya's nuclear research center at Tajura.
u:map:tajoura-nuclear|soviet union.explanation: The document is a US talking-points memo about Libyan-Belgian nuclear talks. In its background section it states that the Tajura research center "was supplied by the Soviet Union." It adds that Libya had many problems dealing with the Soviets. This shows the Soviet Union was Libya's main nuclear partner, and that Libya looked to other countries partly out of dissatisfaction. The memo gives no detail on what was supplied or when. It is one US government assessment, not a Soviet or Libyan record.
established: The memo states that the Libyan nuclear research center at Tajura was supplied by the Soviet Union.
It says Libya had encountered many problems dealing with the Soviets.
It says the Soviet Union had agreed to supply two 440-megawatt power reactors, but no final agreement had been reached.
not_established: The memo does not say what equipment or services the Soviet Union supplied, or when.
It does not describe the Tajura site itself or its operation.
It is a single US source from 1984, and gives no evidence for its claim.

u:french embassy in tripoli|map:lb-us-em.headline: The only source mentions the French Embassy in Tripoli as a talking point; it says nothing linking it to the US Embassy.

u:libyan people's bureau|map:lb-us-embas.headline: The Libyan People's Bureau (Libya's mission in Washington) and the US Embassy in Tripoli are separate offices in different countries, linked only by US–Libya tensions.
u:libyan people's bureau|map:lb-us-embas.explanation: The one document is a 1980 memo from Secretary of State Muskie to President Carter. It concerns a suspected Libyan-linked shooting of a Libyan student dissident in Colorado and the US response to a Libyan campaign of intimidation. The Libyan People's Bureau it refers to is Libya's mission in Washington, not anything in Tripoli. The US Embassy in Tripoli is the American counterpart, but the memo does not describe it. At most, the two stand on opposite sides of the same strained relationship. The link should not be read as a match between places.
established: The memo is dated October 17, 1980 and was sent from Secretary of State Muskie to President Carter.
It reports a suspected Libyan-linked shooting of a Libyan student dissident in Colorado and outlines US responses to Libyan intimidation.
The Libyan People's Bureau mentioned is in Washington, not Tripoli.
not_established: The memo does not show any action by, or at, the US Embassy in Tripoli.
It does not show that the two offices dealt with each other directly.
u:libyan people's bureau|map:lb-us-embas.context: "People's Bureau" was the name Libya gave its embassies abroad after 1979. The US Embassy in Tripoli was closed in 1980 and its staff withdrawn.

u:billy carter|charter oil.explanation: A New York Times article of 23 July 1980 links President Carter's brother Billy to Charter Oil, a U.S. oil company. The article places this inside a wider report on a Libyan plan to win influence in the United States. It matters because it shows how Libya's oil sales could reach into American politics. It says an intelligence report described an individual with political ties, in financial difficulty, who was in communication with Charter Oil.
The article says the report did not name the President's brother as a recipient of Libyan payments.

u:qadhafi|ronald reagan administration d.headline: A 1986 news report says a Reagan White House plan aimed to unsettle Gaddafi, though the Senate found no decision to plant false stories.
u:qadhafi|ronald reagan administration d.explanation: The only source is a 1986 Associated Press article. It follows a Washington Post report that the Reagan administration ran a disinformation campaign against Gaddafi in August 1986. The plan, as the article describes it, was meant to make him think he faced internal opposition and a possible U.S. military move. The Senate Intelligence Committee said it found no policy decision to plant false stories in U.S. media. So the link is real, but it rests on a disputed press report. The sources do not show how far the campaign was carried out. It matters for Tripoli because it shows how Washington tried to pressure Gaddafi in the tense years after the 1986 U.S. strikes on Libya.
established: A Washington Post report described an August 1986 disinformation campaign aimed at Qaddafi.
The AP article says the plan aimed to make Gadhafi believe he faced internal opposition and a possible U.S. military move.
The Senate Intelligence Committee found no policy decision by the administration to plant false stories in U.S. media.
not_established: Whether the campaign was actually carried out, or how much of it.
Whether any false stories reached U.S. or Libyan audiences.
What effect, if any, it had on Gaddafi or on life in Tripoli.

u:1986 us strike|gulf of sidra.headline: In a March 1988 speech, Gaddafi tied the 1986 American strikes to the clash at the Gulf of Sidra and the "line of death."
u:1986 us strike|gulf of sidra.explanation: The 1986 US strike and the Gulf of Sidra are linked in Gaddafi's own words. In this speech he said Americans tried to cross the "line of death" at the entrance to the Gulf, and that scores of Libyans died there in 1986. He held the anniversary event on the Gulf's shore on purpose, to show Libya would defend it. The speech shows how the Libyan leadership told the story. He said that in 1986 the Gulf of Sidra was 'marked and colored' with the blood of scores of martyrs.

The speech was given at Ra's al-Unuf, on the shore of the Gulf of Sidra, as a deliberate show of resolve.

u:map:wheelus|umm aitiqah ecm site.headline: Two 1982 imagery notes place an electronic jamming site beside Umm Aitiqah airfield. Neither note names Wheelus or Okba Ben Nafi.
u:map:wheelus|umm aitiqah ecm site.explanation: Both notes are the same 22 September 1982 U.S. imagery note, found in two CIA files. They say a Soviet-type BIG CAP B radar jammer was newly identified at the Umm Aitiqah electronics countermeasures (ECM) site. The site is described as next to Umm Aitiqah airfield, on the northwest edge of Tripoli. The link to Okba Ben Nafi (the former Wheelus base) depends on Umm Aitiqah airfield being that same base, and the passages do not say so. Without that step, the notes show only that the ECM site sits beside an airfield. The link is therefore a possible one that someone still has to check against another source. It matters because it would show where Libya kept foreign-supplied electronic defences near Tripoli.
established: Doc 1 and Doc 2 both say the ECM site is adjacent to Umm Aitiqah airfield.
Both place the site on the northwest edge of Tarabulus (Tripoli).
Both report the first identification of a BIG CAP B jammer in Libya, and the first outside the Soviet Union and Warsaw Pact countries.

u:public tile and construction materials.headline: A 1982 study named Ra's al-Dali as a possible stone source for Libya's tile and decorative stone industry, including a Tripoli plant.
u:public tile and construction materials.explanation: A Libyan newspaper article from 1982, translated in a U.S. report, describes a study of stone sites for the decorative stone and tile industry. Ra's al-Dali in al-'Aziziyah was one of three hopeful sites, with dark brown, grey and black stone. The link to the Tripoli plant comes from the reader's summary of the article, which says the stone was to be cut and polished at a plant in Tripoli and at al-'Aziziyah. The passage we have does not show that sentence or name the plant, so the link is plausible but not confirmed here. It matters because it shows how Libya tried to replace imported marble with local stone in the early 1980s.
established: A 1981-82 study covered 10 sites in the western and central provinces for raw materials for the decorative stone and tile industry.
Ra's al-Dali in al-'Aziziyah was named as one of three hopeful sites, with dark brown, grey and black stone.
Detailed geological and technical studies and semi-industrial tests were reported to support the suitability of the raw materials.
not_established: The passage shown does not mention the Tripoli plant, or say that Ra's al-Dali stone would be cut and polished there.
It does not say whether quarrying or processing actually began.

timeline.what: The center studied 10 possible stone sites in western and central Libya.
A Libyan newspaper article reported the results, naming Ra's al-Dali as a hopeful site.
The article appeared in the U.S. translation report.

quotes.text: Ra's al-Dali in al-'Aziziyah where the colors are dark brown, grey and black.

doc.t: Near East/North Africa Report No. 2700

u:public tile and construction materials.open_question: The full article text, or company records, would show whether the Tripoli plant was named as the place where Ra's al-Dali stone was cut and polished, and whether that happened.

u:ankara|libyan people's bureau.headline: Two Libyans arrested in Ankara in April 1986 said the Libyan People's Bureau there gave them the grenades.
u:ankara|libyan people's bureau.explanation: A November 1986 CIA paper on Libyan support for terrorism describes an event in Ankara. On 18 April 1986, two Libyans were stopped as they approached the US Officers Club with six Soviet-made grenades. They claimed the grenades came from the Libyan People's Bureau in Ankara. The link is therefore a claim by the arrested men, reported by the CIA, and not a finding the paper confirms. It matters for Tripoli because it shows how Libya's overseas offices, which answered to the government in Tripoli, were suspected of backing attacks after the US raid of April 1986.
established: On 18 April 1986 two Libyans were apprehended near the US Officers Club in Ankara, reportedly about to attack with six Soviet-made fragmentation grenades.
The two men claimed they received the grenades from the Libyan People's Bureau in Ankara.
Two other Libyans were arrested soon afterward as possible accomplices.
not_established: The document does not independently confirm that the Bureau supplied the grenades; it reports only what the men claimed.
It does not say who in the Bureau, if anyone, was involved, or whether orders came from Tripoli.
It does not give the outcome of any investigation or trial.
u:ankara|libyan people's bureau.context: People's Bureaus were what Libya called its embassies after 1979. Ankara is the capital of Turkey. The US air raid on Libya took place in mid-April 1986.

timeline.what: US raid on Libya, which the CIA paper treats as the backdrop to the retaliation attacks.
Two Libyans arrested in Ankara near the US Officers Club with six grenades.
Two more Libyans arrested as possible accomplices.
CIA note attaching the paper on Libyan state support for terrorism.

quotes.text: two Libyans were apprehended as they approached the US Officers Club in Ankara to launch an attack with six Soviet-made fragmentation grenades they claimed they had received from the Libyan People's Bureau in Ankara

doc.t: ATTACHED ARE THE TWO THINGS YOU ASKED FOR EARLIER THIS WEEK FOR YOUR UPCOMING SPEECHES -- THE NUMBERS ON SOVIET AID TO NICARAGUA, ANGOLA, ETC., AND THE EVIDENCE ON SYRIAN, LIBYAN, AND IRANIAN STATE SUPPORT FOR COUNTERTERRORISM.

u:ankara|libyan people's bureau.open_question: Turkish court or police records on the arrests, and any later US or Turkish findings, could show whether the Bureau really supplied the grenades.

u:abeche|map:tajura.headline: A 1983 CIA imagery graphic shows Tajura as a Libyan heavy-lift hub and Abeche as a Chadian airlift point in the same conflict map.
u:abeche|map:tajura.explanation: The two places appear together on one CIA graphic about the Libya-Chad conflict from August 1983. Tajura, near Tripoli, is marked for "heavy-lift activity". Abeche, in eastern Chad, is marked with "probable Chadian airlift activity". The map puts both inside one picture of Libyan logistics and support. The OCR text does not state that anything moved from Tajura to Abeche. The link is that both sit within the same wider war effort, which shows Tripoli's military sites were tied to the fighting in Chad.
established: One August 1983 CIA/NPIC graphic on the Libya-Chad conflict labels Tajura for heavy-lift activity.
The same graphic labels Abeche (spelled variously in the OCR) with probable Chadian airlift activity.
The document's summary links Tajura to tank-related activity and to other Libyan sites such as Sebha, Kufra and Gharyan.
not_established: The passage does not say that Tajura sent equipment or supplies to Abeche.
It does not say Libya, rather than Chad, ran the airlift at Abeche; the label reads 'probable Chadian airlift activity'.
The claim that Abeche was being 'resupplied' by Libya is not supported by the text we have.
u:abeche|map:tajura.context: Libya and Chad fought over northern Chad and the Aouzou Strip through the 1980s, and Libya backed forces there with supplies sent from its own territory.

timeline.what: NPIC prepares a graphic on the Libya-Chad conflict showing Tajura and Abeche among its labelled sites.

quotes.text: TAJURA pred HEAVY-LIFT ACTIVITY

doc.t: LIBYA-CHAD CONFLICT

quotes.text: PROBABLE CHADIAN AIRLIFT ACTIVITY

doc.t: LIBYA-CHAD CONFLICT

u:abeche|map:tajura.open_question: The full, unredacted pages of the graphic and any written text that goes with it might show whether supplies really moved from Tajura to Abeche.

m:artillery-school|hamza-camp|control.headline: Two camps near Tripoli are linked because one news report says the GNA took both from Haftar forces on 23 May 2020.
m:artillery-school|hamza-camp|control.explanation: The link rests only on the reason recorded by the site: that the Government of National Accord (GNA) took both the Artillery and Missile School (also called al-Sawarikh or Missile camp) and Hamza camp from Haftar forces on 23 May 2020. We could not retrieve any text from the cited Al Jazeera article, so we cannot check this ourselves. The link is about a shared event in the 2019–2020 fighting around Tripoli, not a direct tie between the two sites. It sits outside the Gaddafi years themselves. It does show that camps built or used in that era were still military ground decades later. The atlas also notes it is unclear whether the OpenStreetMap "Artillery and Missile School" is the same place as al-Sawarikh camp.
established: The recorded reason says both camps were taken by the GNA from Haftar forces on 23 May 2020.
The cited source is an Al Jazeera article dated 23 May 2020, titled 'GNA retakes military camps near Tripoli'.
not_established: No passage from the article was available, so the claim could not be checked against the text.
It is not shown that the OpenStreetMap 'Artillery and Missile School' is the same site as al-Sawarikh camp.
Nothing here shows a link between the two camps under Gaddafi, or how each was used then.
m:artillery-school|hamza-camp|control.context: From April 2019 forces under Khalifa Haftar fought the UN-recognised GNA for control of Tripoli. The GNA recaptured several positions south of the city in 2020.

timeline.what: GNA reported to have retaken both camps from Haftar forces.

m:artillery-school|hamza-camp|control.open_question: The full Al Jazeera article, or another report from the same day, should be checked to confirm that both camps are named. Satellite imagery or a gazetteer could settle whether al-Sawarikh camp is the OpenStreetMap Artillery and Missile School.

m:fashloum|zawiyat-dahmani|same-place.headline: Fashloum and Zawiyat al-Dahmani are two neighbouring Tripoli districts, with Fashloum lying inland to the south; they are not the same place.
m:fashloum|zawiyat-dahmani|same-place.explanation: The link was recorded as "same-place", but the sources describe two separate suburbs that sit next to each other. Zawiyat al-Dahmani lies between the coast and Fashloom, and Fashloom lies inland to its south. They shared a similar fate in 2011: both were reported cordoned off by security forces on 22 February, and both were reported under opposition control when the Battle of Tripoli began. The older village of Shar al-Shatt, site of the 1911 battle, is tied to Zawiyat al-Dahmani only. So this is a link between neighbours, not between two names for one place.
established: Fashloom lies inland to the south of Zawiyat al-Dahmani, and southeast of Martyrs' Square (DOC 2).
Zawiyat al-Dahmani lies between the coast to the north and Fashloom to the south (DOC 3).
Both areas were reported cordoned off by security forces around 22 February 2011 (DOC 2, DOC 3).
During the August 2011 Battle of Tripoli, fighting was reported in both, listed as separate neighbourhoods (DOC 1).
not_established: Nothing shows the two names refer to the same place; the sources treat them as different districts.
The sources do not give exact boundaries between the two districts.
The sources do not say whether the 1911 Shar al-Shatt village extended into Fashloom.
m:fashloum|zawiyat-dahmani|same-place.context: Wikipedia articles are secondary summaries. The stated reason for the link only shows that the districts are neighbours.

timeline.what: Battle and massacre at Shar al-Shatt, in what is now Zawiyat al-Dahmani (DOC 3).
Both districts reported cordoned off by security forces (DOC 2, DOC 3).
Anti-Gaddafi street protest in Fashloom (DOC 2).
Fighting and opposition control reported in both districts during the Battle of Tripoli (DOC 1).

quotes.text: It lies inland to the south of the suburb of Zawiyat al-Dahmani, and southeast of the Martyrs' Square.

doc.t: Fashlum (Wikipedia)

quotes.text: It lies between the coast to the north, and the suburb of Fashloom to the south.

doc.t: Zawiyat al-Dahmani (Wikipedia)

m:fashloum|zawiyat-dahmani|same-place.open_question: The link would be better recorded as "neighbouring" or "nearby". A detailed map of Tripoli's district boundaries would show where one ends and the other begins.

u:tarhuna|tripoli students' tree plantin.headline: A 1981 Libyan student paper says Tripoli students dug planting holes in the Tarhunah and Ghariyan agricultural projects.
u:tarhuna|tripoli students' tree plantin.explanation: One 1981 article, from the Tripoli paper Al-Talib, describes a student employment program. It says students of the city of Tripoli dug holes for planting trees in the Tarhunah and Ghariyan agricultural projects. Tarhunah is a town outside Tripoli, so this shows city students sent to farm work in the surrounding area. The source is state-run press about student self-sufficiency, so it shows how the program was presented. It does not give numbers, dates or names of schools for this task.
established: A 1981 press article says students of the city of Tripoli dug holes for planting trees in the Tarhunah and Ghariyan agricultural projects.
The article places this within a wider student employment program covering afforestation, construction, cleaning and excavation across Libya.
The same article separately lists Tarhunah students among those working in Awbari.
not_established: The article says the students dug planting holes. It does not say they planted the trees themselves.
It does not give the date, number of students, schools involved or how many trees.
It is a state-aligned account, and nothing independent confirms what was done or whether the work was voluntary.
u:tarhuna|tripoli students' tree plantin.context: In the early 1980s Libyan schools and institutes ran student work programs alongside classes, and the press presented them as national service.

timeline.what: Student employment program reported in Tripoli's Al-Talib, including tree-planting work at Tarhunah.
Article appears in translation in Near East/North Africa Report No. 2414.

quotes.text: The students of the city of Tripoli also dug holes for planting trees in the Tarhunah and Ghariyan agricultural projects.

doc.t: Near East/North Africa Report No. 2414

u:tarhuna|tripoli students' tree plantin.open_question: School records or other 1981 reports could show which Tripoli schools went to Tarhunah, when, and whether the trees were planted.

m:jdeida|abusalim|transfer.headline: Former detainees say some prisoners were held at both Jdeida and Abu Salim, but no source text was available to check this.
m:jdeida|abusalim|transfer.explanation: The atlas links Jdeida prison and Abu Salim prison because former detainees describe being held in both places in Tripoli. The recorded reason also mentions interrogation elsewhere, including in Benghazi, followed by transfer to Jdeida. No source passage could be retrieved for this note, so it rests only on the stated reason and the three sources cited. Taken at face value, the link shows that both prisons were part of the same system for holding political detainees. It does not show which way prisoners were moved between them, when, or how often.
established: The recorded reason says former detainees describe being held in both Jdeida and Abu Salim.
The recorded reason says they describe interrogation elsewhere, including at the 7 April prison in Benghazi, before transfer to Jdeida.
Two interviews on Tarikhi and a 2006 Human Rights Watch report are cited as the sources.
not_established: No source text was available, so none of these claims could be checked against the original wording.
It is not shown whether people were moved directly between Jdeida and Abu Salim, in which order, or on what dates.
The exact building at Jdeida is not documented in these sources.
m:jdeida|abusalim|transfer.context: Abu Salim was the main prison for political prisoners in Tripoli under Gaddafi. Jdeida was a separate civilian prison in the city.
m:jdeida|abusalim|transfer.open_question: The two Tarikhi interviews (Abubaker Shareef and Majda Sahli) and the Human Rights Watch report would need to be read. They could show who was held in each prison, in what order, and in which years.

m:lh-hani-battle-monument|hani|same-plac.headline: A memorial to the 1911 Hani battle is placed in the Hani district of Tripoli, but no source text was available to check this.
m:lh-hani-battle-monument|hani|same-plac.explanation: The two entries appear to describe a monument and the district it stands in. The only reason given is that the monument stands in the Hani district. That is a reasonable link, since a monument is normally in a place with the same name. No source passage could be retrieved, so this note rests on the atlas's own profiles and the recorded reason. The atlas itself says no page it opened names Hani as the Libyan name for the Shar al-Shatt battle. It also says the monument's date and builder are unknown. The link is therefore a sensible inference, not a documented fact. The "documented" label looks too strong.
established: The atlas profile says OpenStreetMap maps two memorial points in the Hani area, named for the Battle of Hani.
The recorded reason is that the monument stands in the Hani district.
not_established: No source text was retrieved, so the cited Wikipedia page could not be checked for this link.
The atlas says no page it opened names Hani as the Libyan name for the Shar al-Shatt battle.
The memorial's date, builder and the year of the battle it marks are unknown.
m:lh-hani-battle-monument|hani|same-plac.context: The Shar al-Shatt fighting of October 1911 was part of the Italian invasion of Libya, when Italian forces held Tripoli and Ottoman and Arab forces counter-attacked from the oasis.

timeline.what: Fighting at Shar al-Shatt, with Italian reprisals after it (per the atlas profile).

m:lh-hani-battle-monument|hani|same-plac.open_question: A map or gazetteer naming the district Hani, and a source that links the Hani memorial to the Shar al-Shatt battle, would settle this. So would a record of who built the monument and when.

u:abdessalam jalloud|map:palace.headline: Two 1979–80 radio and news-agency reports say Jallud received foreign visitors at the People's Palace in Tripoli.
u:abdessalam jalloud|map:palace.explanation: Abd as-Salam Jallud was a senior Libyan leader, and two official reports place his meetings with visiting foreigners at the palace. In July 1979 he received Iran's Mohammed Montazeri at "Ash-Sha'b Palace". In April 1980 he received Pakistan's envoy Agha Shahi at "Al-Chaab Palace". These are two spellings of the same name, People's Palace. The reports suggest the palace was a regular place for receiving official guests. They do not say whether Jallud worked there or what the building was like inside.
established: Tripoli radio (4 July 1979) said Jallud received Mohammed Montazeri, an Iranian revolutionary leader, at Ash-Sha'b Palace.
JANA (26 April 1980) said Jallud received Pakistan's Agha Shahi at Al-Chaab Palace.
Both reports name the same Jallud, with the full name 'Abd as-Salam Ahmad Jallud, and describe him as Staff Major.
not_established: The reports do not say the palace was Jallud's office or home.
They do not say that Ash-Sha'b and Al-Chaab are the same building. That follows from the two spellings of the name and from the map record.
They give no description of the building or its exact location in Tripoli.
u:abdessalam jalloud|map:palace.context: Ash-Sha'b and Al-Chaab are different English spellings of the Arabic word for "the people", so both names mean People's Palace.

timeline.what: Jallud receives Iran's Mohammed Montazeri at Ash-Sha'b Palace.
Jallud receives Pakistan's Agha Shahi at Al-Chaab Palace.

quotes.text: Staff Major 'Abd as-Salam Ahmad Jallud received this morning at Ash-Sha!b Palace Shaykh [as heard] Mohammed Montazeri

doc.t: FBIS Daily Report: Middle East & N. Africa, Vol. V No. 130, 5 July 1979

quotes.text: The meeting, which took place at Al-Chaab Palace, was attended by the foreign secretary.

doc.t: FBIS Daily Report: Middle East & N. Africa, Vol. V No. 085, 30 April 1980

u:abdessalam jalloud|map:palace.open_question: Other records, such as dated visit reports or photographs, could show how often Jallud used the palace and whether he had an office there.

m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-faculty-of.headline: The Faculty of Engineering is recorded as one of the faculties that made up the University of Tripoli, created in 1973.
m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-faculty-of.explanation: This link says the Faculty of Engineering is part of the University of Tripoli, so the two places belong together as faculty and university. The only support is a one-line reason citing a Wikipedia page. We could not retrieve any passage from that page, so we have not checked the wording ourselves. The link is plausible, but nothing here shows when engineering joined or how the building related to the main campus. It helps the reader see that the engineering departments sit within the wider university, whose students and campus figure in the events of the 1970s and 1980s.
established: The record states that the Faculty of Engineering became part of the University of Tripoli when it was created in 1973.
The atlas profile of the university says the Tripoli faculties of the University of Libya became the University of Tripoli in 1973.
not_established: No source text was available to check the stated reason, so the Wikipedia citation is unverified here.
The sources do not say when the engineering faculty was founded or where its building stood; its map position is only the centre of four mapped department points.
Nothing shows that engineering students took part in the 1976–77 protests or the 1984 events.
m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-faculty-of.context: The University of Libya had faculties in Tripoli and Benghazi. In 1973 these were split into separate universities, and the Tripoli one was later renamed Al Fateh University.

timeline.what: The Tripoli faculties of the University of Libya become the University of Tripoli.
The university is renamed Al Fateh University (per the atlas profile).

m:lb-university-of-tripoli|lb-faculty-of.open_question: The University of Tripoli Wikipedia page, or a university history or catalogue, could confirm when the engineering faculty was founded and how it joined the university in 1973.

u:gafsa|tunisia.headline: Qafsah (Gafsa) is a town in Tunisia, and Libyan broadcasts in February 1980 treated the events there as part of a Tunisian uprising.
u:gafsa|tunisia.explanation: Qafsah is a place inside Tunisia, so this link is one of simple geography: a part and the country that contains it. The February 1980 report shows Tripoli radio praising a "revolution" across Tunisia, with Qafsah named first among the towns. It also shows Colonel Qadhdhafi talking about the Qafsah incident and saying Libya had no hand in it. For Tripoli, it shows how the Libyan state spoke publicly about its neighbour and how it answered claims that it had trained saboteurs. The text is poorly scanned, so some of Qadhdhafi's wording is broken.
established: Tripoli's Voice of the Arab Homeland radio, on 9 Feb 1980, named Qafsah among Tunisian towns in a 'revolution' it said covered all of Tunisia.
Qadhdhafi, speaking at Benghazi on 10 Feb, discussed the 'Qafsah incident' in Tunisia and, as summarised, denied any Libyan hand in it.
The same digest has him blaming the Tunisian regime and France for the situation.
not_established: The document does not say what actually happened at Qafsah.
It does not prove who was behind the incident; Libya's denial is only Qadhdhafi's own statement.
The OCR is garbled, so Qadhdhafi's exact words are uncertain.
u:gafsa|tunisia.context: In January 1980 armed men attacked the town of Gafsa in Tunisia. Tunisia blamed Libya, and relations between the two countries became very tense.

timeline.what: Tripoli radio commentary praises the Tunisian 'revolution', naming Qafsah and other towns.
Qadhdhafi, in Benghazi, comments on the Qafsah incident and denies a Libyan role.
FBIS publishes the digest of these broadcasts.

quotes.text: embracing the masses in Qafsah, Safqis, Susah, Qabis, Naftah and in all the Tunisian towns and villages

doc.t: FBIS DAILY REPORT—Middle East & N. Africa, Vol. V No. 029, 11 February 1980

u:gafsa|tunisia.open_question: Tunisian and Libyan records of the January 1980 Gafsa events, and independent accounts of who trained and sent the attackers, would settle the question of Libyan involvement.

m:mitiga|souq-al-juma|same-place.headline: Mitiga airport is in the Souq al-Juma area of Tripoli, but the one source given does not state this or mention the Rada force.
m:mitiga|souq-al-juma|same-place.explanation: The record says Mitiga airport lies in Souq al-Juma and that the Rada force has run the airport and a prison since 2011. The only passage we have is about the August 2011 fighting. It names Mitiga airport and Suk al-Juma side by side as places where fighting went on. That shows they were close enough to be part of the same battle. It does not say the airport is inside the district. The passage says nothing about Rada, a prison, or who has run the airport since 2011. The two Wikipedia pages cited as sources were not among the passages provided. The link is plausible, and it matches the usual description of Mitiga as being in the Souq al-Juma area. Here it is an inference from nearby mentions, not something a source states.
established: The Battle of Tripoli article reports that fighting in Suk al-Juma, Araba district and Mitiga International Airport continued during the August 2011 uprising.
Rebels advanced toward the Mitiga airbase and reportedly surrounded the airport to try to obtain its surrender.
not_established: The passage does not say Mitiga airport lies within Souq al-Juma. It only lists the two together.
Nothing in the passage mentions the Rada force, a prison at Mitiga, or who has controlled the airport since 2011.
The two cited Wikipedia pages were not provided, so their wording could not be checked.
m:mitiga|souq-al-juma|same-place.context: Mitiga is the former Wheelus Air Base, on the eastern side of Tripoli. It is commonly described as being in the Souq al-Juma area. In later years the Rada group, a armed force, has been widely reported to control the airport.

timeline.what: The US hands over Wheelus Air Base, which becomes the Libyan air force's Okba Ben Nafi base.
Fighting in Souq al-Juma and at Mitiga airport continues during the battle for Tripoli.

quotes.text: The entire Tajura district was captured by rebel forces, while fighting in Suk al-Juma, Araba district and Mitiga International Airport continued.

doc.t: Battle of Tripoli (2011) (Wikipedia)

m:mitiga|souq-al-juma|same-place.open_question: The Wikipedia pages on Mitiga International Airport and Souq al-Juma, or a map of district boundaries, would show whether the airport lies inside the district. A recent report on Rada would be needed to confirm the airport and prison claim.

u:ghurdabiyah air base|gulf of sidra.headline: Libyan Su-22 fighters that clashed with U.S. Navy jets over the Gulf of Sidra in 1981 took off from Ghurdabiyah Air Base, near Sirte.
u:ghurdabiyah air base|gulf of sidra.explanation: One source, a Wikipedia article on the 19 August 1981 incident, links the two places. It says two Libyan Su-22 fighters took off from Ghurdabiyah Air Base near Sirte. They were then sent toward U.S. aircraft in the Gulf of Sidra, the waters Libya claimed as its own. The base was where the Libyan response started. The Gulf was where the confrontation happened. The article is about the wider dispute and does not concern Tripoli itself. It helps show how Libya's military reacted to U.S. naval exercises on its coast.
established: The article says two Su-22 fighters took off from Ghurdabiyah Air Base near the city of Sirte.
It says these fighters were the ones involved in the 19 August 1981 incident, in which two Libyan Su-22s were shot down by U.S. F-14 Tomcats off the Libyan coast.
It reports that Libya claimed the whole Gulf of Sidra as its territory, and that Gaddafi called the claimed line the "Line of Death" in 1973.
not_established: The passage does not say whether Ghurdabiyah was the base for other Libyan air activity over the Gulf.
It rests on one Wikipedia article, which in turn cites a U.S. Navy officer's account. No Libyan or primary military record is shown.
u:ghurdabiyah air base|gulf of sidra.context: The Gulf of Sidra lies off Libya's central coast. The U.S. did not accept Libya's claim to it and held naval exercises there on that basis.

timeline.what: Libya claims the Gulf of Sidra as its territorial waters.
Two Su-22s take off from Ghurdabiyah and are shot down by U.S. F-14s off the Libyan coast.

quotes.text: two Sukhoi Su-22 fighters had taken off from Ghurdabiyah Air Base near the city of Sirte.

doc.t: Gulf of Sidra incident (1981) (Wikipedia)

u:ghurdabiyah air base|gulf of sidra.open_question: Libyan air force records or pilot accounts could confirm the base and show how the order to launch was given.

u:libyan people's bureau washington|us c.headline: The US ordered Libya's Washington People's Bureau closed in May 1981, and a Libyan broadcast reacted to that closure.
u:libyan people's bureau washington|us c.explanation: The Libyan People's Bureau in Washington was Libya's embassy-type office in the United States. The one source here is a May 1981 radio digest. It says the US administration closed the bureau and expelled its members, and that a people's committee issued a statement afterward. So the two ends are an office and the act of closing it, not two separate things. The source is a summary of broadcasts, so it gives few details. It does not say why the US acted or how the expulsion was carried out. It matters for Tripoli because it shows how Gaddafi's government handled foreign relations through "people's bureaus" abroad, and how that could lead to a break with the US.
established: A 13 May 1981 FBIS digest covers a people's committee formed at the Libyan People's Bureau in Washington.
The link as read from the document is that the US administration closed the bureau and expelled its members, which prompted the committee's statement.
not_established: The summary gives no reasons for the US decision and no exact date of the closure.
It does not say how many people were expelled or where they went.
It says nothing specific about Tripoli sites or people.
u:libyan people's bureau washington|us c.context: In May 1981 the US ordered Libyan diplomats out of Washington and closed the bureau. Relations between the two countries were poor at the time.

timeline.what: The US closes the Libyan People's Bureau in Washington and expels its members (as reported).
FBIS publishes a digest covering the people's committee statement.

u:libyan people's bureau washington|us c.open_question: The US State Department announcement of the closure, and the full text of the committee's broadcast, would give the date, the stated reasons and the details.

u:china lake california|fort collins, co.headline: A 1981 news report ties a Fort Collins shooting case to a man at China Lake, through phone records.
u:china lake california|fort collins, co.explanation: The article is about the October 1980 shooting of a Libyan student, Faisal Zagallai, in Fort Collins, Colorado. Investigators said they linked Mr. Tafoya, the man charged in Colorado, to Douglas Haden, a civilian at the China Lake naval weapons center in California. The link is said to rest on phone company records and Mr. Tafoya's telephone book. The two places are connected only through the people in the case. Neither place is in Tripoli. The article places Edwin Wilson, a former CIA agent, in Libya, and that is the Libyan thread behind the case.
established: The article reports a Colorado court case in Fort Collins involving Mr. Tafoya.
Investigators said Mr. Tafoya's telephone book and phone company records showed contact with Mr. Haden.
The passage says the evidence linking Tafoya to Haden was found in Tafoya's telephone book, and that phone records showed several calls.

u:libyan people's bureau london|london.headline: The Libyan People's Bureau was Libya's official mission in London, and the June 1980 demonstration and arrests happened at or near it.
u:libyan people's bureau london|london.explanation: The Bureau was Libya's embassy-like office in London, so this link is mainly a place-and-institution one. A second report describes a students' march from the Jamahiriyah Students Union building to the Bureau. For Tripoli, it shows how the government used its London office as a focus for politics and pressure abroad. The report is from Libyan state news and is one-sided.

u:gafsa|qadhafi.headline: In 1981, Tunisian President Bourguiba told a US official that Qadhafi's efforts to destabilize Tunisia lay behind the Gafsa incident.
u:gafsa|qadhafi.explanation: The Gafsa events were an armed attack on the Tunisian town of Gafsa in 1980. A US memo of a 23 May 1981 meeting records President Bourguiba describing the incident and linking it to Qadhafi's efforts to destabilize Tunisia. The link is Bourguiba's own account, written down by a US note-taker. It shows how Tunisia's leaders saw Libya's government as a threat to its neighbours. It also shows how that view was put to the United States when Tunisia asked for defence support.
established: Bourguiba described the Gafsa incident together with Qadhafi's efforts to destabilize Tunisia, in a meeting with Mr. West of the US Defense Department.
He said the insurgents used Soviet arms and killed 45 new inductees, and that Libyan radio told false stories of other cities joining.
He said all the conspirators were caught, and thirteen were condemned to hang and executed.
Bourguiba later mentioned that US support came at the time of Gafsa, and the memo also records Tunisian complaints about Qadhafi's 'exportation of thugs, terrorists, and assassins'.
not_established: The memo gives no independent evidence that Qadhafi or the Libyan government organised, trained or armed the Gafsa insurgents; it only records what Bourguiba said.
The passages do not say how the insurgents were connected to Libya.
The memo is a US summary, not a verbatim record, and the passage is cut off after 'Qadhafi had gone …'.
u:gafsa|qadhafi.context: The Gafsa raid took place in January 1980. It is widely described as an attack by armed Tunisian dissidents who had been trained in Libya, and it badly strained relations between Tunisia and Libya.

timeline.what: Gafsa incident in Tunisia, as described by Bourguiba.
Bourguiba tells Mr. West, a US defence official, about Gafsa and Qadhafi's efforts to destabilize Tunisia.

u:gragur prison tripoli|khamis brigade.headline: A Wikipedia article says the Khamis Brigade was reported to have killed 17 prisoners in a makeshift prison near Gragur, Tripoli, in August 2011.
u:gragur prison tripoli|khamis brigade.explanation: The link rests on one sentence in a Wikipedia article about the Khamis Brigade, the elite security unit led by Khamis Gaddafi. The article places the reported killing of 17 prisoners "near Gragur in Tripoli" on or around 21 August 2011, as rebel forces were closing in on the capital. It describes the place as a makeshift prison, not a long-standing prison building. The article is a secondary summary and gives no eyewitness account, names or sources for this claim. It is best read as a reported event, and it shows how the brigade's detention and killings in Tripoli were recalled at the end of the Gaddafi period.

It does not say who the 17 prisoners were or who gave the order.

m:wheelus|lh-mellaha-wheelus-mitiga|same.headline: Both entries describe one airfield east of Tripoli, known as Mellaha, then Wheelus, then Okba Ben Nafi, and now Mitiga.
m:wheelus|lh-mellaha-wheelus-mitiga|same.explanation: The two entries are the same place under different names. The Wikipedia article says the airfield was built by the Italians in 1923 as Mellaha. It later became the US base called Wheelus. After the Americans left it was renamed Okba Ben Nafi, and in 1995 it became the civilian Mitiga airport. The atlas has one entry for the base as Gaddafi's government took it over and another that follows the whole history. They should be read as one place. The 1970 handover was an early and important step for the new government.
established: The airport was built in 1923 by the Italian Air Force as Mellaha.
The US used it from 1943, and it became Wheelus Air Base after a US airman killed in 1945.
When the Americans left, it was renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base, and the Libyan and Soviet air forces used it.
In 1995 it became a civilian airport with its current name, Mitiga.
not_established: The passage does not give an exact handover date. The atlas notes that sources differ between March and 11 June 1970.
The passage ties the departure to the 1969 coup and the end of the lease. It does not say how the handover was negotiated.
m:wheelus|lh-mellaha-wheelus-mitiga|same.context: Wheelus was the largest US base in Libya. Its closure in 1970 was widely seen as a sign of the new government's break with the West.

u:abdullah senussi|map:abusalim.headline: Abdullah Senussi, Gaddafi's intelligence chief, is linked by two Wikipedia articles to the June 1996 killings at Abu Salim prison in Tripoli.
u:abdullah senussi|map:abusalim.explanation: Two Wikipedia articles connect Senussi to the Abu Salim prison massacre. One says he "was involved" in it. The other says he is suspected of involvement. Abu Salim was a prison in Tripoli, so the link ties a senior security figure to a major event at a known Tripoli place. Both sources are general background articles. They do not describe what he did, and neither cites a court finding on this charge. The reader should treat the link as an allegation or suspicion, not a proven fact.
established: The Senussi article states that in June 1996 he was involved in the Abu Salim prison massacre.
The Politics of Libya article lists his past history as including suspicion of involvement in the massacre.
Both sources describe him as a senior intelligence figure and Gaddafi's brother-in-law.
not_established: What his role was, such as giving orders, planning or being present.
Whether any court has ruled on his part in the massacre. The passages mention only a French conviction in absentia for the UTA bombing.
The two articles differ in wording: one says he was involved, the other says he is suspected of involvement.
u:abdullah senussi|map:abusalim.context: The Abu Salim massacre is widely reported as the killing of many prisoners at the Tripoli prison in June 1996. Senussi was later detained and tried in Libya after 2011.

m:as-bab|as-benashour|event.headline: Two sites hit in the same US air raid on Tripoli on 15 April 1986: Gaddafi's compound, and homes in Ben Ashour that were apparently hit by mistake.
m:as-bab|as-benashour|event.explanation: Both entries describe one event, the US air raid on Tripoli in April 1986. Bab al-Aziziya, Gaddafi's compound, was the main target. The Ben Ashour homes were a residential area where bombs also fell, with civilian deaths and damage near the French embassy. The recorded reason says the bombs meant for the compound landed on Ben Ashour. That helps explain why the raid is remembered for harming ordinary families as well as hitting a military and political site. No source text could be retrieved for this note, so it rests on the stated reason and the two atlas profiles.
established: Both entries place the sites in the same US raid on Tripoli in April 1986.
The atlas profile for Ben Ashour cites a 1987 press report in CIA files that one F-111 mistakenly hit a residential area near the French embassy.
The atlas profile for Bab al-Aziziya names the compound as the main target of the raid.
not_established: No source passage was available here, so the claim that the Ben Ashour bombs were aimed at Bab al-Aziziya was not checked against the cited MERIP or Wikipedia pages.
The exact number of aircraft involved, and which one caused the Ben Ashour damage, is not shown here.
The number of people killed in Ben Ashour is not given in the material provided.
m:as-bab|as-benashour|event.context: The US carried out air strikes on Tripoli and Benghazi on 15 April 1986. It said the strikes were a response to Libyan-linked terrorism.

timeline.what: US aircraft raid Tripoli; Bab al-Aziziya is the main target and bombs also fall in Ben Ashour.
A press report in CIA files says one F-111 mistakenly hit a residential area near the French embassy.

m:as-bab|as-benashour|event.open_question: The MERIP article (1986) and the CIA-file press reports would need to be read to confirm that the Ben Ashour bombs were meant for Bab al-Aziziya, and to give the casualty figures.

u:map:abusalim|tripoli prison.headline: A 1971 US report mentions a plan to free 150 prisoners from "the Tripoli prison," but never names Abu Salim.
u:map:abusalim|tripoli prison.explanation: The 1971 US status report describes a plan to land European mercenaries by sea and free 150 political prisoners from "the Tripoli prison." It says two attempts were made, in early 1971, and that neither landed. The text does not name the prison. Abu Salim is a well-known Tripoli prison, so it could be the one meant, but this document does not say so. The "Tripoli Prison" entry here looks like a general label, not a named site. The link is a possibility only.
established: A US report from May 1971 says the CIA uncovered a plan to land a small European mercenary force by sea in Libya.
The plan aimed to release 150 political prisoners from "the Tripoli prison."
The report says two attempts were made, in late January/early February and in late March/early April, and that neither landed mercenaries.
not_established: The document never names Abu Salim.
It does not say which Tripoli prison was meant, or whether there was only one.
It does not say where the prisoners were held in practice or whether the raid came close to the prison.
u:map:abusalim|tripoli prison.context: Abu Salim is widely known as a major prison in Tripoli, but its use in 1971 is not shown by this document.

Second attempt
US status report written

u:map:abusalim|tripoli prison.open_question: A record naming the prison in this 1971 plan, such as a fuller CIA report or Libyan prison records, would show whether it was Abu Salim.

u:chad|kufra airfield.headline: US imagery notes from 1982 and 1983 show Libyan aircraft at Kufra airfield, possibly preparing for operations in Chad.
u:chad|kufra airfield.explanation: Kufra airfield is in southern Libya, far from Tripoli. Two US photo-interpretation notes describe Libyan combat aircraft there. Both say the aircraft may be linked to operations in Chad. The 1983 note describes Kufra as a major support and logistics base and puts it about 200 nautical miles northeast of the Chad border. Neither note confirms that any aircraft actually flew into Chad. For Tripoli, the link shows how Libya's air power was positioned in the south for the Chad conflict.
established: December 1982: five more SF.260 light ground attack aircraft were seen at Kufra, bringing the total there to nine. The note says this suggests preparations may be under way for operations in Chad.
September 1983: fifteen Flogger fighters were at Kufra, and ten appeared to be preparing to leave.
The 1983 note says Kufra is about 200 nautical miles northeast of the Chad border and serves as a major support and logistics base in southern Libya.
not_established: Neither note confirms that aircraft from Kufra attacked targets in Chad.
The 1983 note says the Floggers may simply have been returning to their home base at Benina; a strike into Chad is only called something that cannot be ruled out.
The 1982 summary describes Kufra as a staging base, but the visible text mainly says the build-up 'suggests' preparations; the passage given is cut off.
u:chad|kufra airfield.context: Libya and Chad were in conflict in the early 1980s, and Libya had forces in northern Chad. This background is not drawn from the two notes.

timeline.what: Note reports five more SF.260 aircraft at Kufra, nine in total, suggesting possible operations in Chad.
Note reports fifteen Flogger fighters at Kufra, ten probably preparing to depart, either to Benina or for a mission into Chad.

u:faya-largeau|sebha.headline: A 1983 U.S. imagery note says tanks heading for Faya Largeau in Chad probably set out from the Sebha area of Libya.
u:faya-largeau|sebha.explanation: Sebha is a town in south-west Libya. Faya Largeau is a town in northern Chad. A U.S. photo-interpretation note from August 1983 spotted a convoy of tanks and trucks in Chad, heading for Faya Largeau. The analysts judged that its equipment probably came from the Sebha area, because tanks and crates were seen at an armored storage area there. This shows Sebha as a likely supply point for Libya's involvement in the Chad war. It helps explain how the Libyan state, governed from Tripoli, backed forces far from the capital. The passage we have for the second document does not show the claim about flights from Sebha.
established: A convoy with six medium tanks on heavy transporters was photographed about 100 nautical miles northwest of Faya Largeau, heading toward it.
The analysts said the convoy's equipment was probably deployed from the Sebha area in west-central Libya.
Their reasoning was that boxes and crates were scattered near T-54/55 tanks at the Sebha armored storage area.
not_established: The note says 'probably'. It does not prove the convoy started at Sebha.

The passage we have does not show the claim of Libyan flights carrying troops and arms from Sebha to Faya-Largeau. Only a summary of the second document (a TV news transcript) was available, and it does not mention Sebha.
Neither document describes anything in Tripoli.
u:faya-largeau|sebha.context: Libya backed rebel forces in northern Chad in the early 1980s, and Faya Largeau was a main objective in 1983.

u:libyan embassy london|london.headline: The Libyan Embassy was in London, and a 1984 shooting of a police officer there led Britain to break relations with Libya.
u:libyan embassy london|london.explanation: The Libyan Embassy in London was Libya's official mission in the British capital, so the link between the two is simply where the building stood. The one source here is a 1984 New York Times article. It refers to "the London Libyan Embassy shooting" of a British police constable and the break in relations with Britain. This matters because the event soured Libya's ties with Britain and Western allies. It also shaped how Tripoli's government dealt with the outside world. The article is mainly about US plans to press allies, and it says little about the embassy as a place.
established: A 1984 US news summary ties a shooting of a British police constable to the Libyan Embassy in London.
The same summary says the shooting was followed by a diplomatic break between Britain and Libya.
The passages mention a 'London mess' and about 8,000 British workers in Libya who were not expected to leave.
not_established: The passages shown do not describe the shooting itself, such as who fired or the date.
They do not say the demonstrations took place outside the embassy. That detail comes from the summary and not from the quoted text.
The article does not discuss the embassy building or daily life in Tripoli.

u:faisal zagallai|qadhafi.headline: Prosecutors suggested Qaddafi ordered the 1980 shooting of Libyan student Faisal Zagallai, who had criticised him; this was a claim, not a proven fact.
u:faisal zagallai|qadhafi.explanation: Faisal Zagallai was a Libyan graduate student at Colorado State University. He was shot in October 1980 and lost the sight of one eye. Two news reports from the trial of Eugene Tafoya say Zagallai openly criticised Qaddafi. One report says prosecutors claimed Qaddafi ordered him killed. The other says only that Tafoya "may have been hired" because of that criticism. The link shows how Libya's government was accused of reaching dissidents abroad. It does not happen in Tripoli itself. Tafoya was acquitted of attempted murder, and neither report shows that Qaddafi gave an order.
established: Zagallai, a graduate student at Colorado State University, was shot in October 1980 and lost the sight of one eye.
Both reports describe him as an outspoken critic of Qaddafi.
Prosecutors at Tafoya's trial claimed Qaddafi ordered Zagallai killed (Doc 1), or suggested Tafoya may have been hired because of the criticism (Doc 2).
Tafoya, a former Green Beret, said he was carrying a CIA message and that the shooting happened in a struggle. He was acquitted of attempted murder.
not_established: Neither report shows evidence that Qaddafi or the Libyan government ordered or paid for the shooting.
The reports do not say who, if anyone, hired Tafoya, and the CIA claim is only Tafoya's own account.
Doc 2 is worded more cautiously than Doc 1 and does not say Qaddafi gave the order.

It says students of the city of Tripoli dug holes for planting trees there.

It does not say whether the two projects were run together or were connected in any other way.
It does not say whether students chose to take part or were required to.

u:public tile and construction materials.headline: The passages shown do not mention the Tripoli tile company at all, so they do not support this link to Ra's al-Dali.
u:public tile and construction materials.explanation: The article is about a 1981-82 study of local stone sites in western and central Libya. Ra's al-Dali in al-'Aziziyah is one of three promising sites. The study found it could supply dark brown, grey and black stone for polished slabs and tiles. The study suggested a tile plant could be set up in al-'Aziziyah.
not_established: The passages never name the Public Tile and Construction Materials Company.
They do not say that samples from Ra's al-Dali were cut or polished in Tripoli, or at any company plant.

u:kufra|matan as sarra.headline: A January 1984 CIA imagery report says a Libyan mechanized infantry unit moved from Kufra to the Matan as Sarra area in southern Libya.
u:kufra|matan as sarra.explanation: The two places are linked by a military movement. A U.S. imagery briefing dated 3 January 1984 says a mechanized infantry unit left Kufra and deployed to the Matan as Sarra area. It gives the unit's equipment as at least 14 BTR-60 armored vehicles, 35 support vehicles and 15 heavy transporters. Other elements stayed behind at a site called Al Jawf. Both places are in southern Libya, far from Tripoli. The link shows how Libya's forces in the south were supported and moved around during the Chad conflict. The document does not mention Tripoli.
established: The briefing says ground activity was highlighted by a mechanized infantry unit deploying from Kufra to the Matan as Sarra area.
The unit is described as BTR-60 equipped, with at least 14 BTR-60, 35 support vehicles and 15 heavy-lift transporters.
The unit was reported near Matan as Sarra Military Camp 1. Remaining elements stayed at Al Jawf military installation.
The same report notes the first deployment of Flogger aircraft to Matan as Sarra airfield.
not_established: The exact dates of the move are not legible in the passages, because the dates are blanked or garbled in the OCR.
The passages do not give the reason for the move or the unit's name.
Nothing here links either place to Tripoli.
u:kufra|matan as sarra.context: In the early 1980s Libya had forces in northern Chad and used bases in southern Libya to support them.

u:aozou airfield chad|matan as sarra air.headline: A 1983 U.S. imagery note says Matan as Sarra airfield in Libya could serve as a base to protect or support Aozou airfield in Chad.

u:chad|faya-largeau.explanation: Faya-Largeau is a town in Chad. The one source here is a U.S. monitoring digest of Libyan state radio from 10 August 1983. This shows how Tripoli's media presented the Chad war to listeners at home. The passage reports a claim. It does not confirm the capture, and it does not describe Libya's own role in any detail.
established: Tripoli Domestic Service, a Libyan state radio service, broadcast on 10 August 1983 that Faya-Largeau had fallen to forces of the 'Chad popular revolution'.
The claim came from Abderahman Moussa, described as the representative in France of the 'legitimate Chad Union Government'. He cited an AFP dispatch.
A second Tripoli broadcast said Goukouni Oueddei led the attack on Faya-Largeau.
The opposing side is described as the 'mutinous forces of Hissein Habre'.
not_established: The passage does not show whether Faya-Largeau was actually captured or held. The claim comes from one side and the broadcast is a report of it.
The text shown does not describe what Libya did on the ground. The summary says only that Libya backed the forces.
The passage is cut off, so the rest of the second broadcast is not seen.

u:edwin wilson|frank terpil.headline: Edwin Wilson and Frank Terpil were former CIA men, business partners, and co-defendants indicted in 1980 over work for Libya.
u:edwin wilson|frank terpil.explanation: Several 1981–82 newspaper items name Wilson and Terpil together as ex-CIA agents who worked with Qaddafi's Libya. One report says a federal grand jury indicted both on 25 April 1980. Another says they were partners with Kevin Mulcahy in a firm called International Technology, Inc., and that Mulcahy had earlier worked for an export firm owned by the two. The link matters because it shows how private deals by ex-agents tied the U.S. to Libya's security and training work. The sources report allegations; they are not court findings.
established: A 1981 AP/New York Times report says Wilson and Terpil were indicted by a federal grand jury on April 25, 1980, on charges tied to Libya: supplying explosive timers, setting up a terrorist training school, and conspiring to commit a political assassination.
A 1981 article on Hersh's story names both as former CIA undercover agents and as Mulcahy's partners in a firm called Inter-Nation Technology, Inc. (OCR text; the name may be garbled).
A 1981 Washington Post Magazine profile says Mulcahy worked for an export firm owned by Wilson and Terpil and describes alleged explosives shipments and training for Libya.
1982 reports say a House committee tentatively found no official CIA involvement in their Libyan activities, but that some CIA employees had contact with them while still at the agency.
not_established: The sources do not prove the charges; they report indictments and allegations.
The passages do not show that the CIA directed or approved their Libyan work; the CIA and the House committee said it did not, though the committee saw remaining discrepancies.
The passages give no detail on where in Tripoli any activity took place, apart from a reported laboratory 'near Tripoli' in one article.

u:gulf of sidra|libyan flight informatio.headline: A 1982 US memo describes both the Gulf of Sidra and the Libyan Flight Information Region as areas Libya claimed or controlled near its coast.
u:gulf of sidra|libyan flight informatio.explanation: The memo is background for a US plan for naval operations near Libya. It lists the Gulf of Sidra claim and the Libyan Flight Information Region (FIR) side by side, as part of the area where the US operated. The FIR is an airspace zone where flight information and alerting services are provided. The memo does not say the two are formally linked. Both places show how Libya's claims reached out from Tripoli over the sea and sky. The link is a shared setting in one document, not a stated connection.
established: In October 1973 Libya claimed the Gulf of Sidra as internal waters, north to latitude 32°30'.
The memo says the Libyan FIR extends north to latitude 34°20'.
The memo says the US held naval exercises in the Gulf of Sidra, some of which crossed into waters Libya claimed.
A November 1972 Libyan communique said foreign aircraft could not fly within 100 miles of Tripoli.
not_established: The memo does not say the Gulf and the FIR are legally or administratively connected.
It does not say the US operations were conducted inside the FIR. That is the AI's reading, not the document's wording.
It does not show what happened in either place in practice beyond the summary given.
u:gulf of sidra|libyan flight informatio.context: The Gulf of Sidra is a large bay on Libya's Mediterranean coast. The US disputed Libya's claim to it and held exercises there to assert freedom of navigation.

u:gabes|tunis.headline: A 1977 U.S. cable links Gabes, where a U.S. ship was present, to Tunisia's dispute with Libya, but it does not tie Gabes to Tunis itself.
u:gabes|tunis.explanation: The cable is from the U.S. embassy in Tripoli in May 1977. It reports a Libyan official complaining about a U.S. naval unit at Gabes during a dispute with Tunisia over the sea floor off the coast, where Libya was exploring for oil. Gabes is a Tunisian port. Tunis is Tunisia's capital. The passage given names "Tunisians" and "Tunisian media", not the city of Tunis. So the link is a loose one: both places belong to the Tunisian side of the dispute. It shows how Libya's quarrel with its neighbour reached the U.S. embassy in Tripoli. It does not show a direct tie between the two cities.
established: On 30 May 1977 the U.S. embassy in Tripoli reported a Libyan protest (demarche) by Under Secretary Atrash about a continental shelf dispute with Tunisia.
Atrash said Libya was surprised by a U.S. naval unit at Gabes. He said it encouraged the Tunisians to act aggressively and asked that it be withdrawn.
Atrash warned that Libya would 'fight back in self defense' if Tunisia attacked.
not_established: The passage does not mention the city of Tunis. The link comes only from 'Tunisians' and 'Tunisian media'.
It does not say what the ship was doing at Gabes, or whether it was withdrawn.
The passage is cut off, so the rest of the cable and any U.S. reply are not shown.
u:gabes|tunis.context: Gabes is a port city in southern Tunisia, and Tunis is the national capital. Libya and Tunisia disputed their offshore boundary in the 1970s, and the case was later taken to the International Court of Justice.

u:libyan people's bureau|suriname.headline: A 1987 CIA memo discusses the Libyan diplomatic presence in Suriname, but the passages shown do not mention a "People's Bureau" or any suspicious activity.
u:libyan people's bureau|suriname.explanation: The memo asks whether Libya had more people in Suriname than a normal embassy-sized group. It says the case for only a normal diplomatic presence is strong: no more than a dozen or so Libyan diplomats and dependents. It also says some contradictory reporting suggests a small number of extra Libyans may have arrived to support the government's fight against an insurgency. The AI's claim that its officials "may be engaged in suspicious activities" goes further than the text, which only raises the possibility of extra, unverified personnel. The link is therefore thin. It shows Libya's reach abroad from Tripoli, but not a documented Bureau activity.

not_established: The passages shown do not name the Libyan People's Bureau in Suriname or say its officials did anything suspicious.
