u:qadhafi|vesco.headline: A 1986 newspaper column says intelligence reports describe Robert Vesco, a fugitive financier, as an adviser who often visited Qaddafi in Libya.
u:qadhafi|vesco.explanation: The only source is a 1986 Jack Anderson column in the Washington Post. It says intelligence reports name Vesco as an adviser to Qaddafi and that he travelled to Libya often to consult with him. The column offers this as "a hint" about how Qaddafi stood up to the oil companies. It gives no dates, places in Tripoli, or details of the advice. The text is damaged by scanning, and the first name "Robert" does not appear in it. The link is second-hand: a columnist reporting what unnamed intelligence reports said. It is useful as a sign of the outside figures around Qaddafi's government, but it does not prove what Vesco actually did.
established: A 1986 Washington Post column says intelligence reports identify Vesco as an adviser to Qaddafi.
According to the column, Vesco went to Libya frequently to consult with Qaddafi.
The column describes Vesco as sought by the U.S. Justice Department, though the scanned text is partly garbled.
not_established: The intelligence reports themselves are not shown, so their dates and reliability are unknown.
The column does not say when Vesco advised Qaddafi, what he advised on, or whether he influenced oil policy.
It does not say where in Libya, or whether in Tripoli, the meetings took place.
u:qadhafi|vesco.context: Robert Vesco was an American financier who fled U.S. fraud charges in the early 1970s. He is widely reported to have lived in several countries afterwards.

It also ties the Tajura suburb to the hospital through events of 2019, not through the Gaddafi years. No passage from the cited HRW report or the Wikipedia page could be retrieved. It cites an HRW piece of 3 July 2019 and the Wikipedia page on the hospital.

Nothing here connects the link to the Gaddafi period.

u:gulf of sidra|tripoli flight informati.headline: The Gulf of Sidra is a stretch of sea off Libya; the Tripoli Flight Information Region is the airspace over and around it that the U.S. Navy named in its 1986 flight notices.
u:gulf of sidra|tripoli flight informati.explanation: In January and March 1986 the U.S. Navy filed notices with international aviation authorities for carrier flight operations in the "Tripoli flight information region". Newspaper reports on the same exercises said the ships and planes might also enter the Gulf of Sidra, which Libya claims as its own waters and airspace. The two places are therefore connected through the same 1986 U.S. naval exercises. They are not the same place. One is a body of water, and the other is an air-traffic zone that reaches out from Libya for many miles. The articles do not say exactly how the zone and the gulf overlap.
established: The Navy's notice said carrier flight operations would run for a week within the Tripoli Flight Information Region, described as airspace extending scores of miles from Libya (Docs 1, 3).
A Pentagon spokesman said aerial maneuvers would take place "in the Tripoli flight information region" and in international waters (Doc 4).
Qaddafi claims the whole Gulf of Sidra and its airspace. The U.S. recognizes only 12 miles of territorial waters, and the warships were authorized to sail in the gulf (Docs 1, 3).
Sources said fleet commanders had been cleared to exercise inside the Gulf of Sidra (Doc 4).
not_established: No article says that the Gulf of Sidra lies inside the Tripoli Flight Information Region, or where its boundary runs.
The reports do not say which flights actually entered the gulf. Doc 1 says planes would begin north of it and work south later.
The articles are press accounts based on anonymous officials. They are not the Navy notice itself.
u:gulf of sidra|tripoli flight informati.context: The Tripoli Flight Information Region is an air-traffic control zone for Libya, so its name does not mean the events took place near the city of Tripoli. The Gulf of Sidra is on Libya's central coast.

timeline.what: U.S. Navy fighters shot down two Libyan fighters above the Gulf of Sidra (Docs 1, 3, 4).
The Washington Post reports that the Navy filed a notice for a week of carrier flight operations in the Tripoli Flight Information Region (Docs 1, 3).
The New York Post reports a new notice of aerial maneuvers in the Tripoli region, and that ships were cleared to enter the Gulf of Sidra (Doc 4).
A Washington Post report describes flight operations off Libya and Scud missile firings into the Gulf of Sidra (Doc 2).

u:marsa matruh|tobruk.headline: Marsa Matruh and Tobruk are named together as the two meeting places of Gaddafi's 1989 talks with Egyptian President Mubarak.
u:marsa matruh|tobruk.explanation: In a October 1989 interview, Gaddafi speaks of his talks with President Mubarak "in Marsa Matruh and Tobruk". He says these sessions led to practical steps between the two countries. Marsa Matruh is on the Egyptian side of the border and Tobruk is on the Libyan side. The link is one of shared events, not of one place causing the other. It shows how Libya and Egypt rebuilt relations in 1989, which affected ordinary people on both sides of the border. The document does not mention Tripoli.
established: The interviewer asks about Gaddafi's talks with Mubarak "in Marsa Matruh and Tobruk".
Gaddafi calls the Marsa Matruh and Tobruk sessions a realistic start that produced agreement on concrete measures for citizens of both countries.
The interview was published in Cairo's Al-Musawwar on 27 October 1989 and translated by FBIS.
not_established: The document does not give the dates of the two meetings or say which took place first.
It does not list the specific measures agreed.
It says nothing about Tripoli or about life in Tripoli.
u:marsa matruh|tobruk.context: Marsa Matruh is a coastal town in Egypt. Tobruk is a coastal town in eastern Libya, not far from the Egyptian border.

timeline.what: Gaddafi and Mubarak hold talks at Marsa Matruh and Tobruk.

u:aozou strip|sebha.headline: A 1982 CIA memo links Sabha, a Libyan training base, to Chadian recruits who were to return to northern Chad and the Aozou Strip.
u:aozou strip|sebha.explanation: The memo says Libya was recruiting Chadians in northern Nigeria and flying them via Benin to Sabha, a training base in southern Libya. They were to go back to northern Chad afterward. It also says military activity in the Aozou Strip was growing. The link is therefore indirect: Sabha is where recruits were trained, and the Aozou Strip is part of the area they were expected to return to. This helps show that Libya's Chad policy depended on bases deep inside Libya, far from Tripoli. The memo does not say that any recruits trained at Sabha went to the Aozou Strip itself.
established: The memo calls Sabha 'a training base in southern Libya'.
Chadians recruited in Maiduguri, Nigeria, were being shipped through Lagos to Cotonou, Benin, and flown from there to Sabha.
The recruits were to return later to northern Chad.
The memo says military activity in the Aozou Strip was growing but not yet substantial.
not_established: The memo does not say that Sabha trainees were sent to the Aozou Strip specifically.
It gives its conclusion about a planned harassment campaign as a present judgment, not as proven fact.
The source of the intelligence is blacked out, so how reliable it is cannot be checked here.
u:aozou strip|sebha.context: The Aozou Strip is a strip of land along the northern edge of Chad that Libya occupied from the 1970s. Sabha (Sebha) is a large town in southern Libya.

timeline.what: National Intelligence Council memo reports Libyan recruiting of Chadians, training at Sabha, and growing activity in the Aozou Strip.

u:kufra airfield|libyan threat to sudan.headline: A 1983 CIA imagery note links Libyan aircraft at Kufra Airfield to preparations for possible hostile action against Sudan.
u:kufra airfield|libyan threat to sudan.explanation: END B is the title of the same 1983 CIA photo-interpretation note that discusses Kufra Airfield. The note says Libyan preparations for "possible hostile actions" were seen at Kufra and Benina airfields and at Al Kufrah barracks. At Kufra it reports a third Blinder medium bomber had arrived. It also mentions Flogger fighters, though the text there is garbled. Kufra is in southeastern Libya, far from Tripoli. The note shows how Libya's military was positioned in the early 1980s, but it does not tie Tripoli to this activity.
established: The note, dated 18 February 1983, says Libyan preparations for possible hostile actions were observed at Kufra and Benina airfields and at Al Kufrah barracks.
A third Blinder medium bomber is reported to have deployed to Kufra Airfield, probably from Umm Aitiqah airfield.
Egyptian reaction to the Libyan preparations is reported at Aswan airfield.
not_established: The text does not say what action was planned, or that Sudan was the target; Sudan is named only in the title.
Much of the document is redacted, and the text about the fighters at Kufra is garbled by the scan.
Nothing here places the decisions or forces in Tripoli.

m:lh-ain-zara-battle|lh-shar-al-shatt|ev.headline: Two battles near Tripoli in the 1911 Italian invasion, Shar al-Shatt in October and Ain Zara in December, are linked as parts of one campaign.
m:lh-ain-zara-battle|lh-shar-al-shatt|ev.explanation: The link is that both battles were fought on the edge of Tripoli during the Italian invasion of 1911. No source passage could be retrieved for this note, so it rests on the recorded reason and the two place profiles. Those profiles give Shar al-Shatt as 23–26 October 1911 and Ain Zara as 4 December 1911, which is about six weeks later. Together they show the Italians first holding the city against a hard attack, then pushing out to take the oasis south of it. The sources do not say whether one battle caused the other.
established: The atlas profiles date Shar al-Shatt to 23–26 October 1911, on Tripoli's outskirts, and Ain Zara to 4 December 1911, about 8 km south of Tripoli.
Both profiles describe Ottoman and Arab forces fighting Italian forces in the same invasion.
The recorded cited sources are the Wikipedia articles on each battle.
not_established: No source text was available to check the link directly, and the Wikipedia articles were not read here.
The sources do not say that either battle caused or shaped the other.
Casualty figures for both battles are uncertain and vary between sources.
m:lh-ain-zara-battle|lh-shar-al-shatt|ev.context: Italy declared war on the Ottoman Empire in September 1911 and landed at Tripoli in October. The war ended in 1912 with Italy taking Libya.

timeline.what: Battle at Shar al-Shatt on the edge of Tripoli; Italians retook the area on the evening of 23 October.

u:aswan high dam|kufra.headline: A 1985 newspaper column links Kufra's water scheme to Egyptian fears about the Nile and the Aswan High Dam.
u:aswan high dam|kufra.explanation: The column says Egypt feared Qaddafi might extend the Kufra pipeline to the Nile in northern Sudan. It also reports a separate plan to bomb the Aswan High Dam, which a defecting Libyan pilot confirmed. Qaddafi himself spoke of linking Lake Nasser, the lake behind the dam, to al-Kufra. The link is real but loose: the column joins the two as parts of a wider water-and-security worry. It does not say the Kufra pipeline was part of the dam plot. It helps show how Libya's water project was read abroad as a political threat.
established: The column says Egyptians feared a secret plan to extend the pipeline from Kufra south and then east to the Nile in northern Sudan.
It reports a plan, confirmed a year later by a defecting Libyan pilot, to bomb the Aswan High Dam.
It quotes Qaddafi as imagining Lake Nasser linked to al-Kufra, the source of the Great Manmade River.
not_established: The column does not show that the Kufra pipeline was actually planned as an attack on the dam or the Nile.
The passage does not give the date or details of the bombing plan, or who else knew of it.
The Egyptian fears and the Western intelligence view are reported, not proved.
u:aswan high dam|kufra.context: The Great Manmade River was Libya's large project to pipe underground water from the desert south to the coast. Lake Nasser is the reservoir behind the Aswan High Dam.

timeline.what: Reported plan to bomb the Aswan High Dam, per the column (date is garbled in the OCR text).
Qaddafi interview with a Cairo newspaper, about linking Lake Nasser to al-Kufra.

u:aswan high dam|kufra.open_question: Egyptian or Sudanese government records, or the pilot's debriefing, could show whether the bombing plan and the pipeline were ever treated as connected.

u:eisenhower|gulf of sidra.headline: In late June 1983, aircraft from the US carrier Eisenhower were reported operating near Libya, and Libya called this a provocation.
u:eisenhower|gulf of sidra.explanation: One news digest from 1 July 1983 links the carrier Eisenhower to American military activity off the Libyan coast. It carries a clandestine radio report that Eisenhower's planes intercepted two Libyan planes. It also carries a Libyan news agency (JANA) statement condemning US aircraft taking off and acting provocatively. The passage we have does not itself name the Gulf of Sidra or say the carrier was in it; the summary says it does, but that part of the text is cut off. The link matters because it shows how the Gulf of Sidra, off Libya's coast, became a place of repeated US–Libyan confrontation that the Tripoli government answered with public protest.
established: A clandestine radio station (Radio Free Lebanon) said on 30 June 1983 that planes from the carrier Eisenhower in the Mediterranean intercepted two Libyan planes.
JANA, the Libyan news agency, on 1 July 1983 accused the US of provocation and intimidation, citing US military aircraft taking off.
CBS, as quoted in the report, said the US Air Force was carrying out special activity opposite the Libyan shores.
not_established: The visible passage does not name the Gulf of Sidra, so the exact location of the Eisenhower's aircraft is not confirmed here.
The interception is reported by a clandestine radio station with 'further details not available'; it is not independently confirmed.
No Tripoli-specific site is mentioned.
u:eisenhower|gulf of sidra.context: The Gulf of Sidra is the waters off Libya's central coast. Libya claimed it as territorial waters, and the US held that it was international water. This dispute led to several naval and air incidents in the 1980s.

u:brega|great man-made river.headline: Brega was the site of a plant that made the large concrete pipes for the Great Man-Made River, and also its entry port.

u:and egyptian seawind exercises|tripoli.headline: A 1986 newspaper report says U.S.-Egyptian Seawind exercises flew aircraft into the Tripoli Flight Information Region so Libyan radar would see them.
u:and egyptian seawind exercises|tripoli.explanation: The Washington Post article describes a secret U.S. plan in August 1986 to make Gaddafi believe another American attack was coming. It says U.S. and Egyptian forces held exercises called "Seawind" in the region that month. According to its sources, aircraft were sent into the Tripoli Flight Information Region, the air-traffic zone around Tripoli, so they would show up on Libyan radar. This matters because it shows Tripoli's airspace being used as part of pressure on Libya, and that the airspace was watched closely. The account comes from unnamed sources and is not confirmed by any other document here.
established: The article says U.S. and Egyptian forces held exercises called Seawind in the region in August 1986.
Unnamed sources told the paper that aircraft were sent into the Tripoli Flight Information Region so they would appear on Libyan radar.

u:kufra|maatan as sarra.headline: A 1983 US imagery briefing lists both Kufra and Maatan as Sarra as southern Libyan sites where Libyan forces were building up.
u:kufra|maatan as sarra.explanation: One US photo-interpretation briefing from August 1983 names both places in a single summary of the Libya-Chad conflict. It says Libya moved some mechanized infantry to Kufra and put long-range artillery near the border at Maatan as Sarra. It also says supply activity continued at key bases in southern Libya. The link is that both were part of the same Libyan build-up, as seen by US analysts. It does not say the two places were connected to each other, and neither is in Tripoli. It matters mainly as a view of what Gaddafi's government was doing in the far south while Chad was at war.
established: The 1983 briefing reports mechanized infantry moved to Kufra.
It reports long-range artillery placed near the border at Maatan as Sarra (spelled 'Matan as Sarra' in the text).
It describes logistics activity at key bases in southern Libya and northern Chad, in support of Libyan and dissident forces.
not_established: The document does not say the two sites worked together or were under one command.
It does not describe any movement of troops or supplies between Kufra and Maatan as Sarra.
It says nothing about Tripoli.
u:kufra|maatan as sarra.context: Kufra is a large oasis in southeastern Libya. Maatan as Sarra is a remote site in the far south near the Chad border.

timeline.what: US imagery briefing reports Libyan forces consolidating in Chad and moving to bases in southern Libya, including Kufra and Maatan as Sarra.

u:ali treiki|libya's mission.headline: Ali Treiki led Libya's U.N. mission in New York until early April 1984, and U.S. officials said he used it to pass money to black activists.
u:ali treiki|libya's mission.explanation: A 1984 Washington Post article says Ali Treiki headed Libya's mission to the United Nations until early the previous month. He then became Qaddafi's foreign minister. Unnamed U.S. officials said the FBI had evidence, from intercepted communications and from watching his contacts with Americans, that he used the mission to pass money to black activists. The article does not name who received money. It also does not show any charge or finding. For Tripoli, it shows how the Libyan government's overseas missions could be used for foreign-policy aims, and how U.S. officials viewed that.
established: The article says Libya's U.N. mission was headed until early last month by Ali Treiki, who is now Qaddafi's foreign minister.
Unnamed U.S. officials said the FBI had evidence that Treiki used the mission to pass money to black activists sympathetic to Libya's aims.
The FBI inquiry grew out of surveillance of the mission that began in 1981, after reports of a possible Libyan-inspired plot against U.S. ambassador Jeane Kirkpatrick.
not_established: The officials did not name any American individuals or groups that received money.
The article does not show the evidence itself, and the sources do not say whether any charges or findings followed.
Treiki's claim or response is not given in the passage.
u:ali treiki|libya's mission.context: Libya's U.N. mission was its official diplomatic office at the United Nations in New York. Ali Treiki served as Libya's U.N. envoy and later as foreign minister.

m:mk-feb2011|dribi|event.headline: The recorded reason says the UN inquiry named al-Dribi among three Tripoli areas where about 15 people were killed on 20 February 2011.
m:mk-feb2011|dribi|event.explanation: The link ties the February 2011 crackdown in Tripoli to one neighbourhood, al-Dribi. The only support is the note's own summary of the UN Commission of Inquiry report (A/HRC/17/44). That summary says about 15 people were killed on 20 February in Fashloum, Tajoura and "al-Dibri". The link would show that the violence reached beyond Green Square into residential districts, as the atlas profile says.

The cited source is the UN Commission of Inquiry on Libya report, A/HRC/17/44.

m:mk-feb2011|dribi|event.context: Protests spread to Tripoli around 20 February 2011, and security forces used lethal force in several districts over the following days. Death counts for the week vary widely.

u:aozou|faya-largeau.headline: A 1983 U.S. briefing note lists Aozou and Faya Largeau as Libyan military sites in northern Chad, with Aozou the main air base.
u:aozou|faya-largeau.explanation: The document is a 1983 U.S. intelligence briefing note on where Libyan forces were placed in northern Chad. It names both places. It says the main Libyan ground force was at Faya Largeau. It says the main Libyan aircraft were at Aozou airfield. The note describes Aozou as the base for resupply flights and close air support for Libyan and Libyan-backed forces in northern Chad. It does not say that Aozou's aircraft flew specifically in the battle for Faya Largeau, so the link is a reasonable reading of the text, not a stated fact. For Tripoli, it shows how far Libya's military reach extended from the capital in the early 1980s.
established: Libyan forces confirmed on imagery were deployed at Faya Largeau, Ounianga Kebir, Ogoui and Aozou.
The primary Libyan ground force deployment in Chad was at Faya Largeau.
Aozou airfield was the main Libyan aircraft deployment, described as the major base for resupply flights and close air support in northern Chad.
Libyan and Libyan-backed forces were said to have recaptured Faya Largeau.
not_established: The document does not say that aircraft from Aozou flew missions against or over Faya Largeau in particular.
The passages given do not give dates or details of the recapture of Faya Largeau beyond that one statement.
The note is a briefing aid and says it should not be used for detailed analysis.
u:aozou|faya-largeau.context: Aozou is in the Aouzou Strip on the Libya–Chad border, and Faya Largeau is a major oasis town in northern Chad. Libya and Chad fought over this region in the 1980s.

timeline.what: U.S. briefing note maps Libyan forces at Faya Largeau, Ounianga Kebir, Ogoui and Aozou.
